articleTitle: 47-year-old surgeon shoots himself dead in UP’s Kanpur
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Police said Singh and his wife had an argument before the incident and that marital differences appeared to be the main reason, though the investigation is underway.
description: Police said the victim's wife heard a loud sound and rushed to the puja room at their home to find the doctor with an injury to his chest
body_raw: A 47-year-old doctor allegedly shot himself dead with his licensed revolver inside the puja room of his three-bedroom flat at Bloosom Apartment in Kanpur, in the early hours of Monday. Police said Sandeep Singh was working as a general surgeon at a government hospital in Kanpur Dehat. No suicide note has been found so far. The incident occurred around 2.30 am, but police received the information only around 6 am from the hospital, following some confusion over jurisdiction. The matter came to light when the victims wife, Kanchan, heard a loud sound from the prayer room. She rushed in and found Sandeep lying on the floor in a pool of blood with injury on chest. She rushed him to hospital and, in the meantime, informed his family members, who live in another part of the district, in the Chakeri area. Doctors declared Sandeep dead on arrival. Police said, the motive behind the drastic step is yet to be ascertained. The post-mortem report is pending. Assistant Commissioner of Police, Kanpur, Virendra Vikram, said the victims family had indicated that the incident may have followed a family dispute. He added that the preliminary inquiry also hinted at this. At the time of incident, Kanchan and their two children - a four-year-old daughter and a two-month-old son - were present at home, said senior sub-inspector, Neeraj Dwivedi. Police said the deceaseds family told them that Sandeep had separated from his first wife, who is also a doctor. The couple had a love-cum-arranged marriage but mutually separated in 2019. Over a year later, Sandeep married Kanchan, who is from Kasganj, in an arranged marriage. Sandeep has a son from his first marriage who lives with his ex-wife.

articleTitle: Create fear in miscreants: Supreme Court on crime against women
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Supreme Court Delhi Police women's safety
description: Hearing a suo motu case on recent rape crimes in Delhi-NCR, the Supreme Court asked the Delhi Police to implement 24-hour monitoring cells and enhance security in vulnerable parks and public areas.
body_raw: Underlining the need to prevent crimes against women and not just arrest the accused after an offence is committed, to ensure that the National Capital Territory remains safe even during late hours, the Supreme Court Monday asked the Delhi Police to put in place a 24-hour monitoring cell for continued surveillance in vulnerable areas. Justice J B Pardiwala, presiding over a two-judge bench, said, . create fear in the minds of all these criminals. Something goes wrong, you are doomed. You need to prevent this at any cost. What is happening today is you catch hold of the culprit. Undoubtedly, you have that skill, you have that promptness, expertise you will apprehend him, he will be arrested, put behind bars. That is not the solution. What is important is to prevent the crime and not just obey the orders. He said that these goons, these miscreants, these anti-social elements will be at high during the upcoming festivals. On September 28, the bench, also comprising Justice K Vinod Chandran - taking suo motu cognisance of incidents of alleged rape of a minor in August on a sleeper bus that travelled nearly 47 km from Greater Noida to Old Delhis Kashmere Gate, the alleged gangrape of a 17-year-old at Astha Kunj Park in South Delhi by three men posing as policemen on September 21, and an alleged gangrape and murder in Northwest Delhi earlier last month - had issued a series of directions for examining the broader institutional failures that may have led to the crimes. On Monday, the bench said there appears to be a feeling that women are not safe in the national capital, especially in vulnerable pockets. Lets try our best to ensure that these types of crimes are not committed repeatedly . there appears to be a feeling that women are not safe in the city, more particularly some vulnerable pockets of the city . So, we need to deliberate a little . the only concern is that the deficiencies, if any, should not lead to, should not facilitate the commission of a crime, said Justice Pardiwala. What is important is to prevent the crime, not what you do after the crime is committed. We have to work together. We must ensure that every young girl, every woman in the NCT of Delhi . should feel safe even at 10 oclock, 11 oclock in the night, whether she is travelling by Metro, whether she is walking on the streets, he added. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, who appeared for the Centre said, We are doing this for our daughters ., adding Mere system being there is not enough. We will have to show that its functioning and it is giving results. The court Monday also sought information on the working status of CCTV cameras installed at vulnerable locations. Referring to the incident at Astha Kunj Park, it sought the status of CCTV cameras and lights installed there and whether security personnel had been deployed. It has been said people warned you about these people criminals even in this unfortunate case, the court noted. Addressing the Delhi Police, Justice Pardiwala said, People should not run away from you. People should come forward to meet you, to talk to you and your response should be such that would repose confidence in a common man. Referring to the September 28 order, Justice Pardiwala said, We impress upon them Delhi Police to take steps as fast as possible so far as these measures which we have suggested. Our immediate concern is to prevent crimes relating to women. Dont let us down. Rise to the occasion, please. Every woman, every girl molested is our sister, our mother. So, it is a huge challenge for the police department of the NCT. Take it up as a challenge, the judge also told the police. Justice Pardiwala added, It is not just installation of CCTV cameras that is going to help you. There has to be a cell. A 24-hour cell, which keeps monitoring what is happening. The bench said it would pass a detailed order in the matter and that the authorities would be given 4 weeks to act on its directions. The top court posted the matter for hearing next on November 16.

articleTitle: Surat Police arrests ‘influencer’ for objectionable content on Mahatma Gandhi
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Bharatiya Gauraksha Manch president Dharmesh Gami of Surat filed the complaint at Umra police station after seeing the video stating that the content would hurt the sentiments of several people.
description: Bharatiya Gauraksha Manch president Dharmesh Gami of Surat filed the complaint at Umra police station after seeing the video, stating that the content would hurt the sentiments of several people.
body_raw: The Surat Cyber Crime Branch arrested a social media influencer for allegedly insulting Mahatma Gandhi in an Instagram reel she uploaded on the eve of Gandhi Jayanti on October 1. Simran Patel, 47, whose account describes her as a digital creator, has one million followers. She uploaded the video featuring a woman showing the picture of Gandhiji on the 500-rupee note in an obscene manner and placing it in a gender context with insulting and objectionable remarks. By the time the complaint was filed, she had deleted the viral video. Patel, who lives in the Adajan area of Surat, was arrested under sections of the Information Technology Act after police investigated the account following a complaint. Her husband has been identified as Amit Patel. Bharatiya Gauraksha Manch president Dharmesh Gami of Surat filed the complaint at Umra police station after seeing the video, stating that the content would hurt the sentiments of several people. Gami told the paper, Our sentiments and respect for the father of the nation, Mahatma Gandhi, were hurt by such an objectionable video. We wanted a criminal case lodged against her so that in the future, nobody dares to commit such an act. Surat police has warned against posting such objectionable content.

articleTitle: Why Harish Rawat’s defiance of AICC deals a blow to Uttarakhand Congress on poll eve
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Congress veteran and ex-Uttarakhand chief minister Harish Rawat
description: AICC leadership issues a stern warning to Rawat for his bid to continue with his statewide yatra, making it clear that “individual campaigns will not be tolerated”.
body_raw: Congress veteran and ex-Uttarakhand chief minister Harish Rawats decision to continue with his Dhanyawad evam Jansamvad Yatra despite a directive from the party high command to call it off has deepened rifts within the state party unit, with the All India Congress Committee AICC leadership warning that his independent outreach could undermine efforts to present a united front ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections. The Congress leadership issued a stern warning to Rawat Monday evening, making it clear to him that individual campaigns would not be tolerated. AICC general secretary in charge of organisation K C Venugopal, in an X post, said Met with Uttarakhand Ex-CM Harish Rawat ji, to discuss on the ongoing campaigns in the election-going state. It was made clear that our campaigns will be taken forward jointly along with all Uttarakhand leaders, solely under the Congress banner under Mallikarjun Kharge ji and LOP Rahul Gandhi jis leadership, with the singular aim of ensuring the partys victory. Venugopal also said Individual campaigns will not be tolerated by the party, and there must only be collective programmes as planned by the party organisation. The party is confident that with the energy and hard work of the entire state unit, we will emerge victorious in Uttarakhand Earlier in the day, Rawat pressed ahead with the Jaspur-Haldwani leg of the yatra, days after AICC general secretary and Uttarakhand in-charge Kumari Selja wrote to him on October 1, asking him not to proceed with the programme. The confrontation has brought into sharper focus differences within the state Congress over Rawats political role and his efforts to remain at the centre of the partys activities in Uttarakhand. In her letter to Rawat, Selja said the party had learnt that he was undertaking the yatra without discussing it with either the state Congress president Ganesh Godiyal or the Uttarakhand in-charge. She also referred to what she called his controversial statements during his recent programmes. The state elections are to be held in the next few months and the party must put up a united front. You will appreciate that any such parallel programme at this juncture will not be in the interest of the party. You may therefore not go ahead with these programmes, the letter read. Rawat, however, made clear that he had no intention of backing down. Hours before beginning Mondays leg of the yatra, he posted on social media There is no stopping now, while calling on his supporters to work to bring the Congress back to power in Uttarakhand and said the resolve was firm for the pride of Uttarakhand. Uttarakhand is due for the Assembly elections in February 2027. On Monday, Rawats yatra began at 11.30 am at Heera Garden in Jaspur in Udham Singh Nagar district en route to Haldwani. Rawat has described the exercise as a public dialogue and thanksgiving campaign, rather than a parallel political programme. A senior Uttarakhand Congress office-bearer close to Rawat said the former CM was continuing with the yatra to strengthen the party ahead of the elections. The yatra is continuing because Rawat ji wants to bring the Congress back to power in the state. Whatever he is doing is in the interest of the Congress and Uttarakhand. Local Congress workers are participating in the yatra and he is getting an overwhelming response from the public, the leader said. The Congress leadership, however, remains concerned about the political message of Rawats independent programme. An AICC leader said the party was already running programmes in the state ahead of the polls and that a separate initiative by Rawat risked reinforcing the perception that it was divided. When there are other party programmes being run ahead of the polls, any such parallel programme by Rawat sends a message to the public that the Congress is a divided house in Uttarakhand. That is not in the interest of the party, the AICC leader said. The leader added that since Rawat had announced Mondays programmes much earlier, the party was keeping a watch on his upcoming programmes and that the matter would be conveyed to the high command. The latest disagreement comes at a difficult time for Rawat within the Congress. Last month, he appeared before the Enforcement Directorate ED in connection with its money-laundering investigation into alleged irregularities in the 2016 Gram Panchayat Vikas Adhikari recruitment examination conducted by the Uttarakhand Subordinate Service Selection Commission. The EDs probe followed searches at multiple locations, including the premises of Chandan Singh Jeena, Rawats former Officer on Special Duty OSD and his current personal assistant. The agency has said it seized or froze assets worth around Rs 1.28 crore, including Rs 32 lakh in cash, around 200 grams of gold and 12 luxury watches. Rawat returned to Uttarakhand last month after spending a prolonged period in Delhi for medical reasons and subsequently led a roadshow in Dehradun. During his yatra in Haridwar last week, a vehicle in his cavalcade carried his photograph alongside the slogan Tiger is back. He is the tallest leader of the Congress in the state. Through such programmes, he is keeping himself in the leading position among the contenders for the CM face, said another party leader.

articleTitle: Former CEC S Y Quraishi: The deleted voter is not a new voter
articleFeaturedImageAlt: form 6 new voter
description: A first-time voter needs registration, using Form 6. A wrongly deleted voter needs restoration, using Form 6X, which can be created in a few hours by the Law Ministry amending the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960
body_raw: The Election Commissions latest instructions mark a U-turn in its approach to the Special Intensive Revision SIR. After an exercise in which about 13 crore names disappeared from draft electoral rolls, the Commission has directed its machinery to identify and re-enrol arbitrarily deleted eligible voters. The change is welcome - even after causing countrywide chaos. But its significance should not be concealed behind administrative language. In instructions issued on September 29 and reinforced at its October 1 meeting with Chief Electoral Officers, the Commission has ordered a special enrolment drive in 20 states and Union territories where SIR has been completed. Officials must compare pre-SIR and post-SIR rolls, identify missing voters, visit their homes and facilitate their enrolment. Political parties may assist. These instructions address two distinct problems. Both deserve attention. First, the young voters. For years, the ECI took pride in encouraging every Indian youngster who turned 18 on every January 1 to register immediately. The Union cabinets 2011 decision to make January 25 National Voters Day reflects this approach. In 2022, another important reform was introduced. Instead of a single qualifying date of January 1, it provided four January 1, April 1, July 1 and October 1. Seventeen-year-olds could even apply in advance. The message was unmistakable Nobody should unnecessarily wait to exercise the franchise after becoming eligible. What happened to that commitment in 2024? The Commission must explain how many young people becoming eligible from 2024 onwards remained unenrolled and why. It cannot now quietly announce a special drive for young voters and expect everyone to forget these questions. Generation Z is entitled to an explanation. The Commission should publish quarterly figures for applications, enrolments, rejections and pendency, identify those affected by its additional requirements, and account for any eligible young citizens who consequently missed elections. Those responsible for unlawful or unjustified administrative obstructions must be held accountable. Announcing a corrective drive is no substitute for explaining why it became necessary. Two, the restoration of deleted voters. Here, the contradiction is even more extraordinary. The Commission has instructed officials to identify people who appeared on the pre-SIR rolls but disappeared from the revised rolls and bring them back on the rolls straightaway. A dramatic surrender indeed. Yet it proposes to bring them back through Form 6. The heading of Form 6 explicitly states Application Form for New Voters. Its declaration requires the applicant to state I am applying for inclusion in Electoral Roll for the first time. How can somebody who has been voting for 20 or 30 years honestly sign such a declaration? There is an additional irony. The same form warns that making a false declaration is punishable under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, with imprisonment extending to one year, a fine, or both. An elector whose name has disappeared is effectively being told to declare that he is applying for registration for the first time. We need to examine the experience of those previously registered voters who reportedly protested against this procedure but were nevertheless forced to submit Form 6. How many complied because they were told that they had no other way of recovering their vote? Why should citizens be placed in a position where recovering their electoral registration requires them to sign a false - and hence illegal - declaration? There is a potentially serious criminal dimension for election officials, too. Under Sections 45 and 49 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, intentional instigation or assistance in committing an offence can constitute abetment. An abettor can face the same punishment as prescribed for the offence. But the larger question is institutional. The Commission is now instructing officials to identify previously registered voters and bring them back through a statutory form designed for first-time applicants. How can it reconcile these two instructions? The solution is straightforward. Introduce an appropriate restoration procedure. Ask for the previous EPIC number and electoral-roll particulars. Verify whether the citizen remains eligible, has shifted residence, is registered elsewhere or has become disqualified. Where necessary, amend the statutory forms through the prescribed legal procedure. I would suggest introducing a new form, say 6X. We must save citizens from expensive and cumbersome litigation when the electoral administration possesses the records needed to examine their claims. A first-time voter needs registration, using Form 6. A wrongly deleted voter needs restoration, using Form 6X, which can be created in a few hours by the Law Ministry amending the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. The Commission has finally recognised the practical necessity of identifying both categories. It must now provide legally appropriate procedures for dealing with them, publish the results and explain the administrative failures that made this corrective exercise necessary. Quraishi is former chief election commissioner of India and the author of An Undocumented Wonder The Making of the Great Indian Election

articleTitle: UWA Chennai campus gets final UGC approval, classes to begin by October-end
articleFeaturedImageAlt: university western australia chennai
description: UWA's first Indian campus officially opened on September 18, 2026, in Andheri East. It began teaching its first cohort in September, with programmes spanning computer science, data science, artificial intelligence and more.
body_raw: The University of Western Australia UWA has received final approval from the University Grants Commission UGC to operate its international branch campus in Chennai. The campus will begin orientation on October 5, with classes scheduled to start on October 19. The 70,000-square-foot campus is located on the seventh floor of One National Park on Velachery Main Road in Chennai. UWA Chennai will offer undergraduate programmes in business management, computer science, data science and advanced computer science with artificial intelligence. Its postgraduate offerings will include a Master of Information Technology and Master of Business Administration MBA. Read IIT Madras begins applications for online executive courses Course fee, schedule and more The Chennai campus is the second UWA campus to begin operations in India. The university opened its Mumbai campus in September 2026. UWA has said it plans to invest about AUD 80 million in its wholly owned campuses in India. The Chennai campus will initially focus on programmes in data science, artificial intelligence, information technology and business. Students will begin with an orientation programme before regular classes start later this month. The opening comes as more foreign universities begin operating branch campuses in India under the UGCs regulatory framework for foreign higher educational institutions. Several such campuses have started teaching or welcomed their first students since the beginning of 2026. Also Read IIT Guwahati taught me more than engineering Coffin dances, Maggi and an events head title Which other foreign universities in India have opened in 2026? Among the numerous that have announced a campus in India, over the past two years, several have begun their intake processes and operating their classrooms this year. The University of New South Wales UNSW opened its Bengaluru campus in August 2026 and welcomed its first students that month. The campus initially offers undergraduate degrees in business, computer science and data science, along with a postgraduate degree in cyber security. Birkbeck, University of London began operations at its Bengaluru campus in 2026. The university received UGC approval to begin teaching from its Whitefield campus and opened it to students for the 2026-27 academic year. Its initial programmes include undergraduate degrees in business management, business analytics and international business, and postgraduate programmes in international business management and business analytics. Also Read IIT Madras, BITS Pilani join hands to promote academic, research opportunities The University of Bristol opened its Mumbai Enterprise Campus on September 10, 2026, and welcomed its inaugural cohort. Located at Cignus Powai, the campus is the universitys first international campus and has an initial focus on areas including data science and finance. The expansion is part of a broader increase in foreign university campuses in India. In an August 2026 response to Parliament, the Education Ministry said UGC had issued 16 Letters of Intent to foreign higher education institutions from Australia, Italy, the UK and the US. At that point, the ministry said the University of Southampton and UNSW had already established campuses in Gurugram and Bengaluru respectively, while four institutions in Mumbai - York, Bristol, Aberdeen and Illinois Institute of Technology - had received approval to start operations. Additionally, the University of York welcomed its first students to its Mumbai campus in September 2026. The Powai-based campus began its inaugural academic year with undergraduate and postgraduate programmes covering computer science with artificial intelligence and cyber security, business and the creative industries. UWAs first Indian campus officially opened on September 18, 2026, in Andheri East. It began teaching its first cohort in September, with programmes spanning computer science, data science, artificial intelligence, cyber security, information technology, business management and an MBA. Chennai is the second UWA campus to follow.

articleTitle: Pune Crime Files | Attacks on gay dating app users rise; reported cases ‘tip of iceberg’
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Pune gay dating app crimes
description: A 19-year-old man and two others attacked a man having sex with another man he met through the Grindr app.
body_raw: Over the last couple of years, there have been several attacks in Pune on men looking for same-sex relationships through apps used by LGBTQIA people, the police and activists said. On September 29, three youngsters allegedly attacked a 22-year-old man having sex with another man he met through the Grindr app. The victim, who hails from Bhosari, and his gay date were attacked by the assailants at a dilapidated building near the Mental Asylum in the Yerwada area around 6 pm, according to the FIR. The other man allegedly ran away to escape from the assailants. The assailants also forcibly transferred Rs 20,000 using the victims PhonePe account, threatened to kill him, and tried to have sex with him, according to the FIR. When he resisted, the assailants dropped him at Vishrantwadi Chowk on a two-wheeler and left, it added. The man approached the police two days later after receiving counselling from YUTAK Trust, which works among LGBTQIA people. Assistant Police Inspector Chandrakant Lohkare said, We probed the bank account into which the accused had forcibly transferred the victims money. This led to the arrest of 19-year-old Devendra alias Karan on the same day. A court remanded him to police custody until October 7 for further investigation. Attempts are underway to arrest the remaining two accused. The police booked the three men on charges including voluntarily causing hurt, robbery, and criminal intimidation. Minor boy lures 25-year-old man In a previous incident, a minor boy lured a 25-year-old man from Warje Malwadi through a gay dating app and called him for a meeting near a shopping mall in Karve Nagar on the night of April 29. The minor then took the man for a long drive. They reached a secluded spot, where the minors aides allegedly attacked the man, stoned his face, snatched his cell phone, and transferred Rs 8,600 from his account. Within an hour after he complained, the police apprehended the minor accused on May 8. His three aides were arrested later. History-sheeter among 5 arrested Earlier this year, the police arrested a gang of five who allegedly robbed three users of a gay dating app between December 28, 2025, and January 11, 2026. According to an FIR registered in these cases, a 27-year-old man received a message on a gay dating app from an ID named ImTop, used by a person identifying himself as Rahil. They decided to meet in Kondhwa around 9 pm on January 11 for a hook-up. But when the man reached the spot, Rahil and his friends allegedly took the victim to an isolated spot and robbed him of his gold ornaments. The police arrested Rahil and four others, including a history-sheeter charged under the stringent Maharashtra Control of Organised Crimes Act MCOCA in the past. The police said the gang members had similarly robbed at least two more men. They targeted men looking for same-sex dating, believing that victims would not file police complaints. Extortion over nude videos In July 2025, when a 22-year-old man went to meet another man he met through a gay dating app, two others forced him to take his clothes off and recorded his videos in a car. Threatening to publicise the videos, they allegedly forced the victim into making online transfers of Rs 8,000. A 24-year-old man was allegedly blackmailed into paying Rs 1.09 lakh between August 2024 and January 2025 by people who befriended him on a gay dating app. The FIR in the case was lodged after YUTAK Trust members met top Pune police officials. Later, in April 2025, the police arrested a gang of four youngsters for allegedly robbing several men from Pune and Pimpri-Chinchwad after luring them through a gay dating app. Many are not willing to approach police LGBTQIA rights activist Bindumadhav Khire said the cases registered represented the tip of the iceberg. Also, gay victims are not targeted only in urban centres, but also in rural parts, for easy money. We have received calls on our helpline from several rural victims. Many are not willing to approach the police due to social pressures, said Khire. Anil Ukarande of Yutak Trust said the police should be prompt in registering the crimes against the LGBTQIA community. These crimes will increase if they go unreported. Efforts like posting reels on such crimes on official social media handles of police establishments should be made to raise public awareness. It will encourage the victims to ignore social taboo and lodge police complaints, he said.

articleTitle: To fight cancer better, count it
articleFeaturedImageAlt: cancer
description: Notification can provide timely information on diagnosed cases, while registries can validate, enrich and analyse it to understand incidence, patterns and trends
body_raw: By Jyotsna Govil A long-standing demand to make cancer a notifiable disease across the country may finally be within reach. If implemented well, this could mark a turning point and change how India counts, plans for and responds to cancer. In its recent order, the Supreme Court asked the 19 states and Union territories where cancer has not yet been declared a notifiable disease to consider doing so. It also asked whether mandatory guidelines from the Centre are needed to bring uniformity. The states should respect the Courts order in its full sense and begin the process without further delay. Experience from states where notification is already in place can provide useful lessons. But differences in reporting and use of information make it difficult to build a comparable national picture. India needs common national guidelines for cancer notification. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare should establish a standard minimum dataset, common definitions and timelines, uniform safeguards and compliance rules. Healthcare providers and laboratories will need training, technical assistance and a practical transition period. The Indian Cancer Society, which completes 75 years in 2026, has long advocated stronger cancer surveillance because better data is the foundation of better cancer care. Notification can provide timely information on diagnosed cases, while registries can validate, enrich and analyse it to understand incidence, patterns and trends. Data is not merely about knowing how many people have cancer. It is about knowing where the disease is, who is affected and where the health system needs to respond. Linked with registry and health-system data, notification can reveal geographic patterns, high-risk populations, delays and dropouts, and show where additional staff, diagnostic capacity or financial support are needed. The implications for health planning are considerable. How does a government decide how many hospitals a district needs, whether facilities are adequate, how many professionals are required or where specialised cancer services should be developed? Such decisions should be based on disease burden and population need. Cancer information must flow from facilities at every level, including smaller hospitals and diagnostic centres, into a system that can bring the data together. States have different levels of technical capacity and some will need the Centres support through training, standardised protocols and digital infrastructure. Reporting must be simple, practical and interoperable with hospital, laboratory and cancer registry systems, including where connectivity is limited. A common digital backbone could provide shared standards while integrating existing systems. CoWIN demonstrated Indias ability to operate digital public-health infrastructure at national scale. Cancer notification requires a different architecture, especially for longitudinal information, interoperability and privacy, but deserves the same ambition. Reliable data can also improve planning for medicines, diagnostics, radiotherapy and emerging therapies by helping governments, healthcare providers and the pharma industry anticipate demand and improve availability. Data protection, however, must be non-negotiable. Cancer information is deeply personal. Any national system must safeguard access, privacy, cybersecurity and permitted uses of information, with clear rules on identifiable data and anonymisation. Better notification may initially make Indias cancer numbers appear higher. This should not be interpreted as a sudden increase in prevalence. More comprehensive reporting will identify cases previously outside formal records an initial rise may simply mean we are seeing the problem more clearly. Over time, consistent data can identify trends and gaps in care, strengthen research, guide resources and help policymakers assess whether interventions are improving outcomes. Most importantly, it can move cancer planning from estimates towards evidence. The SC has opened the door. States should move promptly, while the Centre provides the standards, technical support, digital infrastructure and safeguards needed to make notification work consistently. Ultimately, this is about making every cancer diagnosis count. A diagnosis should not remain confined to an individual hospital record when, with appropriate privacy protection, it can help show where cancer occurs, where care is falling short and where resources are most urgently needed. We should use this moment not merely to count cancer cases, but to build the knowledge India needs to fight cancer more intelligently, more equitably and more effectively. The writer is chairperson, Indian Cancer Society, Delhi Branch

articleTitle: Inside Sourav Joshi’s luxury bungalow: Multi-crore car collection, private lift, 3 kitchens
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Inside 27y old 40M Youtuber Sourav Joshi's bungalow
description: One of India's biggest YouTuber, Sourav Joshi showed off his luxury Haldwani bungalow as filmmaker-choreographer Farah Khan visited him. When Farah asked if he wants to do films one day, Sourav said YouTube pays him much better.
body_raw: Sourav Joshi is considered as one of the biggest vloggers in India, with around 42 million subscribers on YouTube. However, not many are aware that he owns a lavish bungalow in Haldwani, Uttarakhand. In her latest vlog, filmmaker-choreographer Farah Khan visited his house, with her cook Dilip. The 27-year-old Youtuber Sourav and his wife Avantika Joshi gave a tour of their luxury bungalow. In the beginning of the vlog, as soon as Farah and Dilip reached Souravs house, the filmmaker pointed out at a plot on the other side of the road, revealing the YouTuber is constructing another bungalow there. He also pointed out that the house will be designed in such a way that it has a lot of greenery, so the view from their present house is pleasant. As soon as they entered his house, Sourav Joshi introduced Farah Khan to his joint family, that lives together there. The contemporary living area had a posh neutral color palette, with a double-height ceiling. The main highlight was a wooden display cabinet embedded in one side of the wall, which had artifacts and decorative pieces kept on every shelf. The couch had a subtle off-white tone, with indoor plants of various heights placed around. After chatting in the drawing room, the hosts gave a tour of their basement, which included a private gym space and parking area. Sourav Joshi, who loves collecting cars, owns a Ferrari, Thar, Mercedes Benz G-Class G-Wagon, and many other cars. The YouTuber also bought a mustard-black coloured limited Trophy edition Defender roughly priced at Rs 1.6 crore on road recently. ALSO READ Farah Khan says hosting Lock Upp is more complex than Bigg Boss Have to be careful As soon as they stepped upstairs, there was a beautiful temple room. The home temple was decorated with hanging marigold flowers on the walls. The wooden paneling featured a huge Om symbol, with idols placed on an elevated platform. My mother likes doing bhajan, keertan, so everyone sits here to do it, Sourav said. Then, the hallway of Sourav Joshis luxury bungalow led to a white-finish open kitchen. The huge windows in the modern layout allowed sunlight, making the area brighter. Along with the minimalist cabinets and countertops, there was also space for a breakfast bar setup with casual dining. When they walked inside, there was a second kitchen, where the family actually cooks their food. You have made such a Sooraj Barjatya coded, Maine Pyaar Kiya type of a house, Farah Khan complimented. The entire ground floor consisted of around 3-4 rooms, for his parents, grandparents, uncle-aunt, and guest rooms. The newlyweds Sourav and Avantika, who got married last year in November, live on the first floor. The model had a private lift installed, to travel to the upper floor, which is built for all the children in the family Souravs real brothers and cousins. The first floor also has its own kitchen for late-night cravings, a gaming room, and many more exciting bits. Their balcony shows a hilltop view of Nainital and Bhimtal. Your house is very beautiful. I am also going to turn my house white and neutral after this. Sourav then flaunted his smart home, to control light, fans, and other electronics. Avantika and Sourav also gave a tour of their walk-in closet, which Farah called inspired by Kardashian sisters. There were many other spaces on the level, including, a studio with a sunroof and a huge terrace. Towards the end of the vlog, the vloggers mother made the popular Kumaoni thali for Farah Khan and Dilip.

articleTitle: How long does it take to fix a pothole? A Delhi teen is tracking it
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Parth Anand, 15, started building the platform in March this year.
description: The platform uses AI to identify the agency responsible for a road, file complaints and publicly track whether potholes are repaired.
body_raw: In October 2025, Parth Anands parents were driving to Delhis Karol Bagh to buy clothes for his grandparents anniversary when their motorcycle hit a pothole. They fell off the vehicle and suffered fractures. It took them about three months to recover. For Anand, the accident was difficult to dismiss as just another bad-road mishap. He noticed that the pothole appeared to have been there for some time. He reported the pothole through the Municipal Corporation of Delhis MCD system. But responses, he found, could take three to four months. What struck me was that more and more people were complaining, but the authorities were still not responding. That frustration kept growing, he said. That experience eventually became the starting point for Project Sadak. In March this year, the 15-year-old began building a platform that would do more than collect pothole complaints. It would identify the agency responsible, send the complaint to it and, crucially, leave a public trail of what happened next. Building the platform Anand built the first platform himself, working on it alongside school - he studies at St Francis de Sales School in Janakpuri - during a roughly three-hour window between tuition and his commute home. He later used AI to develop the platform further. As of September, the platform had recorded 1,815 reports across India, including more than 220 from Delhi. Bengaluru accounts for more than 1,500, while other reports have come from Rajasthan, Uttarakhand and Kerala. More than 20 repairs have been documented through the platform. In Vikaspuri, two potholes reported through Sadak in April were fixed in about five days, Anand said. In Bengaluru, a complaint filed in June was followed by a repair within two days. Anand said his analysis of pothole complaints in the city found that repairs typically take three to four months. The number of reports also rose during the monsoon, increasing by 25 in cities such as Bengaluru and Delhi, he added. How does it work? A resident first uploads a photograph and location of the damaged road. The report then goes through an AI-assisted verification process to identify whether the image actually shows a pothole and to detect duplicate reports. The system also asks the person reporting the pothole to classify the nature of severity. Anand said this determines how the platform follows up with authorities. Once a report is verified, an AI agent identifies the authority responsible for that particular road and files a complaint with it. Depending on the road, this could mean agencies such as the MCD or National Highways Authority of India NHAI. The AI agent also follows up through email. Each report, Anand said, is photographed, geotagged and timestamped, and its status remains publicly visible. What makes it different is that existing channels like MCD 311 PWD helplines take complaints, but citizens rarely see what happens next - and theres no public record of how long the fixes take. Sadaks focus is primarily on public tracking, said Anand. Where AI came in Initially, Anand built the platform using his own coding knowledge. As the project grew more complex, he began using AI to further develop and scale it. The basic reporting form was easy to build myself. It got complex once real reports started coming in. One of the problems was duplicate reporting. Many people report the same pothole, so the system has to tell if two reports are the same spot using GPS and photos, he said. Alongside the project, Anand said he is working on AI research in mechanistic interpretability with Prof Manolis Kelliss lab, at MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory CSAIL, and is an Emergent Ventures fellow. The project also received a grant from the Lift Off Grant, an independent microgrant programme, which was used to meet the development costs of the project. On future plans, Anand said he had discussions with another country about adapting the platform to meet its national reporting requirements, and was in talks with an automotive technology company to deploy instant pothole-fixing machines, which could raise awareness about Project Sadak and the need for faster repairs. But the larger problem Anand wants to tackle is simpler than the technology behind Sadak getting people to stop treating potholes as an unavoidable part of city life. The issue of potholes is not new. Its very basic. But everybody suffers from it. They see it and ignore it, he said.

articleTitle: Kainchi Dham drowns in tourists after Hanuman Ansh release, district may act to ease pressure
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Kainchi Dham is located in the Kumaon hills (Express)
description: ‘We usually expect about 25,000 people visiting the shrine every day, but the long weekend saw a crowd of more than 35,000 every day,’ the DM told Express.
body_raw: For kilometres, cars crawled through the Kumaon hills towards Kainchi Dham over the long weekend, bumper-to-bumper on the mountain road. Pilgrims got out and walked along the roadside and families waited for hours, while vehicles heading towards Mukteshwar were caught in the same gridlock as those arriving for darshan. Videos circulating online over the weekend showed long lines of cars, buses and two-wheelers around Bhimtal, Bhowali and Kainchi, with reports of journeys that ordinarily take a few hours stretching much longer. The congestion has prompted the Nainital administration to consider opening an alternative route to ease pressure on Kainchi Dham. Speaking to The Indian Express, Nainital District Magistrate Lalit Mohan said that the administration is considering a new standard operating procedure under which an existing bypass connecting the Kainchi area towards Almora and Ranikhet could be opened to divert traffic as a solution to the crowd. The district administration will meet temple authorities, police and other stakeholders on Tuesday to finalise crowd-control measures, he said. We usually expect about 25,000 people visiting the shrine every day, but this weekend, since October 2, we have seen a crowd of more than 35,000 every day. Both the pilgrims and the locals use the same road to Kainchi, which also goes up to Mukteshwar, causing a traffic jam for hours, Lalit Mohan said. He said traffic had been cleared from the Mukteshwar side on Sunday. What explains the surge? Mohan attributed the latest surge to two factors the end of the monsoon, when travellers who had avoided the hills because of rain and landslides return, and the release of Hanuman Ansh, the film based on the life and teachings of Neem Karoli Baba. When The Indian Express reported on Kainchi Dham last month, Hanuman Ansh, made on a reported budget of Rs 2 crore, had grossed around Rs 300 crore worldwide. Its success has introduced Neem Karoli Baba, who died in 1973, to a younger audience far removed from the generation that knew him during his lifetime. It is learnt that 24.34 lakh people visited Kainchi Dham in the first six months of 2026, compared with around eight lakh visitors in the entire previous year. The surge has even prompted Hanuman Ansh director Vishal Chaturvedi to urge devotees to check the situation before travelling to Kainchi Dham. There is a huge crowd at Kainchi Dham at the moment. we should all check the situation there before going, he said, adding that visitors should avoid a situation where children and women in your family are suffocating in the crowd or are stuck in a traffic jam. He also suggested that devotees consider other sites associated with Neem Karoli Baba if Kainchi remains overcrowded. The hills are choked The proposed diversion comes as Uttarakhand is already building an 18.15-km Kainchi Dham bypass from Sanatorium to Ranighat. Eight kilometres were completed and hot-mixed earlier this year, and hill-cutting on another 10.15 km is done too. A motor bridge is also being built to connect the bypass with the Bhowali-Almora highway. The state has separately built the Bhowali bypass and a 30-metre double-lane bridge over the Shipra River to ease congestion in the area. The states Public Works Department has also identified the Talla Ramgarh-Ratighat road as an alternative route connecting Kainchi with Ramgarh, Mukteshwar, Lohaghat and Champawat, saying its strengthening could significantly reduce traffic pressure. A state planning document notes that Uttarakhand receives tourists equivalent to roughly 300 per cent of its resident population, compared with 185 per cent in Himachal Pradesh, and warns that hill destinations once known for walking and trekking are increasingly being choked by vehicles. The National Green Tribunal has recently taken on record a scientific carrying-capacity study covering major pilgrimage sites including Kedarnath, Hemkund Sahib, Gangotri and Yamunotri, reflecting a wider debate over the limits of tourism and pilgrimage in the fragile Himalayas. Kainchi has already had its own carrying-capacity study. A Tourism Department study conducted in 2025 found that 64 per cent of devotees came only for darshan and returned the same day, while 82.4 per cent were from outside Uttarakhand. Nearly two-thirds were aged between 15 and 30. Parking was the biggest infrastructure complaint, with 74 per cent of respondents dissatisfied with parking facilities. At the temple, authorities said the situation remained manageable. Pradeep Bhatt, who works in Kainchi Dhams accounts section, said authorities have deployed additional police personnel inside and outside the temple. The crowd has swelled due to the long weekend. Police are taking extra precautions. The police force is now being placed inside and outside the temple too. So far it has been managed all right, he said. By Monday, the immediate crisis had eased. Dheeraj Tiwari, 27, who runs his familys business beside the temple entrance, said the worst congestion lasted a day or two. The administration has now cleared everything out. Today everything looks normal. It was the long weekend that created a lot of flow of pilgrims, he said. For residents, however, the problem is measured differently. Mani Bharadwaj, who formerly worked at Hotel Monal, about 500 metres from the shrine, and lives in Bhowali, said the disruption extended beyond tourists. Today things seem to have gone back to normal, but over the weekend the locals faced a lot of problems. When thousands of vehicles are stuck on the same road, it affects everyone-people going to work, bringing supplies, travelling for medical needs or simply trying to get home. Locals have no separate road. The same infrastructure has to serve pilgrims and local residents. Every time there is a huge rush, locals bear the disruption. There needs to be a permanent solution rather than waiting for every long weekend and then putting more police on the roads, he said.

articleTitle: 7-month pregnant sarpanch faces no-trust motion, Chhattisgarh High Court steps in
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Chhattisgarh High Court sarpanch pregnant no-confidence motion
description: Referring to Supreme Court observations recognising the right to health as part of the right to life and emphasising maternity protection, the court noted that removal of elected women representatives should not be treated casually.
body_raw: A seven-month pregnant village sarpanch has received temporary relief in a no-confidence motion after the Chhattisgarh High Court deferred the proceedings, saying elected panchas ward members have a statutory and democratic right to seek her removal, but authorities must also ensure she gets a fair opportunity to respond without compromising her health or that of her unborn child. Justice Amitendra Kishore Prasad was hearing a petition filed by one Manisha Raj Chouhan, the elected sarpanch of Siriyagarh gram panchayat in Sakti district, challenging a September 21 notice issued for a meeting to consider a no-confidence motion against her. The meeting was scheduled for noon on October 1 at the panchayat building. The right to health has been recognised as an integral facet of the right to life guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India. The authorities are required to balance both aspects, namely, the statutory right of the Panchas to seek consideration of a no-confidence motion and the right of the petitioner to receive a fair and reasonable opportunity to participate in the proceedings without compromising her health or the health of her unborn child, the court said on October 1. The proceedings began after nine panchas submitted an application on September 17, saying they had lost confidence in Chouhan and seeking her removal. She received the notice on September 24 and challenged the process, saying supporting material had not been supplied to her and that she had not received seven clear days to prepare for the meeting. Financial allegations According to the states submissions recorded in the order, the panchas had filed affidavits alleging that Chouhan had misappropriated Rs 10 lakh, Rs 75,564, Rs 25,750 and Rs 1,91,600, and that the related works had not been completed. The state said the prescribed authority had considered the allegations and, after verification, found sufficient grounds to initiate the no-confidence proceedings. Chouhan argued that the prescribed authority had called for records from the chief executive officer of the panchayat body but issued the notice without waiting for the report. She also said documents relating to the allegations had not been provided to her. The high court said simply calling for records and issuing the notice before receiving them would not automatically invalidate the proceedings. The question was whether any mandatory legal requirement had been violated or whether the procedure had caused substantial prejudice to Chouhan. However, the court found significance in her complaint that the material relied upon for the no-confidence motion had not been supplied. The principles of fairness and natural justice require that the affected elected representative should have reasonable knowledge of the material relied upon against her, the court said, adding that this was necessary for her to effectively participate in the proceedings. Notice period also questioned The court also considered Chouhans objection to the notice period. The notice was dated September 21 but received by her on September 24. The meeting was fixed for October 1 at noon. The court noted that she, therefore, had seven calendar days from actual receipt of the notice to the scheduled meeting. It said the question of whether the legal requirement of seven days notice had been complied with had to be examined with reference to the date of service or receipt, particularly since Chouhan claimed that she had not received seven clear days to prepare for the proceedings. The court did not hold that the notice was legally defective. It directed the prescribed authority to consider Chouhans objection. Pregnancy a key consideration The high court then considered Chouhans medical condition. She had stated that she was around seven months pregnant and placed her Matru Avam Bal Suraksha Card on record. The court noted that the respondents had not specifically disputed her pregnancy. Referring to Supreme Court observations recognising the right to health as part of the right to life and emphasising maternity protection, maternal health and dignity, the court also noted observations that removal of elected women representatives, particularly in rural areas, should not be treated casually and that fairness, natural justice and democratic functioning must be respected. At the same time, the court made it clear that pregnancy did not automatically stop the no-confidence process. The right of the elected Panchas to move a no-confidence motion is also a statutory and democratic right, it said, adding that the court could not bar such proceedings just because the elected sarpanch was facing inconvenience. Chouhan was directed to submit a fresh detailed application before the prescribed authority, Dabhara, raising her objections regarding the notice period, non-supply of supporting material and her medical condition, along with relevant documents. The authority was directed to consider the application objectively and in accordance with law, while taking into account her medical condition and the legal rights of the panchas. If necessary, it could defer the proceedings and fix an appropriate future date. It was also directed to provide Chouhan the material on which the proposed motion was based, subject to the material being part of the record and legally disclosable.

articleTitle: The migrant in Germany, caught between nativist politics and an open policy
articleFeaturedImageAlt: afd, germany
description: While the election results may not erode Germany’s broader appeal, and a migration architecture that remains comparatively open as Anglophone destinations tighten policies, perceptions are a two-way street. Hard-right rhetoric may convince skilled Indians to view Germany as a temporary corridor to onward migration
body_raw: By Shairee Malhotra Elections in the East German states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania gave the far-right Alternative fur Deutschland AfD two striking victories, marking the German far rights first landslide since the Third Reichs fall in 1945. The elections also increased the partys vote share in Berlin. Chancellor Friedrich Merzs Christian Democrats suffered a historic defeat in all three elections. From failing to enter the Bundestag in 2013, the nativist, anti-immigrant AfD rose to second place in the 2025 federal elections, becoming Germanys largest opposition party. It has exploited grievances over economic stagnation, pairing broader discontent with demands for severe restrictions on immigration. This has profound consequences for Germany, the EU, and India. In 2022, India and Germany signed a Migration and Mobility Partnership Agreement MMPA to facilitate easier two-way mobility for students and professionals. As Germany grapples with demographic challenges of ageing populations, mass retirements and declining birth rates, the MMPA provides up to 3,000 annual job seeker visas for qualified Indian professionals. However, while Germany invests in creating structural legal pathways to address its acute labour shortages, its electoral politics portrays migration as a threat. With Indian nationals tripling from 86,000 in 2015 to 280,000 in 2025, the German Institute for International and Security Affairs describes India as the most important country of origin for labour and education migration. Around 1,38,000 Indians work in skilled occupations including STEM fields, IT, healthcare - sectors central to the German economy, but struggling with the largest worker deficits. A Bertelsmann Foundation study estimates that Germany would need 400,000 fresh immigrants annually to address worker shortages, likely to number 1.3 million by 2030. The AfDs proposed incentives to bring back Germans living abroad and baby bonuses can hardly bridge such gaps. But with the far-right boom, skilled Indians considering a future overseas may also rethink Germanys allure. As migration rules are determined at the federal level, the far-rights rise may not lead to a direct abrogation of German migration laws or agreements. Yet, there is already sound evidence of an increasingly hardening political atmosphere on migration. In 2025, Merzs CDU sought to restrict migration through a proposed parliamentary law supported by the AfD. Thus, even as they try to keep the AfD out of office by upholding the firewall, the latters influence is changing how mainstream parties approach migration. States control aspects of public services, policing, and education, where far-right ideology may create an uneasy climate. Hate crimes doubled in Germany from 2019 to 2023. The AfDs rhetoric explicitly differentiates between irregular migration that burdens domestic welfare systems and skilled legal migration that contributes to German society. Yet, rather than migration status, external traits such as skin colour shape day-to-day encounters and prejudices. While the election results may not erode Germanys broader appeal, and a migration architecture that remains comparatively open as anglophone destinations tighten policies, perceptions are a two-way street. Hard-right rhetoric may convince skilled Indians to view Germany as a temporary corridor to onward migration. As Indo-German relations expand across the bilateral spectrum, the mobility of skilled professionals acts as a bridge, also linking both countries research and innovation ecosystems, particularly in domains such as digitalisation and AI. How policymakers reconcile political and economic realities will determine Germanys fate as Europes industrial powerhouse and its attractiveness as a migratory destination. The writer is deputy director, Strategic Studies Programme, ORF

articleTitle: 10,107 women candidates clear JEE Advanced, highest in 6 years
articleFeaturedImageAlt: women in IIT
description: While the qualification rates for most categories improved, the figures for general and OBC candidates dropped.
body_raw: For the first time in six years, the number of women candidates qualifying the JEE Advanced crossed the 10,000 mark in 2026, shows the Joint Implementation Committee JIC report by IIT Roorkee, which conducted the JEE Advanced this year. According to the JIC report, a total of 43,112 female candidates registered for JEE Advanced. Of these, 40,562 appeared in both papers and 10,107 qualified. The success rate among registered women candidates rose from 21.7 in 2025 to 23.4 this year. One in four registered women candidates qualified this year, compared with roughly one in five last year. The top female candidate scored 280 marks mathematics 101, physics 86, chemistry 93, securing All India Rank 77. Among the 3,814 female students who got admission, 37 secured seats through the gender-neutral pool, the report said. Read IITs, IIMs see more women joining than ever as placements and salary packages rise The qualification rate for Scheduled Caste SC and Scheduled Tribe ST candidates also saw a sharp jump of 9.8 and 8.1 percentage points, respectively, from last year. In 2026, a total of 15,856 SC candidates and 6,379 ST candidates qualified in JEE Advanced, whereas last year it was 12,499 and 5,008, respectively. The number of Economically Weaker Section EWS candidates qualifying the entrance exam also went up from 6,291 to 6,377. The report also shows a decline in the number of general category candidates qualifying for the entrance exam this year. Last year, a total of 16,154 students from the general category qualified the exam. The number dropped to 15,883 this year, with the qualification rate declining from 43 to 39.8. articleTitle: Mere presence at protest no proof of crime: Rajasthan High Court shields 23 agitators
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Protest Rajasthan High Court Unlawful Assembly Crime dissent Constitution Legal News
description: The high court was hearing a petition by 23 residents of Hanumangarh district seeking protection from coercive action in a criminal case arising from their alleged involvement in a large public demonstration.
body_raw: Being part of a protest does not make a person criminally liable for everything that happens in the crowd, the Rajasthan High Court has said, noting that mere presence at a large demonstration cannot by itself establish individual criminality. The court said investigators must distinguish between a persons presence at a gathering and specific acts attributed to them, while balancing the right to dissent with the states duty to maintain public order. Justice Farjand Ali was hearing a petition filed by 23 people from Hanumangarh district in connection with a criminal case arising from a public protest and issued notice to the state and police directing that no coercive steps be taken against the petitioners in the meantime. The right to voice dissent, to assemble peacefully and to espouse a cause, subject of course to the reasonable restrictions permissible in law, constitutes an essential facet of the constitutional scheme governing a democratic polity. A protest, by itself, cannot be equated with criminality merely because the expression of dissent causes inconvenience or displeasure to the authorities, the court said on September 28. It added that at the same time, the constitutional protection available to peaceful expression cannot be permitted to become a shield for acts which are, independently and specifically, alleged to constitute cognisable offences. The distinction between the two assumes significance while considering the entitlement of an individual to protection during the pendency of investigation, it said. Mere presence not participation The case arose from allegations linked to a public protest in which a large number of people had assembled. Against this backdrop, the court considered whether every person present at such a gathering could be subjected to the same degree of criminal culpability without specific attribution of individual acts. The petition was filed by 23 residents of Hanumangarh district. The petitioners were represented by Senior Advocate Vineet Jain and advocate Kunal Upadhyay, with Additional Advocate General Deepak Choudhary and public prosecutor Narendra Gehlot appearing for the state. Making it clear that it was not deciding whether the allegations in the criminal case were true or whether any of the petitioners were ultimately guilty, the high court examined whether the material placed before it, at this stage, justified subjecting the petitioners to coercive action just because of their alleged association with or presence in the larger protest assembly. The court acknowledged that the allegations included acts allegedly committed by certain members of the gathering. If those allegations were ultimately established against the persons responsible, the court said, they could attract legal consequences. But those allegations could not automatically be extended to everyone who was present at the protest. Mere presence at the place of demonstration, without more, cannot ipso facto be treated as proof of participation in each and every overt act allegedly committed during the course of such assembly, Justice Ali said. The court said this distinction assumes considerable significance where a protest involves a very large number of people. Simply being part of a gathering and actually participating in a particular alleged act are not necessarily the same thing. Criminal liability must be linked The court said that in cases concerning public protests, particularly large gatherings, the investigating agency would have to undertake the exercise of separating individual culpability from general allegations relating to the assembly. Criminal liability is individual in character, the court observed. Ordinarily, it said, criminal liability cannot be fastened on a person merely by association with a gathering unless the ingredients of the particular offence are otherwise attracted against that person. The observation does not mean that people participating in protests are immune from criminal proceedings. Justice Ali recognised the states legitimate authority to regulate public protest and assemblies in the interest of public order. The court also noted that the right to voice dissent, assemble peacefully and espouse a cause is subject to reasonable restrictions permissible in law. It said it was not required at this stage to return a finding either with regard to their culpability or the truthfulness of the allegations. The court also said the issue was not merely a dispute between private parties. It concerned the manner in which citizens right to participate in democratic expression and the power of the state to maintain public order operate within their respective constitutional fields. Finding that the matter warranted examination before any precipitative or coercive action was permitted against the petitioners, the high court decided to intervene without expressing any opinion on the merits of the allegations or the defence of the petitioners. It issued notice and directed that the matter be listed after four weeks. In the meantime, the court ordered that no coercive steps shall be taken against the petitioners.

articleTitle: ‘Dead insect’ in sealed Rs 50 fruit drink bottle, Bombay woman wins Rs 1.25 lakh
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Bottle Orange fruit beverage Maharashtra Consumer Dispute Redressal Commission
description: The Maharashtra state consumer commission rejected the beverage company’s technical objections and upheld Rs 1.25 lakh compensation over a dead insect found in a sealed bottle.
body_raw: The Maharashtra State Consumer Dispute Redressal Commission recently upheld a district commissions order that held a beverage company liable for deficiency in service and confirmed a payout of Rs 1.25 lakh to a woman who had filed the consumer complaint in 2012 after she found a dead insect inside a sealed beverage bottle. While dismissing the appeal, Presiding Member Nisha Amol Chavhan and Member Vijay Premchandani said that the beverage companys attempts to defeat a legitimate consumer grievance through technicalities and procedural hair-splitting regarding lab accreditation and typographical errors are unacceptable. The appellant the beverage company is a large-scale manufacturer producing consumable beverages. The standard of care required in bottling plants is absolute. The presence of a dead insect in a sealed beverage is a gross violation of food safety standards and constitutes a severe deficiency in service and an unfair trade practice, the September 30 order read. The state commission further observed that the presence of a macroscopic foreign biological entity is a manufacturing and packaging defect that occurred at the plant, completely independent of the products expiry date. According to the judgment of the district commission, the woman had alleged that she had bought a 1-litre bottle of an orange fruit-based beverage worth Rs 50 along with some other grocery items on October 23, 2011, from a shop, which was one of the authorised sellers for the beverage company. The woman had claimed that when she took out the bottle from the refrigerator to serve her guests, she saw a dead insect floating inside the bottle even before the seal of the bottle was opened. The woman alleged that her guests were shocked and disgusted by the sight and were not able to consume anything for the rest of the evening, because of which she and her family members were embarrassed. On November 2, 2011, the woman sent a legal notice to the beverage company, as a result of which a consumer response co-ordinator of the company visited her home for inspection of the said defective product and admitted after his evaluation that there was a serious and fatal deficiency in service on the part of the company and apologised for the same. The woman stated that she was also asked to share a few photographs of the defective product so that it could be shown to the quality control department and her grievances would be redressed. However, even after following the instructions of the consumer response co-ordinator and issuing a final reminder, there was no response from the company. Consequently, on January 27, 2012, the woman filed a consumer complaint with the South Mumbai district consumer commission. The district commission, by its judgment on August 30, 2018, held the beverage company and the authorised seller liable for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice, ordering them to pay Rs 50 as the refund of the bottle and Rs 1 lakh as compensation for the mental torture. The shop and the company were further directed to pay an additional sum of Rs 25,000 to the woman as litigation costs. The beverage company approached the state commission to appeal against the order of the district commission. Past shelf life The beverage company contended that the district commission had wrongly relied on a precedent involving a solid food item where visual inspection was sufficient and that the lab to which the defective product was sent for testing was not an appropriate laboratory as per law and its report was legally invalid and cannot be relied upon. The company alleged that the woman had unexplainedly delayed sending the bottle for testing until it was past its 4-month shelf life and had initially refused to hand over the bottle to the manufacturer, because of which she prevented a timely scientific testing of the product. As per the order, the woman did not appear before the state commission despite being served notices, and hence the case continued ex parte. Macroscopic object On the allegation that the woman had refused to give the bottle to the company for testing, the state commission stated that we find no fault in the consumers actions. Handing over the primary piece of physical evidence to the very party accused of the manufacturing defect, prior to initiating legal proceedings, would have jeopardised the consumers case. The state commission observed that the appellant contended that the product was tested past its 4-month shelf life. This argument is fundamentally flawed. The expiry of a products shelf life leads to natural degradation, fermentation, or spoilage of the juice it does not spontaneously generate a dead insect inside a sealed bottle. Regarding the objection to the labs visual inspection, the state commission held that the primary mandate for the lab in this instance was to verify package integrity to ascertain whether the factory seal was intact and to confirm the presence of the foreign object. When a macroscopic object like a dead insect is present in a sealed container, the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur the thing speaks for itself is highly relevant. Chemical analysis of the liquid is secondary when the physical contamination of a sealed consumable item is visibly established, and the seals integrity is confirmed. Accordingly, the judgment passed by the district commission was confirmed and upheld. Takeaway The ruling establishes the obligation of companies producing beverages and food items to ensure proper packaging and manufacturing of its products and that the concerns of the consumers must not be ignored, causing them unnecessary inconvenience. For consumer-related grievances, individuals may contact the consumer helpline in their respective states and union territories Maharashtra 1800-22-2262 or call the National Consumer Helpline at 1915for assistance. articleTitle: Higher airfares likely as IndiGo hikes fuel charge over fuel price rise
articleFeaturedImageAlt: The revised fuel charges will apply to all bookings made from 00:01 am on Tuesday, which means that booking already made will be unaffected by the charge revision.
description: IndiGo described the latest increase as a “measured and relatively modest adjustment”, saying a significantly larger increase would have been required to fully offset the rise in fuel costs.
body_raw: With jet fuel prices remaining elevated on a sustained basis amid the West Asia crisis, IndiGo on Monday announced hikes in its distance-based fuel charges for domestic and international flights from Tuesday October 6. The hikes in fuel charge are bound to lead to a further increase in airfares, which have already been high due to the impact of the West Asia war. Jet fuel is a major cost element for airlines as it accounts for over 40 of their operating expenses. While the increases on domestic flights range from Rs 100 to Rs 350 per sector, a large number of international passengers will face substantially larger increases compared with the fuel charges announced by the airline in April. The fuel charges for international flights have been hiked by up to Rs 2,500 per sector. The revised fuel charges will apply to all bookings made from 0001 am on Tuesday, which means that booking already made will be unaffected by the charge revision. ATF prices have remained volatile in recent months, especially following geopolitical issues in the Middle East. The continuous rise in the fuel prices, with the latest month-on-month increase exceeding 14, has taken ATF costs to levels that are amongst the highest in the last decade. Given that Aviation Turbine Fuel makes up a significant share of airlines operating costs, this rise is expected to impact airlines cost structures and network economics, including those of IndiGo, said the countrys largest airline, which operates over 2,200 flights a day. IndiGo described the latest increase as a measured and relatively modest adjustment, saying a significantly larger increase would have been required to fully offset the rise in fuel costs. The fuel charge was introduced in March, in the early days of the West Asia war, and was last revised on April 1. IndiGo regrets the additional burden these revised fuel charges may place on its customers. However, the decision reflects the sustained increase in operating costs and the evolving market environment. IndiGo will continue to monitor the situation and make relevant adjustments as and when appropriate. IndiGo remains committed to giving wings to the nation by offering affordable, convenient and consistent travel to customers, the airline said. Details of IndiGos revised fuel charge For domestic flights up to 500 km in distance, like Delhi-Jaipur, the levy has been hiked by Rs 100 to Rs 375. For a flight distance of 500-1,000 km like Delhi-Ahmedabad, the new fuel charge will be Rs 600, up from Rs 400. The increase in fuel charge will be Rs 300 for flights with distance between 1,000 and 1,500 km like Delhi-Mumbai, taking the levy to Rs 900. For 1,501-2,000 km like Delhi-Bengaluru, the new levy will be Rs 1,150 versus Rs 800 earlier, an increase of Rs 350. Similarly, for flights with a distance of over 2,000 km like Delhi-Thiruvananthapuram, the new levy of Rs 1,300 is Rs 350 higher than the charge announced on April 1. As for international flights, those to and from countries in the Indian subcontinent will attract a surcharge of Rs 1,000 for distances up to 500 km, up from Rs 900 per ticket. For flights with distances beyond 500 km but within the subcontinent, the levy has been hiked by Rs 500 to Rs 3,000. For West Asia, flights with a distance of up to 2,000 km will have a surcharge of Rs 5,500, higher by Rs 2,500. For over-2,000-km flights to and from this region, the new levy of Rs 5,500 is higher by Rs 500 from the charges announced on April 1. As for Southeast Asia and China, flights with a distance of up to 2,000 km will have a surcharge of Rs 5,500, up from Rs Rs 3,500. Flights with distances beyond 2,000 km will also attract Rs 5,500, an increase of Rs 500. Flight to and from Africa will see the surcharge rising to Rs 6,000, an increase of Rs 1,000. Flights to and from Greece and Turkey will have a surcharge of Rs 10,000, up from Rs 7,500. There is no change in the Rs 10,000 fuel charge on flights to and from the rest of Europe.

articleTitle: BJP’s list of 8 for Rajya Sabha poll: 2 women candidates, 1 big name dropped
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Hardeep-Singh-Puri_
description: Ten Rajya Sabha seats are falling vacant in Uttar Pradesh, eight of which are currently held by the BJP, while the SP and the BSP hold one each.
body_raw: The Bharatiya Janata Party BJP Monday announced its eight picks for the October 16 Rajya Sabha poll in Uttar Pradesh, fielding two women candidates. Union Minister Hardeep Singh Puri, whose term in the Upper House is at an end, was not on the list of nominees, which party insiders indicated shows the Central Council of Ministers is due for a shakeup. Former Lok Sabha MP Priyanka Singh Rawat and Shruti Gangwar, Jharkhand Governor Santosh Gangwars daughter and a prominent member of the Uttar Pradesh BJP, were among the partys nominees in the politically important state. Dharampal Singh, Radhakant Ojha, Prakash Pal, Vidyasagar Sonkar, Gopi Krishna Pandey, and Ram Pratap Singh Chauhan were the others. Ten Rajya Sabha seats are falling vacant in Uttar Pradesh, eight of which are currently held by the BJP, while the Samajwadi Party SP and the Bahujan Samaj Party BSP hold one each. How the numbers add up Currently, the BJP-led NDA holds 150 seats in the 245-member Rajya Sabha, while non-NDA parties account for just over 100 seats. The UP Assembly currently has 396 members in the 403-member House, following the death of seven MLAs in the past 11 months. Each Rajya Sabha candidate, therefore, will require 37 first-preference votes to win. The October 16 polls is going to be a tough contest between the BJP and the Samajwadi Party SP. The BJP and SP have the numbers to win seven and two seats respectively out of the 10 at stake. The timing of the polls adds to the intrigue as they come months before the Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections likely to be held early next year. The BJP has 255 MLAs and its NDA allies add another 33 Apna Dal S 13, RLD 9, SBSP 6, and NISHAD Party 5. This takes its tally to 288. With the support of Puja Pal unaffiliated MLAs Manoj Pandey, Rakesh Pratap Singh, and Abhay Singh who were expelled from the SP in June 2025 for cross-voting in the 2024 Rajya Sabha polls and two MLAs of the Raja Bhaiyya-led Jansatta Dal Loktantrik, the NDAs effective strength reaches 294, two short of the required 296 37 for each first-preference votes to ensure victory of eight candidates. Of the 10 seats that will go to polls, the BJP holds eight at present.
