articleTitle: Inside India’s ‘mini Israel’ deep inside the Himalayas as local police steps up vigil
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Dharamkot aerial view
description: For decades, visitors from Israel have been coming down to Dharamkot in Kangra district in search of peace. The village, too, has adapted itself to cater to its guests. The conflict in the Middle East has, however, kept many of them away this year.
body_raw: On a misty afternoon, a group of six men on three motorcycles stop near the link road adjoining Mcleodganj. Mini Israel kitthe hai? Which way to the Mini Israel?, they ask in Punjabi. A local villager looks towards them and raises his finger. Just park your bikes here and trek upwards. Dharamkot is little ahead. Separated by two kilometres and joined by the Dhauladhar range, Mcleodganj and Dharamkot are a world apart in many ways. Walking up, the Buddhist prayer flags, the swanky cafes, and the aroma of momo and Laphing in Mcleodganj give way to signboards in Hebrew, home-style bakeries, and the whiff of freshly baked challah bread signalling the arrival of Dharamkot. These days, the administration has intensified vigil in and around Dharamkot. Although so far, we have not received any request from any Israeli national at Dharamkot about their security, we are ensuring a strict vigil in and around, Superintendent of Police of Kangra district, Kulbhushan Verma says. A patrolling team has been assigned the task to patrol village streets twice a day. We also have details of every foreign national, including Israelis staying there. SSP Verma says that there was an isolated incident earlier when unknown people made some graffiti on walls nearby Dharamkot to hurt the sentiments of Israeli visitors. We had lodged an FIR immediately and our investigation concluded that some mischievous elements did this. There was nothing more to it, he says. Dharamkot is around 240 kms from Himachals capital Shimla. Its closest city is, however, Dharmshala and the nearest airport-around 20 kms-is in Gaggal, Kangra. No one-neither locals nor the Israelis-can quite put a finger on why this small village in Kangra district became a favourite of the Israeli travellers. One such Israeli is Mayya from Yavne. Now 39, Mayya was just 18 when she first visited India in 2008. I dont exactly remember where I got the idea to visit Dharamkot during my first trip. I think I had just heard a lot about this place from many people. she says. What followed was an inseparable bond that continues even today, she says as she fondly looks at her husband Gopal Subramanium. Born and raised in Chennai, Gopal too has a Dharamkot story of his own but one he is not willing to part with. I left my home at the age of 18. I dont want to get into details of the circumstances in which I left. I came to Dharamkot in the early 2000s, says the 50-year-old. Mayya met me in 2008, and later, we decided to get married, he says as a matter-of-fact. I think it was my destiny. To come here and meet him, Mayya chips in. She is clearly the more romantic one. The couple runs a small guest house in Bhagsu Nag, right next to Dharamkot. We used to run a guest house in Dharamkot too but left it after the lease expired, explains Gopal. The couple are parents to two children A daughter, Sansa 8, who was born in Israel and a son, Agam 5, born in Kangra. I do keep visiting Israel and have Israeli citizenship. But now I am no less an Indian, says Mayya, seated in the verandah of their guesthouse, which doubles as a small bistro, as clouds hang low, signalling an impending spell of rain. To an outsider, Mayya and her family may seem an anomaly but for the locals in Dharamkot, she barely raises an eyebrow. Mayya is not the only one from Israel who established herself here. There are a number of Israelis, who have made Dharamkot their second home over the years, Gopal says. They come to India on tourist visas again and again after short intervals. Many have started their own ventures to earn a livelihood. Fond of Israelis Local residents of Dharamkot say they have a special fondness for these Israeli guests and make sure that they feel at home. They keep to themselves, dont haggle or create a fuss, and are generally well-behaved, a local shopkeeper says. Besides, our livelihood is dependent on the tourists. We get along well. Hence, the dip in the number of Israeli tourists this season, in the wake of the war with Iran, has left them wistful. The emptiness hangs heavy in a jewellery shop in a congested, narrow lane deep inside Dharamkot. Artist Vrindavan Dass, popularly known as Raju Dadda, who traces his roots to Kolkata, is sitting on a chair, the wall next to him covered with pages carrying instructions written in Hebrew. Israelis dominate this place. They come here frequently. They want to keep themselves busy and jewellery-designing workshops are one component of this goal, Raju says. Besides jewellery workshops, you will find music lessons, classes to make musical instruments, and yoga workshops here. Another shop owner Aditya Singh is from Rajasthan. My jewellery shop is more of a workshop than a shop, where we train people, especially foreigners, to make different jewellery designs, he says. Today, though, there is not a single student inside the workshop. Raju attributes this to several factors, including the ongoing Middle East crisis, heavy monsoon and, foremost, the increasing arrival of domestic tourists. It is common knowledge among locals that Israelis like to keep to themselves. One reason behind their preference for Dharamkot is its secluded nature, which could afford them their own space, a local resident explains. Hence, the arrival of domestic tourists, many of whom come looking for content for their social media reels, seems to be a downer for many of them. Mayya is not sure if the war is the major reason for the dwindling number of Israelis visiting Dharamkot. This situation is quite normal back in Israel now. Indeed, some problems exist. There are no direct flights and tourists have to come through connecting flights. That makes the journey more expensive, she says. Gopal, however, gives another reason. A lot of youngsters, who would have otherwise travelled to India, may be busy. the military service is mandatory there, he says. Similar views were expressed by Dor Stroul, 37, who is on his second visit to Dharamkot. Some problems are being faced by people who are still serving in the defence services. Otherwise, I dont believe there is much of a hurdle despite the ongoing Middle East crisis, says Stroul, who is a tech professional back home. Asked about his own military experience, he says, I was not found fit for the defence service during my medical examination. While Adityas jewellery store was bereft of Israeli visitors, a few steps ahead, a musical-instrument shop is echoing with the sound of a lone flute. In one corner of Madan B N Music Workshop, 23-year-old Yoni, a first-time visitor to India, is practising his fingerwork on the instrument. Lone student on the flute I came here in July. I have been learning the flute for the last fortnight. I would like to learn and practise here for the next three months, says Yoni, who declines to share his full name and profession in Israel. I am a native of Nepal, but two generations of my family have settled in Dharamshala. My grandfather and father were also musicians. Our relationship with Israelis goes back a long way., Music instructor Madan says. Today, you see only one person sitting in my workshop. But there have been days when it remained crowded with foreign students round-the-clock. Like Raju, Madan also attributes the dip in the expected rush to the glut of domestic tourists. It has led to a few unsavoury incidents, he whispers. War, too, could be a reason, he shrugs. You cant attribute it only to the Middle East conflict, though. I personally believe that when the rush of domestic tourists increases here, the number of Israeli tourists reduces. Apart from this, during the monsoon, Israelis move towards destinations like Leh, Ladakh, he adds. As the congested trail continues alongside a natural drain nullah running through the middle of Dharamkot, a striking red-coloured, three-storey building comes into view. While you can walk into the neighbouring cafes and shops without a hitch, entry here is strictly guarded. It is Dharamkots Chabad House and a sign announces it in Hebrew and English. The Chabad House is situated on land that was once taken on a long lease by a group of Israelis. We are not allowed to enter this building. But this place is revered by people from Israel, says Deepu, who runs a cafe, The Bamboo Chick, next door. They assemble here once or twice a week and pray. This building also serves as a transit point for visiting Israelis. There is a group that arranges everything for anyone, who comes from Israel until the person is able to make their own arrangements, Deepu explains. Once a remote shepherd village Raju Raj, 69, a local resident, attempts to explain how Dharamkot transformed from a remote shepherd village into this Mini Israel. Initially, Dharamkot was a village dominated by the shepherd Gaddi community. Their main sources of livelihood were rearing livestock, small-scale farming and daily wage jobs. I am also not clear how and when Israelis started reaching this village, but one thing is for sure - it is all due to the presence of His Holiness the Dalai Lama at Dharamshala near Mcleodganj in the 1960s. His presence changed this entire landscape, says Raj. Although Jewish people from Israel have no connection with him, the Dalai Lama matters, he says. As foreigners started arriving here, they began establishing their own avenues. They cant purchase land here, so they started taking it on lease. People from other states in India, such as Rajasthan, West Bengal and Goa, have also taken land on lease and are running businesses, especially in the hospitality sector, he says. The village, too, caught up and made sure to create a hospitable environment for its Israeli guests. A number of locals speak Hebrew, shops have no photography, videography allowed signage because Israeli visitors seek complete privacy. A number of outlets double up as money exchange centres too. Kaka Ram, 59, another native of Dharamkot, says the transformation of the village has been such that it would now be difficult to locate a house that depends entirely on agriculture and cattle rearing-their ancestral trade. Every house in this village has a homestay, guest house, cafe or eating joint, rustling up all kinds of food, especially dishes such as falafel, pita and shakshuka, he adds. Earlier a gram panchayat, Dharamkot now comes under the Municipal Corporation of Dharamshala. Kangra District Tourism Development Officer Vinay Dhiman says, Foreigners want to explore more and more. The area around Dharamkot is full of adventure activities. There is the Triund hiking trail, the Laka Glacier. Experienced mountaineers can scale Moon Peak. Even Bir-Billing, a paradise for paragliders, is in Kangra district. All these things attract foreign tourists. According to information available with the State Tourism Department, approximately 8.26 lakh tourists visited Kangra district in 2025-2026. Nowhere is the quest for calm of these Israeli residents and tourists more evident than it is at Tushita Meditation Centre. Most of the disciples who come here to undergo short-and long-term courses of 15 to 30 days are from Israel, Alejandro, 34, a teacher of philosophy from Columbia, tells The Indian Express. At present, there are 22 students, including me, undertaking a course at Tushita. Around 16 out of 22 are Israelis. A dream of a simple life Like Mayya, Daniela, 29, from Tel Aviv, and her partner Yonatan, 34, are nurturing a dream of making Dharamkot their second home. At a restaurant in the heart of the village, they order Tibetan food while sitting at a low bajot-style table and begin narrating their story. While Daniela is visiting for the second time, it is Yonatans first time in both India and Dharamkot. We first met in Chile in South America in 2018. Since then, we have been friends. I visited Dharamkot in 2021. This place was so beautiful and appealing that I wanted to visit it again and again. This visit is also special because this time, Yonatan is accompanying me, says Daniela. Yonatan, who works in the technology sector, says, I had heard a lot about Dharamkot. The couple says though they have visited many countries - Thailand, Malaysia, Nepal, to name a few-it is in this small Himachal village where their heart seems to have found its destination. We would never miss an opportunity to settle in Dharamkot, they say, almost in unison. It feels like home.

articleTitle: Keralam CM calls out ‘unnecessary’ angioplasty: Who needs a stent, who doesn’t?
articleFeaturedImageAlt: angioplasty
description: Cardiologists explain when angioplasty can be life-saving, when medicines may be enough and why finding a blockage does not automatically mean a patient needs a stent
body_raw: Kerala Chief Minister V D Satheesans call for a campaign against unnecessary angioplasty - a procedure to open a narrowed or blocked heart artery with a small balloon, often followed by placement of a stent to keep it open - has sparked a debate among doctors. Satheesan said some hospitals were carrying out angioplasty despite there being no medical need for it, putting the focus on a procedure that can be life-saving in some situations but may not be necessary in others. The Indian Medical Association IMA has agreed that unnecessary investigations and treatment should be avoided, but has cautioned against broad claims about unnecessary angioplasty. Such statements, it said, could undermine patients trust in doctors and even prompt some to delay or refuse procedures that are genuinely life-saving. Kerala is among the countrys largest users of coronary stents, ranking third in reported stent use after Maharashtra and Karnataka, according to National Interventional Council data. Cardiologists say angioplasty is not required for every patient with chest pain, but it should not be delayed when a patient is having an acute heart attack, when blood flow to a part of the heart is suddenly blocked because of blood clotting over broken plaque, depriving the heart muscle of oxygen. The decision, they stress, has to be made on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the patients clinical condition, investigation findings and risk factors. What is an angioplasty? An angioplasty is a procedure to open a narrowed or blocked heart artery with a small balloon, often followed by placement of a stent or a mesh bridge to keep it wide enough for oxygenated blood to flow. Modern stents are drug-coated with clotting medicines and are designed to last a lifetime. When do we need angioplasty? Coronary angioplasty can be life-saving when performed promptly during a heart attack. However, in non-acute situations or stable coronary artery disease, when the hearts arteries are narrowed, predictable and do not pose an immediate emergency its role is more limited. Several large studies have shown that, for most patients with stable disease, routine angioplasty and stenting do not provide additional protection against death or heart attack compared with treatment with medicines only, says Dr Ambuj Roy, professor of cardiology, All-India Institute of Medical Sciences AIIMS, Delhi. According to him, stent or bypass surgery is particularly considered when there are high-risk coronary blockages that place a large amount of heart muscle in jeopardy, or when troublesome angina chest pain persists despite an adequate trial of medical therapy. At the IMAs research cell in Kerala, convenor Dr Rajeev Jayadevan says stenting is not like repairing a blocked water pipe. It is a complex decision that is personalized to the individual patient sitting before the doctor, guided by established scientific society guidelines, diagnostic findings and specialized medical training. What percentage of plaque is required for testing? According to protocol, a coronary artery blockage generally requires at least 70 narrowing or 50 in critical areas like the left main artery before a stent is considered necessary. Mild blockages under 50 are typically managed non-invasively through diet, lifestyle changes, and medications like statins. For moderate, borderline blockages between 50 and 70, we need to test functional blood flow to determine if the heart muscle is actually deprived of blood before deciding whether to place a stent, says Dr Balbir Singh, chairman, Cardiac Sciences, Max Healthcare. Who should get an angiogram? the heart imaging test In patients with chest pain who are not having a heart attack, doctors first estimate the pretest probability or how likely the patient is to have significant coronary artery disease. This estimate is based on factors such as age, sex, the nature of the symptoms and other risk factors, including smoking, family history and existing medical conditions. If the estimated probability is very high - above 85 - guidelines may support proceeding with coronary angiography. If it is very low - below 15 - further testing for coronary artery disease may not be necessary, says Dr Akshay Ashok Bafna, HOD Cardiology at Rajarshi Chhatrapati Shahu Maharaj Government Medical College, Kolhapur. Whats the reason for patient anxiety? Unfortunately, information asymmetry can limit a patients ability to make a truly informed choice. Faced with an angiogram showing a 70 or 90 blockage, patients understandably depend heavily on their treating cardiologist to explain whether a stent is likely to prolong life, prevent a heart attack, relieve symptoms or add little to good medical therapy, explains Dr Roy. It is the overuse of stents in these situations that has, at times, brought an otherwise lifesaving treatment into disrepute. This has in recent times been amplified due to wide availability of insurance schemes. Unfortunately, we have seen that it has at times led to an opposite and potentially dangerous consequence patients refuse stents even during an acute heart attack, when timely angioplasty can save lives and preserve heart muscle, he says. Dr Jayadevan concurs that a treatment that was clinically necessary can easily be perceived as unnecessary when viewed without the full medical context. The complex factors leading to a specialists clinical decision are rarely known to an outside observer. Whenever there are specific concerns or apparent protocol issues, they should be investigated through appropriate statutory medical bodies and clinical audit forums, rather than through generalised public commentary. If public trust is eroded, the real tragedy is that people facing life-threatening heart conditions may hesitate to seek evidence-based scientific interventions, sometimes falling victim to unproven treatments, Dr Jayadevan adds. Dr S Ganapathy, surgeon and public health activist, points to another source of anxiety for patients the difficulty of interpreting cardiac tests without the right clinical context. Even normal variations in an ECG can differ with age, he says. An ECG of a 30-year-old is different from that of a 50-year-old, he explains, noting that variations in ECG waves can sometimes add to a patients anxiety when they are not properly explained. Such anxiety, he says, can make patients particularly vulnerable to inappropriate medical advice. Some people can prey upon these anxieties, he cautions, making it important for patients to understand that an abnormal-looking test does not, by itself, mean that an invasive procedure such as angioplasty is necessary. Ask the right questions Dr Bafna argues for precise framing of the question. Instead of asking Is angioplasty necessary?, the appropriate question should be, Is angioplasty necessary for this particular patient, at this particular time, based on the available scientific evidence? Patients, too, should be encouraged to participate in treatment decisions. They should understand why a procedure is being recommended, what alternatives exist, what the expected benefit is, and what risks are involved, says Dr Bafna. The public messaging should not be to avoid stents but to stent the right patient at the right time. Greater public awareness, shared decision-making and audit of adherence to evidence-based indications are essential to achieving this, adds Dr Roy.

articleTitle: Hanuman Ansh box office: Neem Karoli Baba film earns just Rs 20 lakh less than The Vvaan on 9th Tuesday
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Hanuman Ansh box office collection day 61: Neem Karoli Baba biopic earns just Rs 20 lakh less than Sidharth Malhotra's The Vvaan: Force of the Forrest.
description: Hanuman Ansh box office collection day 61: The Neem Karoli Baba biopic slipped down below the daily mark of Rs 1 crore after 41 days, only to bounce back to that figure on its ninth Tuesday.
body_raw: Hanuman Ansh box office collection day 61Vishal Chaturvedis devotional film Hanuman Ansh, which features Shobhinaw Satyaa as revered spiritual guru Neem Karoli Baba, continues to hold its own in front of new releases even in its ninth week at the domestic box office. While its daily earnings pale in comparison to Ajay Devgn-starrer crime thriller Drishyam 3, its on the verge of surpassing those of the holdover release - Sidharth Malhotra-starrer action adventure fantasy film The Vvaan Force of the Forrest. After over 60 days, Hanuman Ansh has earned Rs 385.62 crore gross and Rs 326.48 crore net in India, and Rs 425.52 crore worldwide. Hanuman Ansh box office collection - Week 9 On its ninth Tuesday day 61, Hanuman Ansh took advantage of the discounted ticket prices to get back into the Rs 1 crore range. It garnered exactly Rs 1 crore from 1570 screens, a 33.33 growth from its ninth Monday day 60 collection of Rs 75 lakh from 1475 screens. That was, in fact, the first time in 41 days of its historic box office run that the films daily earnings went below the Rs 1 crore mark. Ever since Day 18, Hanuman Ansh has been consistently earning more than Rs 1 crore every day, all the way till day 59. It finally fell below that threshold on its ninth Monday, owing to massive competition from Abhishek Pathaks Drishyam 3, which amassed Rs 21 crore from over 16,000 shows on its first Monday, as per Sacnilk. However, despite the competition, Hanuman Ansh has managed to secure around 1500 screens even in its ninth week. Its ninth weekend is testimony to its enduring appeal, since the film collected Rs 3 crore on Sunday day 59, Rs 2.10 crore on Saturday day 58, and Rs 2.25 crore on Friday day 57, which was a holiday on the occasion of October 2, celebrated as Gandhi Jayanti. The impact of Hanuman Ansh is not limited to only the box office, but also the cultural ethos of Indian society. Nainital District Magistrate Lalit Mohan told The Indian Express earlier this week that partly owing to the film, daily visitors have increased by 10,000 over this past long weekend at Kainchi Dham, the spiritual site associated with Neem Karoli Baba in Uttarakhand, prompting the district management to devise an alternate route to avoid congestion. Made on a modest budget of Rs 2 crore, Hanuman Ansh has now earned almost 213 times at the worldwide box office. It initially opened at just Rs 25 lakh on August 7 and collected Rs 1.10 crore in its opening week at the domestic box office. However, following the upsurge in week 3, the weekly collections kept multiplying. After over two months at the domestic box office, with no streaming premiere in sight, Hanuman Ansh is just a couple of crores away from surpassing the domestic box office collection of Sunny Deol and Varun Dhawan-starrer period war drama Border 2 Rs 329.70 crore to become the second highest grossing Indian film this year, after Ranveer Singh-starrer spy thriller Dhurandhar 2 The Revenge Rs 1108.90 crore. Hanuman Ansh was released internationally by Hombale Films over a month after its domestic release on September 11. Since then, its collected Rs 39.90 crore at the overseas box office in less than a month. Its dubbed Telugu version is slated to release in cinemas this Friday on October 9, which may further complement its unprecedented box office run. Vvaan box office collection day 12 Meanwhile, the holdover release from a couple of weeks ago September 25, Deepak Kumar Mishras The Vvaan Force of the Forrest has also been impacted by the Drishyam 3 wave. It collected Rs 1.20 crore from 1990 screens on its second Tuesday day 12, benefitting from discounted ticket prices, to register a 26.30 growth from its second Monday day 11 earnings of Rs 95 lakh. Thats also the first instance when Vvaan went below the daily earnings mark of Rs 1 crore so far. Over its second weekend, it earned Rs 3.25 crore on Sunday day 10, Rs 2 crore on Saturday day 9, and Rs 3.25 crore on Friday day 8 at the domestic box office. Its opening weeks cumulative earnings stand at Rs 53.60 crore in India. Also Read Fahadh Faasil says wont get half of Rs 300 cr as Bethlehem Kudumba Unit earns Rs 326 cr Thus, the total box office collection of Vvaan now adds up to Rs 76.30 crore net and Rs 64.25 crore gross in India. It has collected Rs 7.20 crore internationally, which makes its worldwide gross earnings go up to Rs 83.50 crore. Given the current trajectory, Vvaan needs to pick up pace if it aspires to cross the coveted Rs 100 crore mark in India, or even globally.

articleTitle: Soundarya Rajinikanth says parents ‘changing’ male-dominated dynamic at home: ‘My rocks during divorce’
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Soundarya Rajinikanth
description: Soundarya Rajinikanth opened up about love, marriage and how her parents Rajinikanth and Latha are evolving beyond the male-dominated dynamics she grew up witnessing at home.
body_raw: Soundarya Rajinikanth, who is currently promoting her latest production, Love, which is streaming on Netflix, recently opened up about her own experiences with love and marriage. She also spoke about how her parents, Rajinikanth and Latha, are now changing and moving away from the male-dominated dynamics at home that were once accepted without question. Having gone through a divorce nearly a decade ago, Soundarya recalled how her parents stood by her throughout the difficult phase. Speaking about partnership and how the idea of love evolves at different stages of life, Soundarya told Nayandeep Rakshit, I think we grew up in a generation where it is probably male dominated at home. It is changing with my parents now. Not earlier. As you grow older, the concept of love also changes. What was love for me when I was 20 was not love for me when I was 40. So that changes. So even my parents were learning. Having given love a second chance with her marriage to actor Vishagan Vanangamudi, Soundarya said she and her husband follow a simple formula in their relationship. In my marriage, there is a formula we have where we say, you meet me halfway and I will meet you halfway. It is never my way or yours. We live by it, she said. In the same interview, Soundarya also recalled the difficult period surrounding her divorce from her first husband, businessman Ashwin Ramkumar. She credited her parents with being her biggest source of support during that time. I think it is very important because for a girl, the first man she has in her life is her father and her first friend is her mother. And that just gets stronger and stronger as children grow up. In my difficult times, my parents stood up with me like rock support and I couldnt have done it without them, she said. ALSO READ Drishyam 3 Box Office Collection Day 5 Updates Ajay Devgns film makes it to top 5 highest-grossing Bollywood films of 2026, earns Rs 341 crore worldwide Soundarya said that her failed marriage did not make her question the institution of marriage. Instead, it helped her realise that she may have simply been in the wrong relationship. When my first marriage failed, it didnt make me stop believing in the institution of marriage. It was just a wrong relationship. When I came out of that, I took my time to heal and I couldnt wait to be back in that institution because I believe in it. I believe in commitment that you can be openly proud about and I am very happy to be married again. Soundarya Rajinikanth divorced Ashwin Ramkumar in 2017, two years after they welcomed their son, Ved. According to statements from Soundarya and Ashwins lawyers at the time, the couple had been living separately for seven months before the divorce, after their misunderstanding over various issues reached a point of no return. The couple had tied the knot in September 2010. Meanwhile, Soundaryas latest production, Love, is currently streaming on Netflix. Directed by filmmaker-actor Balaji Mohan, the film marks his return to the directors chair. He is also gearing up for the release of his Hindi debut, Nayyi Navelli, starring Yami Gautam in the lead role.

articleTitle: Repo rate hiked by 25 bps to 5.50 pc: Why RBI has hiked interest rates; EMIs set to rise
articleFeaturedImageAlt: sanjay malhotra
description: GDP growth in FY27 hiked 40 bps to 7.1 pc; Inflation forecast up to 5.2 pc
body_raw: The Reserve Bank of India RBI has increased its policy repo rate by 25 basis points bps to 5.50 per cent, marking the first rate hike since February 2023 and signalling a shift towards tighter monetary policy amid rising inflationary pressures, elevated crude oil prices and a challenging global interest-rate environment. The Monetary Policy Committee MPC has changed the policy stance to calibrated tightening from neutral indicating further hike in the interest rates is a likelihood. The MPC has also hiked the growth projection from 6.7 per cent to 7.1 per cent in FY27 in the wake of the higher economic activity in the country. The panel also raised the inflation forecast to 5.2 per cent for FY27 from 5 per cent previously. The decision by the policy panel to hike rates comes after nearly two years of monetary accommodation. The increase is expected to push up borrowing costs across the economy, affecting interest rates on home, personal and vehicle loans, while also providing some support to deposit rates. RBI Monetary Policy Meeting October 2026 LIVE Announcing the monetary policy, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said high frequency indicators show economic activity holding momentum in the second quarter albeit with some moderation when compared to first quarter. The policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or pause, depending on the evolving conditions, Malhotra said. The RBIs move follows growing concerns that inflationary pressures are becoming more broad-based. Retail inflation rose to 4.82 per cent in August, remaining above the central banks medium-term target of 4 per cent for the third consecutive month, although it continues to remain within the RBIs tolerance band of 2-6 per cent. The last rate hike-when it was hiked from 6.25 per cent to 6.50 per cent - occurred in February 2023, making any potential increase the first in over three-and-a-half years. Governor Sanjay Malhotra hinted at policy recalibration due to signs of inflation normalizing, while Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta acknowledged that conditions for a rate hike may arise during the year. Recent CPI data shows headline inflation at 4.82 in August, marking the third consecutive month above the 4 medium-term target, though still within the RBIs 2-6 range. Forecasts project inflation to rise to an average of 5.9 in Q4 2026 before moderating in the following quarters. As inflation risks persist, a more extended rate hike cycle may be on the horizon. Why has the RBI raised rates? The decision comes against a backdrop of rising food and energy prices, weather-related disruptions and higher crude oil prices. Maharashtra has declared drought in about 265 of its 358 talukas, while the possibility of drought has also been flagged in Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan. Reservoir levels across India are around 20 per cent below last years levels, raising concerns about agricultural output and the rabi crop. The possibility of El Nino conditions extending into 2027 remains another key risk to the inflation outlook. Global developments have added to the pressure. Crude oil prices have risen above 100 a barrel amid geopolitical tensions, raising concerns about imported inflation and Indias external balance. The West Asia conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war have also added uncertainty to the global economic outlook. At the same time, global interest rates remain elevated. The US Federal Reserve recently raised its policy rate by 25 bps to 3.75-4 per cent, while US benchmark yields have also risen sharply by 53 bps to 5.31 per cent in a month. The benchmark 10-year bond yield in India has gone up by 25 bps to 7.21 per cent in a month. A narrowing interest-rate differential with the US could increase pressure on Indias financial markets and currency, making the RBIs policy response more important. Foreign investors have been pulling out funds from India in the wake of the rise in yields in the US. What does the rate hike mean for borrowers? The increase in the repo rate is expected to feed into lending rates, particularly for loans linked to external benchmarks. Home, personal and vehicle loan borrowers could see their equated monthly instalments EMIs rise as banks pass on the higher cost of funds. Loans linked to the marginal cost of funds-based lending rate MCLR may also become more expensive. Banks, however, have flexibility in revising MCLR-based rates depending on their funding costs, liquidity conditions and deposit mobilisation. Deposit rates could also rise marginally as banks reassess their funding requirements. The extent of any increase will depend on liquidity and broader funding conditions. Savers and depositors would like to see the deposit rates going up as high retail inflation has cut into their savings. Inflation risks remain broad-based The RBIs decision to hike retail inflation to 5.2 per cent comes as price pressures extend beyond food and perishable commodities. Higher energy prices, food inflation and weather disruptions are adding to the risks. Analysts expect retail inflation to peak at around 6 per cent in the third quarter and average about 5 per cent in FY27. The possibility of sustained inflation above the RBIs target has strengthened expectations that monetary policy may remain tighter for longer. Economists have pointed to the widening gap between consumer and wholesale price inflation, with rising input costs gradually spreading across farming and non-farming sectors. Growth outlook The rate increase comes amid strong economic growth. Indias GDP grew 7.8 per cent in the first quarter of FY27, beating expectations, with consumption, investment and exports supporting momentum. GST collections, automobile sales and bank credit have also remained healthy. While analysts expect FY27 growth at 7.3 per cent, RBI was conservative in its assessment and raised its growth projection to 7.1 per cent from the earlier estimate of 6.7 per cent. However, higher crude prices, elevated global interest rates, geopolitical tensions, trade-policy uncertainty and weather disruptions pose risks to growth in the coming quarters. The 25-bps increase to 5.50 per cent therefore marks an important change in the RBIs policy direction. With inflation becoming broader and global financial conditions remaining tight, the central bank faces the challenge of containing price pressures without significantly weakening domestic growth.

articleTitle: ‘Caregiver’s transfer inhumane’: Rajasthan High Court quashes bank manager’s posting
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Rajasthan High Court bank manager caregiver thalassemia transfer
description: The court found that the bank failed to consider its Equal Opportunity Policy before transferring the manager – whose brother with thalassemia required blood transfusions every 15 days – to a branch 1,000 km away.
body_raw: Calling the transfer of a UCO Bank manager caring for his 75 per cent permanently disabled brother with thalassemia not only arbitrary but also inhumane, the Rajasthan High Court has quashed his proposed posting nearly 1,000 km away. The court held that the bank could not mechanically apply its routine transfer policy without considering its own safeguards for employees caring for persons with disabilities. The court said the managers brother required regular blood transfusions and depended wholly on him for his medical treatment, personal care and financial support. Justice Anoop Kumar Dhand was on October 5 hearing a petition filed by UCO Bank manager Rahul Agrawal against his transfer from Baneti branch in the Jaipur zone to Bhadwa branch in the Ahmedabad zone. The transfer order was issued on May 16 and the bank rejected his representation seeking cancellation of the transfer on September 8. Transferring a care-giver of a person suffering from Thalassemia, who requires blood transfusion on every 15-20 days, to a place 1000 km away, where no such facility or family support is available, without any reasonable consideration, is not only arbitrary but also inhumane and violative of Article 21 of the Constitution of India, which includes right to health and right to live with dignity of both the disabled dependent and the petitioner, the court said. The dispute centred on UCO Banks Equal Opportunity Policy for 2024-27, which contains specific provisions for employees caring for persons with disabilities. The high court found that the bank had failed to meaningfully consider those safeguards before transferring Agrawal to a branch around 1,000 km away from his present posting. Brother dependent on him for treatment According to the order, Agrawals younger brother, Ashish Kumar Agrawal, suffers from thalassemia and has 75 per cent permanent physical disability. His disability was certified by the Department of Medical Health, Government of Rajasthan, on April 19, 2022. The petitioner told the court that his brother was wholly and solely dependent on him for his day-to-day survival, including regular blood transfusions, medication, personal care and financial support. He also submitted that there was no other person in the family to look after his brother. tha The court noted that this dependency was not raised for the first time during the litigation. It had already been declared by Agrawal and recorded in the banks service and HR records. The bank had not disputed the dependency in its reply. The banks own Equal Opportunity Policy became central to the dispute. The policy, framed for 2024-27, contains provisions relating to the transfer and posting of persons with disabilities and their caregivers. It says a person with disability should not be posted far from their residence if this creates difficulties in commuting. It also provides that an employee caring for a dependent daughter, son, parent, spouse, brother or sister with specified disability may be exempted from routine transfer or rotational transfer, subject to administrative constraints. Bank cites promotion, long posting UCO Bank opposed Agrawals plea, arguing that its transfer policy required officers to be transferred after promotion. Agrawal had been promoted from Scale-I to Scale-II through an order dated April 1, 2026. The bank also pointed out that he had remained posted at Baneti and nearby places in the Jaipur zone since January 2018 and had spent around eight years there. It argued that there was no malice or mala fide intention behind the transfer and that several officers had been transferred because of administrative requirements. The high court, however, found that the bank had failed to demonstrate that it had properly considered the special policy while dealing with Agrawals representation. It described the September 8 rejection order as a non-speaking order because it did not explain why his request for retention or exemption under the Equal Opportunity Policy had not been considered. It held that the order was arbitrary and discriminatory and violated Articles 14 equality and 16 equality of opportunity in employment of the Constitution. The Special Policy framed by the respondent-Bank is, therefore, not an act of charity but a statutory obligation. It has a binding force, the court said, adding that the bank cannot be allowed to frame a policy for public display and then act contrary to it. Administrative constraints cant defeat protection The court acknowledged that transfer is ordinarily an incidence of service and courts generally do not interfere with transfer orders. But it said this principle is not absolute where a transfer violates legal rules or a binding policy, is arbitrary or falls within other grounds for judicial review. It held that the banks special policy had binding force and was intended to provide reasonable accommodation to employees caring for persons with disabilities. The expression administrative constraints, the court said, could not be treated as an omnibus or mechanical exception that defeated the protective purpose of the policy. Any departure from the exemption had to be based on genuine, relevant and demonstrable administrative exigencies. The court found that the transfer order did not refer to the disability certificate, the special policy or the relevant caregiver provisions, calling it a classic case of non-application of mind. It said the circumstances were particularly serious because Agrawals brother required blood transfusions every 15 to 20 days. The judge also made it clear that Agrawal could not claim permanent immunity from transfer. It noted that he had already served at his present place for more than seven years. The bank could hence consider transferring him to another station where a vacancy existed, provided it first considered his circumstances and the special policy. The high court quashed the May 16 transfer order and directed the bank to allow Agrawal to continue at his present posting until his case was reconsidered under the Equal Opportunity Policy and in light of his brothers medical condition and dependency.

articleTitle: ‘Missing’ land around KCR’s farmhouse: BRS leader, family to get notices

description: Revanth Reddy has ordered officials to investigate the 45-acre gap and look into possible irregularities in the state’s land records.
body_raw: Telangana Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy Tuesday ordered an inquiry into 45 acres of land in Siddipet districts Erravalli village that officials could not account for during a recent survey. The land is adjacent to a farmhouse owned by Bharat Rashtra Samithi BRS chief K Chandrashekar Rao, where he has retreated and spends most of his time after his partys defeat in the December 2020 Assembly elections. Last month, officials found a discrepancy in the land records during a routine exercise to identify land for distribution to beneficiaries in Erravalli and Venkatapuram villages of Markook mandal. In Survey No 325 of Erravalli village, records show that the parcel should contain 388 acres. However, the survey team could identify only 343 acres, leaving 45 acres unaccounted for. In a meeting Tuesday night, Reddy ordered an inquiry and directed officials to scrutinise whether any irregularities existed in the Dharani portal, which hosts land records. The chief minister sought details of Erravalli land, and directed officials, including Chief Secretary Sanjay Jaju and CMO Principal Secretary V Sheshadri, to issue a notification to identify the missing 45 acres. As KCR and his family members own land near Survey Number 325, officials would issue notices requiring them to submit their land records. The CM instructed officials to distribute the land identified in Survey Number 325 to eligible beneficiaries and landless local farmers. Reddys allegations During recent public meetings, Revanth Reddy has questioned and accused KCR and his family of amassing disproportionate wealth during the partys regime between 2014 and 2023. At a public meeting in Sircilla recently, he demanded that KCR and his son K T Rama Rao, popularly known as KTR, disclose the details of the properties they owned, as well as those of nephews T Harish Rao and Santosh Kumar. He said KTR built a farmhouse in Janwada village, while his sister Kavithas farmhouse is in Shankarpally, Harish Raos in Moinabad, and KCRs farmhouses are in Erravalli. He questioned where all these properties came from. He also ordered the construction of a Telangana Martyrs Colony for the families of those who sacrificed their lives during the Telangana movement and who belong to that area. The government will allocate housing plots to the martyrs families and develop the colony with all necessary infrastructure. The chief minister assigned the Housing Department responsibility for the colonys construction and ordered officials to ensure the project is completed by June 2 next year. The chief minister also suggested establishing a Young India Integrated School and an education hub on the available lands within the limits of Velikatta village in Kondapaka Mandal.

articleTitle: Grinding your teeth at night without knowing it? Here’s what it does
articleFeaturedImageAlt: teeth
description: From worn enamel and sensitive teeth to jaw pain and headaches, sleep bruxism can cause damage before you realise there is a problem
body_raw: Lisa Shah, in her late 40s, frequently complained of morning headaches and increasing tooth sensitivity. She did not realise she was grinding her teeth at night until dentists noticed characteristic wear patterns during an examination, recalls Dr Bibhakar Ranjan, a Germany-based dentist and preventive oral health advocate. After wearing a custom-made night guard and addressing contributing factors, her teeth were protected from further wear and there was an improvement in jaw discomfort, he says, underscoring why bruxism, or teeth grinding, needs greater attention and awareness among patients as well as dentists and doctors so that it can be identified early. In India too, experts associated with the Indian Dental Association IDA, say several studies have reported an increasing prevalence of the condition across different population groups. According to estimates across various studies, sleep and awake bruxism collectively affect approximately 10 to 30 per cent of the general Indian population, with varying degrees of severity, from occasional to frequent episodes. There is also a high correlation with anxiety, academic or occupational stress and modern lifestyle habits, says Dr Jayesh Rahalkar, consultant orthodontist and past president of the Indian Dental Association, Pune. Studies have shown that the rates can rise significantly in high-stress or physically demanding environment. For instance, studies in India show awake bruxism rates as high as 68 per cent among professional weightlifters and elevated levels among dental students facing academic and clinical stress, Dr Rahalkar says. The Indian Dental Association traditionally observes Oral Health Month during October and November to promote better oral hygiene and preventive care across India. What is bruxism? Grinding or clenching of teeth? Bruxism is the medical term for the involuntary or subconscious clenching, grinding or gnashing of teeth, which can happen during waking hours or while sleeping, Dr Rahalkar says. Symptoms can range from morning headaches, dull pain around the temples, sore or tight jaw muscles and facial pain to increased tooth sensitivity and enamel wear. According to Dr Rahalkar, several factors have been linked to bruxism, including psychological stress, anxiety, sleep disorders and lifestyle habits such as heavy alcohol consumption, tobacco use and high caffeine intake. Over time, dentists say, persistent grinding can make teeth increasingly sensitive to hot and cold, while also causing cracks, fractures and, in severe cases, significant pain. Dr Ranjan says patients may not even realise that they are clenching or grinding their teeth while asleep. It is only when there are jaw pain, headaches or worn teeth that dentists often identify the signs during a check-up, he says. Bruxism is on the rise due to increased stress and sleep disorders. It is known to affect 20 per cent of the population, says Dr Mohit Kheur, consultant at Deenanath Mangeshkar Hospital and professor at M A Rangoonwala Dental College, Pune. Types of disorder Bruxism can broadly be classified as sleep bruxism and awake bruxism. While sleep bruxism occurs during sleep and may involve rhythmic or sustained clenching and grinding, awake bruxism is more commonly characterised by clenching or holding the teeth together while a person is conscious. Experts say awake bruxism may be associated with periods of stress, anxiety or intense concentration, while sleep bruxism may occur alongside other sleep-related problems. In many cases, however, people may be unaware of the habit, particularly when it occurs during sleep. Rise in use of night guards, but they do not address the underlying cause With growing awareness of bruxism, dentists are seeing greater use of night guards, which are designed to separate the upper and lower teeth and reduce the damage caused by repeated clenching and grinding. According to Dr Ranjan, a custom-made guard can provide an important layer of protection, particularly in patients who have already developed signs of tooth wear. By creating a barrier between the teeth, it can help limit further enamel loss and reduce the risk of cracks, fractures and damage to existing dental restorations. However, a night guard is primarily a protective measure and does not eliminate the factors responsible for bruxism. A custom-made mouthguard doesnt cure the underlying cause of grinding, Dr Ranjan says. Identifying and addressing triggers such as stress, anxiety or sleep-related problems therefore remains important. In cases where prolonged bruxism has already damaged the teeth, restorative treatment may also be required. Worn-down teeth due to grinding can be restored with dental fillings or crowns, Dr Ranjan says.

articleTitle: Implants ‘broke’ thrice after procedure, Punjab dentist to pay UK citizen Rs 79,000
articleFeaturedImageAlt: consumer commission dentist
description: The Punjab State Consumer Commission was hearing the dentist’s appeal against the district commission order directing him to refund Rs 64,000 spent on the dental implants and pay Rs 15,000 compensation.
body_raw: The Punjab State Consumer Commission has upheld a Rs 79,000 payout for a patient whose dental bridge allegedly broke three times after treatment by a Jalandhar-based dentist. While upholding the award of a district consumer commission, the state body did not buy the dentists argument that a person who spent a huge sum of money on dental implants would knowingly chew hard food that could harm his teeth. The Punjab State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission judicial member Harinderpal Singh Mahal and member Kiran Sibal were hearing an appeal filed by a Jalandhar dentist against an April 17, 2023 order of the District Consumer Commission, Jalandhar. The state commission, on September 28, noted the district commissions observation that it cannot be presumed that a person who has spent so much amount for fixing the implants would chew hard food knowingly fully well that it may cause harm to his teeth. The dispute began in March 2018 when the complainant, a UK resident, approached the dentist after his tooth bridge needed replacement. According to the complaint recorded in the order, the dentist advised two implants and a bridge costing Rs 64,000. After the complainant returned to the UK, the bridge became loose within about three months. Subsequent attempts to replace or repair it also failed. Bridge failed repeatedly According to the complainant, he was told after the first problem that the plastic crowns would have to be removed and replaced with stone crowns during his next visit to India. He returned in March 2019, but the replacement bridge broke in the middle after five months. He again approached the dentist and was advised to return the following year. In March 2020, another procedure was carried out, but the new bridge also failed and broke into two pieces. The complainant said he was again promised that the problem would be corrected on his next visit. He could not travel to India in 2021 because of the Covid-19 pandemic and eventually got a denture fitted by a dentist in the UK for 500, stated in the complaint to be equivalent to about Rs 50,000. The complainant claimed Rs 64,000 towards the implants, Rs 1,500 for X-ray and reception charges, Rs 10,000 in taxi fares and Rs 50,000 towards the replacement denture. The dentist disputed the complaint, saying the patient had been informed about the procedure and had signed a consent form. He said three implants had initially been advised at Rs 97,000, but the patient opted for two implants and an overhead bridge costing Rs 64,000. The dentist also contended that the bridge could have broken because the patient chewed hard or sticky food despite being advised against it. He said he had replaced the bridge without charging the patient and again advised him not to eat hard or sticky food. Commission rejects dentists plea The dentist argued that there was no defect in the implants and that it was the bridge that had broken. His counsel contended that any liability should therefore be limited to the cost of the bridge. The commission rejected the argument, noting that the record specifically mentioned charges for the dental implants but did not specify any separate amount charged for the bridge. It therefore found no basis to limit the liability as suggested by the dentist. The commission recorded that the bridge became loose about three months after the initial treatment, was replaced, and that a later porcelain-fused-to-metal bridge broke after five months before being replaced again. Finding no merit in the appeal, the bench dismissed it and upheld the district commissions direction to pay Rs 64,000 towards the amount spent on the implants and Rs 15,000 as compensation. The commission also directed that the Rs 39,500 deposited by the dentist while filing the appeal, along with any interest accrued, be remitted to the complainant after 45 days from the sending of certified copies of the order to the parties. Takeaway Consumers should keep treatment records, payment receipts, consent forms and communication with the dentist when undergoing costly dental treatment. If treatment repeatedly fails and a dispute arises over responsibility, these records can help establish what treatment was provided, what was paid for and what went wrong. Consumers facing similar grievances may contact the consumer helpline in their respective states Punjab helpline1800-425-1082 or dial the National Consumer Helpline at1915for assistance. articleTitle: INDIA allies not happy with Gandhis’ ‘impromptu’ protest, Congress firefights
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Lok Sabha LoP Rahul Gandhi, with Congress MPs Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and Deepender Singh Hooda, stages a sit-in protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar at Akashvani Bhawan, in New Delhi on Tuesday. (AICC/ANI Photo)
description: Voices from among the allies feel what was a joint Opposition protest turned into a “Rahul Gandhi show”. Some also questioned the Congress leaders’ insistence on meeting the Election Commission when the protest was against them.
body_raw: Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra stole the show at the INDIA bloc march to the Election Commissions office in Delhi on Tuesday with the sit-in at Akashvani Bhavan. But this has upset Congresss allies, many of whom feel Tuesdays mega protest eventually became a Gandhi siblings show. The Gandhis, they feel, grabbed the spotlight with the sit-in at Akashvani Bhavan, the All India Radio headquarters, while other Opposition leaders were detained and taken away to police stations. Sources said KC Venugopal, Congresss general secretary organisation, told other INDIA bloc parties that the Congress leadership acted in the moment and that he regretted the mistrust created because the allies were not kept in the loop. Voices from among the allies feel what was a joint Opposition protest turned into a Rahul Gandhi show. Some also questioned the Congress leaders insistence on meeting the Election Commission when the protest was against them. What happened on Tuesday About 200 Opposition MPs gathered at Parliaments Makar Dwar on Tuesday before marching to the Election Commission office to demand the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the Chief Election Commissioner, over issues linked to the Special Intensive Revision of voter rolls. Delhi Police had cordoned off all roads leading to the poll panels office, and as the Opposition march reached Akashvani Bhavan, senior Opposition MPs, including Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, were detained, put on buses and taken to police stations. An impromptu move In a move the Congress described as impromptu, the Gandhi siblings entered the Akashvani Bhavan and staged a sit-in for hours. According to Congress sources, Rahul Gandhi planned to enter the Akashvani Bhavan complex and exit through the back gate, right opposite to the Election Commission office. But when police locked the back gate, the Gandhi siblings and other party leaders, including Venugopal, Pawan Khera and Imran Pratapgarhi, staged a sit-in at the Akashvani Bhavan, demanding a meeting with the Election Commission. The Gandhi siblings and Congress leaders with them were detained late in the evening and released later. An FIR has now been filed. Congress leaders said the Akashvani Bhavan sit-in was not part of the plan and that the Gandhi siblings pulled off a surprise move. The Congress leaders didnt know about the protest, so the allies also didnt know, said a Congress leader. Congress leaders defended the decision to protest at Akashvani Bhavan, calling it spontaneous. How could we have predicted this? And the MPs of other parties could have come back, and some of them did. The Congress has ensured all allies feel included, said a Congress leader. Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge will be hosting a lunch for INDIA bloc MPs at Sagar Ratna restaurant in Janpath. Why allies are not happy Todays protest was an INDIA bloc protest. But eventually it became a Congress and Rahul Gandhi protest, said a source in the INDIA bloc parties. articleTitle: IIM Ahmedabad tweaks PGP shortlisting, lists graduation disciplines
articleFeaturedImageAlt: IIM Ahmedabad CAT
description: The basic eligibility criteria remain unchanged. Candidates must hold a bachelor's degree or an equivalent qualification with at least 50 per cent marks or equivalent CGPA.
body_raw: The Indian Institute of Management IIM Ahmedabad has made minor changes in the selection criteria for admission to its two-year Post Graduate Programme PGP in Management for the 2027-29 batch. This time, they have introduced a new classification of undergraduate disciplines and revised the way candidates academic backgrounds are assessed. IIM Ahmedabad has divided undergraduate degrees into 18 broad disciplines for its admission process, including engineering and technology, computer science and information technology, medical and health sciences, commerce, accounting and finance, economics, agriculture and allied sciences, social sciences, arts and humanities, law, management, mathematics, pure sciences, professional courses, fashion and design, journalism and media, architecture and planning, hospitality and food sciences and others. The change is part of the revised admission process for the PGP programme. IIM-A uses candidates academic performance, CAT-2026 scores and other components to shortlist applicants for the subsequent stages of selection. Read Indian student Pratyush Prabhakar elected VP of Academic Affairs at Harvard Kennedy School Under the new policy, candidates graduation marks will be awarded rating scores ranging from one to 10. Candidates scoring up to 55 per cent in graduation will receive one point, while those scoring above 55 to 60 per cent will receive two points. The rating increases to three points for scores above 60 to 70 per cent, five points for above 70 to 80 per cent, eight points for above 80 to 90 per cent and 10 points for scores above 90 per cent. IIM Ahmedabad has also retained a gender-diversity component in its selection process. Non-male candidates will receive three points under this component, while male candidates will receive no points. The basic eligibility criteria, however, remain unchanged. Candidates must hold a bachelors degree or an equivalent qualification with at least 50 per cent marks or equivalent CGPA. The minimum requirement is 45 per cent for candidates belonging to the Scheduled Caste SC, Scheduled Tribe ST and Persons with Disability PwD categories. The degree should involve at least three years of education after completing Class 12 or an equivalent examination. Candidates appearing for their final-year bachelors degree examination or awaiting results can also apply, subject to the conditions specified by the institute. Also Read IITs, IIMs see more women joining than ever as placements and salary packages rise For the 2027-29 batch, candidates must also be at least 19 years old as on June 30, 2027. IIM Ahmedabad has retained the minimum CAT-2026 qualifying cut-offs. For General and Economically Weaker Section EWS candidates, the overall cut-off is 95 percentile, with an 85 percentile sectional cut-off. The corresponding overall cut-offs are 90 for NC-OBC, 85 for SC and 75 for ST candidates. In the notice, the institute has clarified that these are minimum qualifying cut-offs and meeting them does not guarantee a call for the next stage of the admission process. The revised admission policy is applicable to candidates seeking admission to IIMAs PGP for the 2027-29 academic session.

articleTitle: Citing postpartum psychosis, court acquits mother sentenced to life for killing infant
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Gauhati High Court mother infant baby postpartum psychosis
description: The woman allegedly told the police that she did not like her daughter from the day she was born, but the court said her statement was inadmissible as it could have been made under police pressure or influence.
body_raw: A case in which a mother was convicted for killing her 38-day-old daughter took a different turn before the Gauhati High Court, which found that she may have been going through the rare mental health condition of postpartum psychosis.The court acquitted the woman in the 2016 case, holding that her confession was inadmissible as it raised concerns of police pressure. Justices M Zothankhuma and Rajesh Mazumdar on October 6 allowed the womans appeal against her conviction and life imprisonment by the trial court in September 2023. The court mentioned that postpartumpsychosis is a severe mental condition which develops following delivery, and scientific research has pointed out that childbirth is a potent trigger for severe mood disorder. The woman had allegedly told the police that she did not like her daughter from the day she was born. Her confessional statement is to the effect that she was mentally unwell and that she did not like her daughter from the day she was born. On trying to understand the case where a mother does not like her newborn child, we have come across rare cases of infanticide due to Postpartum Psychosis, the court said. Postpartum psychosis is a rare and severe mental health condition that can develop after childbirth and is distinct from postpartum depression. The court added that women with this health issue can lose touch with reality, and its symptoms may include delusions, hallucinations, severe mood symptoms and cognitive symptoms. The court, however, said it was not required to decide whether the woman actually had postpartum psychosis, but noted that the issue should have been considered by the trial court before convicting her. Infant goes missing The womans husband lodged a complaint in 2016 stating that his daughter, who was one month and eight days old, had gone missing during the night. During questioning by the police, his wife allegedly confessed in the presence of local witnesses that she had killed the child on October 14, 2016, and thrown the body into the Dikhow River. The husband, however, said that when he had inquired about the missing infant, the wife stated that she did not know where the baby was. The woman was represented by advocate D Baruah. Can put mother, child in danger The court pointed out that some symptoms of postpartum psychosis can be fleeting and changeable. It noted that there is a risk to babies in around 35 per cent of postpartum psychosis cases, as mothers going through the condition may act on false beliefs, incorrectly handle their babies, become severely confused or behave unusually. The court added that such behaviour can be temporary and is caused by the effect of postpartum psychosis on the brain. The National Library of Medicine in the National Centre for Biotechnology Information states that postpartum psychosis is rare, affecting one and two per one thousand women. However, postpartum psychosis can develop rapidly and place the life of the mother and infant in danger, the court mentioned. It noted that the mothers confessional statement was signed by a woman head constable who was present when it was recorded. The same makes the said confessional statement inadmissible as evidence, as the accused cannot be said to be completely free from police pressure or influence at the time of making her confession, it added. The court held that the womans conviction could not be sustained solely on the basis of the inadmissible confession and that an admission made during the hearing on sentence could not be treated as additional evidence for conviction. It thus set aside the conviction and acquitted her of the charge of murder.

articleTitle: Food safety scandal in Mumbai to blackmail: Extortion bid behind ‘rat in dosa’ video
articleFeaturedImageAlt: rat in dosa tukaram mundhe FDA
description: Mansi Acharya and her sister Kinjal allegedly came to collect the money. However, instead of arresting them, the police served them notices, a police officer said.
body_raw: The Borivali Police have booked two sisters for allegedly threatening hotelier Jai Kishore Shah with a police case over a viral video of a rat allegedly found in a dosa unless he paid them Rs 25 lakh. According to the complaint, the amount was negotiated down to Rs 7 lakh, of which Shah allegedly paid Rs 1 lakh in advance on September 30. On October 5, Shah allegedly agreed to meet the sisters and pay the remaining Rs 6 lakh. Acting on his complaint, the Borivali police arranged for the meeting to take place at the same hotel. Mansi Acharya and her sister Kinjal allegedly came to collect the money. However, instead of arresting them, the police served them notices, a police officer said. According to the police, on September 24, Acharya, along with a child and two men, visited Radhakrishna Hotel-Banquet-Fast Food on L T Road in Borivali West to eat Mysore Masala Dosa and other dishes. While eating about half a dosa, a person accompanying her, identified as Amit Trivedi, allegedly found a rat in his dosa. Acharya created a ruckus at the hotel, called the police, and made a video. According to Shahs complaint, the video went viral on September 26, after which the Food and Drug Administration FDA suspended the hotels licence on September 28, forcing it to shut down. Shah alleged that Acharya threatened to lodge a police complaint against him and circulate the video further unless he paid her money. He approached the Borivali police on September 29, alleging that he had been threatened with further circulation of the video and a police case if he did not pay. He further alleged that between October 1 and 5, Acharya repeatedly contacted him on WhatsApp and demanded the remaining Rs 6 lakh, threatening to approach the police and circulate the video. Police booked both under Section 308 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for extortion.

articleTitle: ‘Imaandaar CM’ hoardings flood poll-bound Punjab. But why are people upset?
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Bhagwant Mann hoarding
description: Ludhiana residents have questioned why honesty "needs an announcement or publicity", and why crores of taxpayers' money was being spent to issue a "self-certified honesty declaration".
body_raw: With less than six months to go for the Punjab Assembly elections, the ruling Aam Aadmi Party AAP in Punjab is fighting a paradox. While the Punjab and Haryana High Court has ordered a high-level CBI probe into the serious corruption allegations linked to Chief Minister Bhagwant Manns office, the roads, highways and streets in the state, especially in the states largest city, Ludhiana, are speaking otherwise. Huge hoardings declaring CM Mann as imaandaar honest have flooded Ludhiana at intervals of every few meters across the city- from highways, chowks, roadsides to streets. Not just Ludhiana, but the imaandaar CM hoardings have cropped up across the state -- drawing sharp reactions from the Opposition parties as well as residents. Residents in Ludhiana have questioned why imaandaari honesty needs an announcement or publicity, and why crores of taxpayers money was being spent to issue a self-certifiedhonesty declaration for the CM when polls were just months away, and people would be the only judge. The critics are also pointing to CM Manns own words, before he became the CM, when he had flayed other parties for advertising false claims. In Ludhiana, huge hoardings declaring Mann as imaandaar CM have been installed on Ferozepur Road, with his smiling face and a caption Imaandaar CM 90 households getting 600 units of free power. The honesty hoardings have also been put prominently in posh locations of Ludhiana West constituency such as Pakhowal Road near Hotel Park Plaza, Aggar Nagar locality on Ferozepur Road, near Sidhwan Canal Pakhowal Road, etc apart from highways and roundabouts. Ludhiana-based RTI activist and an environmentalist Kuldeep Singh Khaira said it is high time linguists update the definition of honesty. After the High Court order, even the word imaandaar must be thinking, What do I really mean? Now it feels we have to update the definitionof honesty. Those who are really honest never really sing about it. They dont need to announce it. Harjot Benipal, a worker of Akali Dal Waris Punjab De, said This has also probably happened for the first time in 70 years that a CM is declaring himself as honest. Sandeep Singh, a resident, said If a CM has to scream through hoardings that he is honest, there is something fishy. Moreover, can the AAP issue a White Paper on who has paid for this flood of hoardings in the city? Residents question why crores have been spent just to portray him as clean. Polls are a few months away. Let the people decide, said another resident, Kanav Sharma. Harminder Taneja, another resident, said Why is so much advertising needed if you are really honest?From where is so much money coming to spend on advertising? From the pockets of people. Echoing the view, Rashpal Singh, a student, said What kind of honesty is that when you have to shout about it through billboards?Taxpayers money is being used to promote the CMs honesty this is also a first in 70 years. With the AAP heavily banking on its kattar imaandaar a die-hard honest party pitch for the election campaigns, and the phrase repeatedly used by AAP national convenor Arvind Kejriwal to describe his party leaders, the residents are also taking a dig at the party for omitting kattar in the billboards. The AAP government must sue the creators of these hoardings. How dare they miss the word kattar and write onlyimaandaar for the honourable CM, said a resident, requesting anonymity. Another resident, Prince Vij, said Bhagwant Mann is such an Imaandaar CM that he has to waste taxpayers money to tell everyone that he is honest. What a waste of public funds Pulling out an old video of Mann criticising previous governments for wasting money on billboards and hoardings, senior Congress leader and MLA Sukhpal Singh Khaira highlighted the splurge of the Imaandaar CM. He alleged that CM Mann and AAP supremo Arvind Kejriwal used to trap others with their word power. Now, theygot caught in their own words today Once they made fun of banners, and today they are running the government based on flexboards themselves. Claims are of honesty, but development exists only on paper and hoardings Before taking over as the CM, Mann had criticised previous governments for wasting public money on banners and hoardings. What kind of development is this that has to be advertised via banners? Had hospitals actually been built, they would be visible. After 9.5 years, this is fake development being shown on banners, Mann was heard saying in the video. CMs corruption stench has reached Delhi SAD Senior SAD leader and former minister Bikram Singh Majithia also took potshots at Manns honesty hoardings. Chief Minister keeps walking around holding a board that says, I am honest, while corruption in his offices has been simmering so long that its stench has reached DelhiPeople have started reading the boards and writing underneath Yeah, we got it OK, TATA, BYE BYE he wrote on X. Punjab BJP president Kewal Singh Dhillon said What kind of honesty is this that advertisements are required to publicize it? Ludhiana BJP president Sunil Moudgill, in a statement issued on Tuesday, said that the Punjab government has put hoardings of Honest CM across the state, but they should be replaced with Dishonest CM. The High Court has ordered a high-level CBI probe into corruption allegations in the working of the Chief Ministers Office CMO and his Officer on Special Duty OSD Rajbir Singh Ghuman, but the CM is protecting corrupt individuals. Despite the ED writing to the Punjab Government three times, they did not get it probed. What does this prove? he asked. Imandaar CM exposed Ravneet Singh Bittu Former union minister and BJP leader Ravneet Singh Bittu posted on X Bhagwant Mann, who has put up billboards across Punjab proclaiming himself as Imandaar CM, has been exposed today.Acting on the direct orders of the Honble Punjab and Haryana High Court and an ED report, the CBI has registered an FIR against the Punjab CMs OSD along with 5 others, conducting coordinated raids across 8 locations.Behind the self-promoted billboards of integrity lay severe allegations of institutionalized corruption-from auctioning IASIPS transfers and manipulating government tenders to fixing land CLUs and leaking confidential policy drafts for pecuniary gain.Integrity was confined to advertisements, while power was blatantly abused behind closed doors. Hoardings are part of routine campaign However, Ludhiana AAP president urban Jatinder Singh Khangura said that such hoardings are a part of the routine campaign of the party that we run from time to time. CM Mann is the most popular face of our party, and he will lead our election campaign for 2027. His honesty doesnt need any proof. We have no idea who has paid for these hoardings-the party or the government. However, AAP Punjab spokespersons - Malwinder Singh Kang, Baltej Singh Pannu, and Neel Garg - were not available for comments.

articleTitle: Ola, Uber banned in Chandigarh. Drivers have a workaround. So do cops
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Chandigarh bike taxi ban, Chandigarh taxi ban, Chandigarh bike taxi crackdown, Chandigarh Police taxi crackdown, Uber ban Chandigarh, Ola ban Chandigarh, Rapido ban Chandigarh, inDrive ban Chandigarh, banned bike taxis Chandigarh, app-based taxis Chandigarh, Chandigarh transport rules, Bharat Taxi Chandigarh, Chandigarh news, Indian Express news
description: The crackdown has so far resulted in action against 915 vehicles in Chandigarh, making it the authorities’ biggest drive yet against unauthorised app-based transport services.
body_raw: The ride may be banned, but getting one is still surprisingly easy. In Chandigarh, drivers of app-based taxis and bike taxis linked to Uber, Ola, inDrive, and Rapido are finding new ways to stay on the road - and the police are finding new ways to catch them. From switching phones to airplane mode to cancelling bookings just before the ride begins, drivers are adopting tactics to evade enforcement, while Chandigarh Police are booking rides themselves on banned platforms to catch them in the act. The cat-and-mouse game has so far resulted in action against 915 vehicles - 812 challaned and 103 impounded - in what authorities describe as their biggest crackdown yet on unauthorised app-based transport services. Modus operandi The drivers allegedly put their phones on airplane mode, ask passengers to pay the amount shown, cancel the ride just before starting, and go offline while plying routes where police are not normally deployed. Drivers also allegedly ask passengers to tell the police they found the cab parked and hired it directly. When the police catch the driver, he quickly puts his phone on airplane mode. Meanwhile, the Chandigarh Police book cabs through the banned apps themselves to catch drivers red-handed. After stopping a vehicle, they check the drivers phone and apps to establish whether the cab is being operated through a banned platform. More bikes than cabs According to State Transport Authority STA data, bike taxis accounted for the bulk of the violations, with nearly 70 per cent of all vehicles found operating in Chandigarh, underlining the scale of their continued operation in the city. Data shows as many as 569 bike taxis were challaned and 67 impounded, taking the number to 636. Among the 208 taxis, 194 were challaned and 14 impounded. Despite the ban, app-based two-wheeler services and taxis both have a significant presence on city roads, a STA senior officer told The Indian Express. The Chandigarh Administration had also written to the Centre seeking a GPS-based mechanism to restrict the operation of the suspended aggregator apps within Chandigarh. The move was proposed as the apps remain accessible despite suspension of their licences, allowing drivers to continue accepting bookings. The ban Earlier this month, Chandigarh Administration suspended the licences of Uber and Rapido for six months. STA said the two companies had failed to comply with mandatory requirements covering driver insurance and training, fares, vehicle eligibility, safety and other operational norms, despite being given several opportunities to meet the conditions. The action followed the Union Territory administrations earlier suspension of Ola and inDrive over alleged violations related to driver welfare and training. However, the ban has made commuting difficult for passengers, with fewer options and, at times, higher fares due to reduced competition. Although the Bharat Taxi app is an alternative, many commuters still dont know about it, leaving them struggling to find affordable rides.

articleTitle: Virat Kohli refutes claim he visited Premanand Ji Maharaj for Rs 5 cr: ‘Out of deep faith’
