articleTitle: Rules for body-worn cameras by cops: Court asks Centre to decide in 6 months
articleFeaturedImageAlt: delhi police
description: The Delhi High Court refused to pass any directions on a PIL seeking an SOP on such cameras used by police personnel
body_raw: The Delhi High Court Wednesday refused to issue directions on a public interest litigation PIL seeking a standard operating procedure SOP for use of body-worn cameras by police personnel. It, instead, directed the government to consider the plea as a representation and take a decision on it within six months. A bench of Acting Chief Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Arun Bhardwaj was hearing the PIL by advocate Chahat Raghav. The lawyer sought an SOP on use of body-worn cameras by the Delhi Police, its operation, and the memory and storage of data collected through such cameras. Senior advocate Akhil Sibal, representing the petitioner, argued, There has to be an SOP, until there is some sort of law. it is different from facial recognition technology which has concerns about surveillance, profiling, privacy. if we have a mechanism or defined way of using it, then it will go a long way in addressing some of these concerns. Time and again, we are left with allegations and counter allegations. The question is ultimately of accountability. body-worn cameras are used, but it is all sporadic, no SOP, no chain of custody, preservation or access. Purpose is to rather than having this chaos. there has to be some way for accountability.There has to be some procedure that needs to be laid down, it will benefit the whole process, Sibal added. He also referred to media reports stating that amid allegations of police excesses during the SIR protests, Delhi Police and Rapid Action Force RAF deployed at the protest site have been issued directions to wear body cameras. Meanwhile, Additional Solicitor General ASG Chetan Sharma, representing the Centre, suggested to the court that the PIL can be treated as a representation. Sibal resisted the proposition, urging that it is not the governments case that they are unaware of the use of body-worn cameras. He urged, Let them place some reply before the court. representation will serve no purpose, its not something that they are not aware of. The court recorded in its order, The use of body-worn cameras by police can be inferred from not only tender issued but also use of the same by the traffic police. The SOP is informed to not be in existence. In such an event, there might not be any provision in the police manual. However, since the statement is made from ASG, we deem it appropriate to take the same on record. We direct the respondents to communicate the decision on framing of SOP regarding use of body-worn cameras within six months.

articleTitle: World Bank ranks India among top 10 in AI readiness
articleFeaturedImageAlt: AI
description: India among top 10 emerging markets in AI readiness: The World Bank report titled 'India and Artificial Intelligence: Seizing the Development Opportunity, ' released in October 2026, ranked India among the top 10 emerging-market performers in AI readiness.
body_raw: World Bank Ranks India Among Top 10 in AI ReadinessThe World Bank Group has recently released a report titled India and Artificial Intelligence Seizing the Development Opportunity under the India Development Update IDU. According to the World Banks latest report, India has emerged among the top 10 leading emerging-market performers in artificial intelligence AI readiness, supported by its large technical workforce, globally integrated IT sector and digital public infrastructure. Recent developments in Indias economy place it in a medium-term and global context. The report also suggested that even though aggregate long-term impacts remain uncertain, existing analysis shows that labour market substitution risks are lower than in advanced economies so far due to a smaller share of cognitive jobs, with significant potential for productivity jobs. According to the World Bank, AI holds significant promise for enhancing productivity and transforming public service delivery in India. However, the institution noted that the technologys long-term effects on employment and overall economic stability remain uncertain. To reach its full capacity, the report suggested that this can only occur through broadening AI adoption beyond large urban firms, building worker capabilities, strengthening infrastructure, leveraging AI in public services, and establishing adaptive governance frameworks. Private AI investment in India soared to 4.1 billion 36,231.7 crore in 2025, more than triple the previous year, reflecting surging investor confidence in the nations tech ecosystem. At the same time, employment across Indias Global Capability Centres expanded to 2.36 million, prompting the World Bank to note AIs potential for driving development while cautioning over its uncertain long-term impact on labour markets. A policy research working paper titled Beyond the AI Divide A Simple Approach to Identifying Globaland Local Overperformers in AI Preparedness, published by the World Bank, notes that in the landscape of the global AI Divide, nations perform along three distinct economic tiers.At the top, high-income economies such as Singapore and the United States dominate global rankings through deep capital and mature regulatory frameworks. Below them, upper-middle-income countries such as China and Malaysia act as regional tech gateways that weaponize state infrastructure to rapidly scale compute power. Meanwhile, lower-income economies such as India and Rwanda go beyond their economic weight, defying resource constraints through aggressive policies, massive engineering talent, and digital public infrastructure to close the gap. A core team of analysts, including Ran Li, Vincent Tsoungui Belinga, Aurlien Kruse, Tanvir Malik, Naresh Kumar, Mohini Gupta, Utz Johann Pape, Ayago Esmubancha Wambile, and Nishtha Kochhar, authored the report under the guidance of World Bank leads Hoon Sahib Soh, Sebastian Eckardt, and Paul Procee.

articleTitle: Why does a university in Gujarat celebrate Gandhi Jayanti on Oct 7?
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Mahatma Gandhi spinning the charkha, a symbol of Swadeshi, self-reliance and resistance to British rule (Wikimedia Commons)
description: Gujarat Vidyapith, which the Mahatma established in Ahmedabad in 1920, celebrates ‘Rentiya Baras’ every year – Gandhi’s birthday in accordance with the Vikram Samvat. This Oct 7, it took the charkha to 350-odd schools across Ahmedabad.
body_raw: Five days after the people and government of India observed Gandhi Jayanti, the university the Mahatma founded in Ahmedabad celebrated his birthday on Wednesday October 7. Gujarat Vidyapith traditionally observes Gandhijis birthday in accordance with the Hindu Vikram calendar. As part of this years celebration, it took the charkha to around 350 municipal schools across Ahmedabad to spread Gandhijis message of swadeshi. When was Gandhiji born according to the Hindu calendar? Gandhi was born on Bhadarva Vad Baras, that is, the 12th day dwadashi of the sixth month of the Hindu lunisolar calendar, known as Bhadrapada, in the year 1925 of the Vikram Samvat, which corresponds to October 2, 1869 of the Gregorian calendar-the date universally recognised as his birthday. The Vikram Samvat, which is used by many Hindus to determine the dates of religious rituals and festivals and for making astrological calculations, started in 57 BCE-that is, 57 years before the Gregorian calendar, which is the standard international civil dating system in use around the world. 2026 corresponds primarily to Vikram Samvat 2083, which began on March 19-20 of this year. The official Indian national calendar follows the Shaka Samvat, which began in 78CE. The Gujarat Vidyapith has been celebrating Gandhis birthday by the Hindu Vikram Samvat calendar as Rentiya Baras for the past 90 years. Why is the Mahatmas birthday called Rentiya Baras? Rentiya means spinning wheel in Gujarati, which Gandhi used to spin khadi. He had wanted to dedicate his birthday to the charkha, and desired that the day should be celebrated as Rentiya Baras. Ravindra Pancholi, associate professor of Social Work at Gujarat Vidyapith, told The Indian Express When a demand was raised by his Gandhis followers to celebrate his birthday, Gandhiji said that he did not like it, and that this day his birthday according to the Vikram Samvat could instead be observed as Rentiya Baras. So, from around 1929-30 began this tradition of celebrating Gandhis birthday as per the Vikram Samvat calendar as Rentiya Baras, and not as Mohan Jayanti or Gandhi Jayanti, Pancholi 55, who is grandson of the late Gujarati writer and educationist Manubhai Pancholi Darshak, said. Why did Gandhi want to use the imagery of the charkha? For Gandhi, the charkha or spinning wheel was the most potent symbol of Indian self-reliance. He saw the charkha as an instrument of economic, political, and moral resistance against the British. Gandhi first wrote about the symbolism of the charkha in Hind Swaraj in 1909. After he started living in the Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad in 1917, he started to experiment with spinning and weaving by hand, and promoted khadi hand-spun, hand-woven cloth as an alternative to cloth made in the mills of Lancashire in Britain. Gandhi saw khadi and the charkha as a path to Indian self-sufficiency and non-violent resistance to colonialism. Besides the political and economic imperative of Swadeshi, he also encouraged the act of spinning to promote the dignity of labour and to identify with the poor. How has the Gujarat Vidyapith taken this message forward on Gandhis birthday? As part of the Non-Cooperation Movement that he launched in August 1920, Gandhi called for a boycott of schools and colleges under the control of the British government. In opposition to Lord Macaulays colonial education system that worked to sustain the interests of Empire, Indian nationalists established five Vidyapiths to provide anti-colonial education to Indian youth. Gujarat Vidyapith, which was founded on October 18, 1920 by the Mahatma himself, was one of these five Vidyapiths. Today, it is one of the national universities with a charter from the Government of India and seeks to promote Gandhijis ideals of service-oriented education, the Gujarat Vidyapith says on its website. To this end, the university has been celebrating Rentiya Baras in different ways every year, Advaita Dave, Public Relations Officer of the Vidyapith, said. Last year, our staff and students spun charkha at the Sabarmati Riverfront for around an hour and a half. Apart from Swadeshi, the idea was to spread the message that spinning the charkha is a kind of yoga as well, which helps one to improve concentration, Dave said. Pancholi said that in earlier years, students of the Vidyapith have taken part in Akhand Kantan or non-stop spinning on the occasion of Rentiya Baras, taking turns to spin the charkha continuously for 12 hours in batches of 20-25, with each batch spinning for two hours. What happened on Rentiya Baras this year? The Gujarat Vidyapith organised a special program on October 7 to take Gandhis ideals of Swadeshi, self-reliance and khadi to students of schools run by Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation. Around 200 volunteers and more than 1,800 students of Gujarat Vidyapith will visit 351 schools across 48 wards of Ahmedabad city. They will demonstrate the spinning wheel before school students and explain its significance, along with Mahatma Gandhis ideas of Swadeshi and self-reliance. Through this program, the message of the spinning wheel will reach more than 1,35,000 students, the Vidyapith said in a statement issued ahead of Rentiya Baras.

articleTitle: Amid Rahul & Priyanka’s ‘Sting’ moment, PepsiCo gets court relief
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Rahul, Priyanka Sting
description: Granting temporary relief, the Delhi High Court stayed the FSSAI’s order against PepsiCo over use of the “Energy Drink” label for its products
body_raw: During Tuesdays INDIA bloc protest, Rahul Gandhi offered his sister Priyanka a red drink. She looked at it with suspicion, sniffed it, and took a small sip. The video of the exchange went viral, prompting speculation that the drink was PepsiCos Sting. The viral moment came on the same day the Delhi High Court gave the beverage firm temporary relief in a case concerning Sting. On Tuesday, PepsiCo India Holdings Private Ltd and Monster Energy India Private Limited were before the court to seek an interim stay on the Food Safety and Standards Authority of Indias order to the two companies to discontinue using the energy drink description for its products. The products included PepsiCos Adrenaline Rush Energy Drink-Ultimate Performance and Sting Energy, and Monster Indias Monster Energy and Predator Energy. The food regulator had issued the order on the ground that using energy drink as a label for the product constitutes misbranding and misleading. Justice Amit Mahajan, on October 6, stayed the FSSAIs June 30 order against the two companies covering the four products, along with any consequential action taken by the regulator. The court noted that the order had been passed without issuing a show-cause notice to the beverage makers or giving them an opportunity to be heard. It also sought responses from the Health Ministry and the regulator and listed the matter for November 5. Last month, Red Bull India Pvt Ltd had approached the court with a similar grievance. It, too, was directed by the FSSAI to discontinue using the energy drink description for its caffeinated products. The HC had stayed the FSSAI action on similar grounds. The three companies argued that their products fall under the relevant food category and that the regulator had previously clarified that they could use the term Energy Drink. They contended that the regulator could not take a somersault and subsequently state that use of the term could amount to misbranding.

articleTitle: Mumbai civic body cracks down on tax defaulters, puts Imperial Grand Palace Hotel up for auction
articleFeaturedImageAlt: imperial grand palace
description: This will be the first time since 1984 that the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) has auctioned attached properties to recover pending tax dues.
body_raw: In a major move to recover tax dues and boost revenue, the Mumbai civic body has put three commercial Mumbai properties, including the famous Imperial Grand Palace Hotel at the Royal Palms in Aarey Forest, up for auction. This will be the first time since 1984 that the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation BMC has auctioned attached properties to recover pending tax dues. This is also the first time the BMC has attached a property linked to the contentious Royal Palms project to recover property tax. In total, the BMC will be auctioning three properties to recover Rs 74.98 crore. According to civic records, the Imperial Grand Palace Hotel auction shall recover pending dues of Rs 41.52 crore. The Royal Palms project, a contentious project that took off in the 1990s, aimed to transform a portion of the Aarey Forest into a luxury venue for leisure activities by constructing a chain of hotels, restaurants and a golf course. The project, however, nosedived after the properties got entangled in several financial cases. The current outstanding tax from this property stands at Rs 41.52 crore. The proprietors have been sent multiple notices, and we have had meetings with them. However, despite multiple deliberations, they have failed to pay the pending dues. Therefore, we have attached the property and will be putting it up for auction soon, a civic official told The Indian Express. The property has a carpet area of 38,143 square meters and has 422 rooms. It is located in a quaint corner of the Aarey Forest. The Imperial Palace was a five-star hotel listed as part of the Royal Palms project. In the early 2000s, this hotel was a preferred venue for luxurious activities however, its popularity dwindled after 2012. At present, the property lies unused and in a dilapidated state. Civic officials said the last conference recorded in this hotel was in 2012. Besides this hotel, the civic body will auction another commercial property in Malad Kurar for Rs 3.46 crore and another in Bandra for Rs 30.6 crore. In February, civic authorities attached 12 properties to recover pending dues up to Rs 269.62 crore. Civic officials said that after these properties were listed, some of their owners reached out and settled their claims while the remaining owners approached the court. The civic body put them up for auction after the owners of these three properties didnt make any effort to save them. Of the 12 properties that were listed, management of six properties settled the bill while six properties are still listed as default subjects. Of these six properties, two are open land parcels. Since the court has ordered us to revise the existing method of calculating the tax rate on land, we will be sending them a fresh bill. One of the remaining owners approached the court, and the case is sub judice. As a result, we will be putting out these three properties for auction, the official said. The civic authorities levy property tax on all real estate and commercial properties located within the BMC jurisdiction. Once the property owners default on paying taxes, the civic authorities send them notices, adding penalties. If owners still do not pay the taxes, these properties are seized or attached temporarily and put up for auction after legal proceedings. Property tax is one of the highest sources of revenue for the BMC, and this year, it has collected Rs 7,611 crore against an annual target of Rs 7,341 crore till March 31.

articleTitle: Rate hike: Behind the RBI’s pivot, a need to safeguard price stability
articleFeaturedImageAlt: rbi rate hike
description: The interaction between persistent supply shocks and strong demand warrants particular attention. Economic history suggests that when supply-driven price pressures coincide with robust growth, inflation often broadens beyond a narrow set of categories
body_raw: The shift in stance by the RBIs Monetary Policy Committee MPC, accompanied by a rate hike in its October review, was hardly unexpected. Monetary policy is shaped principally by domestic growth and inflation dynamics, with global developments playing a secondary role. Recent developments on both fronts increasingly pointed towards a recalibration of policy. This year was marked by an unusual combination of shocks and uncertainties. Yet, despite the conflict in West Asia and unresolved tariff-related turbulence, Indias economy has remained remarkably resilient. Growth has stayed robust, while inflation, particularly core inflation, has thus far been relatively contained. However, the balance of risks has begun to shift. Since the MPCs August review, upside risks to inflation have become more pronounced. Three factors stand out. First, the conflict in West Asia, marked by repeated cycles of escalation and de-escalation, has kept commodity markets volatile. Recent developments have pushed up crude prices again, with the Indian crude basket, as estimated by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell, returning to its April peak. Reflecting this, we now expect crude prices to average 88-93 per barrel this fiscal, compared with our earlier forecast of 82-87 per barrel. Even if geopolitical tensions ease, crude prices may remain elevated as damaged infrastructure is repaired and depleted inventories rebuilt. In such a scenario, another round of pass-through to domestic petrol and diesel prices appears likely. While higher pump prices could temper demand and ease pressure on oil marketing companies, they would also raise inflation through both direct and indirect channels. Food inflation represents a second major source of vulnerability. Food prices are the most volatile component of Indias inflation basket, and recent increases reflect both base effects and emerging supply concerns. To be sure, the relationship between monsoons and food inflation is not linear. Not every rainfall-deficient year has led to higher food inflation, and the governments free food programme for nearly 800 million people, alongside healthy rice buffer stocks, provides an important cushion. Nevertheless, the 2026 monsoon has ended with rainfall 13 per cent below the long-period average and over 42 per cent of districts in India classified as deficient. More importantly, the problem extends beyond the aggregate shortfall. The spatial distribution and timing of rainfall have been particularly unfavourable, making this one of the most disrupted monsoon seasons of the past decade. The implications extend beyond the current kharif season. Weak monsoons can impair rabi production by reducing soil moisture and reservoir levels. As of October 1, reservoir storage was 12.2 per cent below normal and 20.4 per cent lower than a year earlier. Crisils Deficient Rainfall Impact Parameter DRIP points to broad-based stress, with cotton, tur and bajra among the most vulnerable crops. Intensifying El Nino conditions, combined with supply disruptions linked to the West Asia conflict, are exerting upward pressure on food prices worldwide. Particularly notable is edible oil inflation, driven by weather-related disruptions in Southeast Asia and rising biofuel demand. According to the World Meteorological Organisation, the probability of a strong El Nino extending into early 2027 is close to certainty, raising the risk of extreme weather events and supply disruptions. Given that India imports over 55 per cent of its edible oil requirements, elevated global prices and currency weakness continue to keep domestic edible oil inflation elevated at around 20 per cent. The impact of the monsoon on agricultural output and food prices, then, will remain one of the most important variables for policymakers to monitor this year. Inflation risks, however, are no longer confined to supply-side shocks. Demand-side pressures also appear stronger than previously anticipated. GDP growth in the first quarter was not only above trend but also exceeded previous expectations, and the second quarter is also doing well. Reflecting this momentum, the RBI has raised its growth forecast for this fiscal to 7.1 per cent from 6.7 per cent earlier. Crisil likewise expects growth of 7.0 per cent. The interaction between persistent supply shocks and strong demand warrants particular attention. Economic history suggests that when supply-driven price pressures coincide with robust growth, inflation often broadens beyond a narrow set of categories. Early signs of such generalisation are becoming visible in core inflation, with price pressures gradually spreading beyond food and fuel. Global developments reinforce the need for caution. Bond yields in advanced economies have risen much more sharply than in India, reflecting persistent inflation and growing concerns over fiscal sustainability. Consequently, the spread between US and Indian 10-year government bond yields has narrowed to roughly 200 basis points, compared with over 400 basis points a few years ago, reducing the relative attractiveness of Indian government securities for foreign investors. At the same time, major central banks remain in tightening mode. The US Federal Reserve raised rates by 25 basis points in September, and markets continue to price in further tightening. The European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan have also maintained a tightening bias in response to persistent inflation pressures. Indias liquidity situation adds another layer of complexity. The RBIs efforts to mobilise foreign currency non-resident deposits have been highly successful, strengthening foreign exchange reserves and improving balance-of-payments resilience. However, these inflows have also injected substantial liquidity into the financial system. Consequently, financial conditions eased through August, and liquidity remains abundant. This creates a degree of tension, albeit transitory, between prevailing monetary conditions and the tightening bias increasingly warranted by growth and inflation dynamics. Taken together, these developments explain the RBIs policy shift. Inflation risks are becoming more broad-based, growth remains resilient, global monetary conditions continue to tighten, and domestic liquidity remains ample. Policymakers will need to remain highly vigilant on price developments. While future actions will remain data-dependent, the possibility of another rate hike this year can no longer be ruled out. The writer is chief economist, Crisil

articleTitle: ‘80% NDA, 20% PDA’: Yogi Adityanath back with claim ahead of Assembly polls
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Yogi Adityanath 80-20 UP Assembly polls
description: Since the Samajwadi Party has not fielded a third candidate, there will be no contest between it and the BJP in the Rajya Sabha polls.
body_raw: After the Samajwadi Party SP decided not to field a third Rajya Sabha poll candidate from Uttar Pradesh, paving the way for the unopposed election of its two and the ruling BJPs eight candidates to the Upper House, Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath said on Wednesday that the state would again see an 80-20 fight in upcoming Assembly polls. Adityanath said in Lucknow that the Rajya Sabha elections would predict the Assembly election results. Yeh ladaai 8020 ki fir aa gai hai. 80 per cent NDA me, aur 20 per cent PDA me. Aur PDA ka kya haal hone wala hai, yeh aapke saamne fir aane wala hai The fight has again become 80 and 20. Eighty per cent in NDA and 20 per cent in PDA. PDAs fate will be before everyone, he said at the Seva Jyoti Yatra-Viksit Bharat Sankalp Sabha, which marks Prime Minister Narendra Modis completion of 25 years in elected office. Since the SP has not fielded a third candidate, there will be no contest between it and the BJP in the Rajya Sabha polls. The SP has renominated veteran leader Ram Gopal Yadav, uncle of party president Akhilesh Yadav, and fielded Reliance executive Dhanraj Nathwani as its second Rajya Sabha candidate. The party has enough strength in the Assembly to get its two candidates elected to Rajya Sabha. The SP chief first floated the abbreviation PDA-Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak backward classes, Dalits, and minorities-in June 2023. The formulation was projected as the SPs social coalition against the BJP-led NDA, with Akhilesh repeatedly claiming, PDA hi NDA ko harayega it is the PDA that will defeat the NDA. Ahead of the 2022 Assembly elections, Adityanath had remarked that the Assembly election contest would be an 80 per cent vs 20 per cent fight, with the 20 per cent interpreted as a reference to the population of the minorities in the state. Adityanath later defended his 80 vs 20 remark. In an interview with ANI, he said, Its a reaction to an action. I spoke about 80 vs 20. Eighty per cent support the Bharatiya Janata Party BJP, while 20 per cent always oppose. We havent spoken about caste or religion.

articleTitle: Rahul Gandhi detained again: How does detention differ from arrest, what rights do detainees have?
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi is detained at Akashvani Bhawan on Tuesday. (Gajendra Yadav)
description: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita does not define 'detention' per se. Instead, it gives police a set of powers that allows them to stop, remove or temporarily hold people in certain situations, including when a crime has actually taken place.
body_raw: Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi was detained on Wednesday October 7 as Opposition leaders protested in New Delhi demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Election Commissions Special Intensive Revision SIR exercise. This was the second time in as many days that the Congress leader had been detained - on Tuesday, too, he along with Opposition leaders including Priyanka Gandhi Vadra was taken into custody by Delhi Police after protesting for nearly eight hours inside Akashvani Bhavan in New Delhi. On Wednesday, before Gandhis latest detention, police had registered a case of trespass into the Akashvani Bhavan premises. Since October 2, Delhi police have detained hundreds of protesters, including Advocate Prashant Bhushan, and AISA national president Neha Bora. Legally speaking, what exactly is detention? How does it work? And what rights does law provide to police and detainees? How does detention differ from arrest? Police, under the law, are empowered to maintain law and order, particularly during protests and demonstrations. In practice, this may sometimes look like an arrest and at other times a detention, often because these terms are used interchangeably. Arrest is a formal act of police taking a person into custody in connection with an offence, marking the beginning of criminal proceedings. Once a person is arrested, a range of constitutional and statutory safeguards immediately come into play. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita or BNSS, which replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure or CrPC does not define detention per se. Instead, it gives police a set of powers that allows them to stop, remove or temporarily hold people in certain situations, including when a crime has actually taken place. This is why disputes arise after protests. Someone may be taken away by police, kept in custody for several hours, and released without any case being registered. To the person involved, it can feel very much like an arrest. Legally, however, police may say that they were exercising preventive powers rather than arresting the individual for an offence. Senior Advocate Sanjay Hegde drew a distinction between a formal arrest and the short-term custody often seen during protests. They are temporarily not allowed to leave wherever they are detained, and they are not put under a formal arrest either, he told The Indian Express. Advocate Soutik Banerjee told The Indian Express that the distinction is often used to avoid the scrutiny that accompanies a formal arrest. The police know that the power to arrest cannot be exercised casually when there is no cognizable offence punishable with more than seven years being committed by the protestors. If they are arrested, courts will come down heavily on them. That is why they choose to abduct people and release them within hours, he said. A cognizable offence is one for which police can arrest without a warrant. Section 170 of the BNSS allows preventive action before any offence is committed. A police officer, knowing of a design to commit any cognizable offence may arrest, without orders from a magistrate and without a warrant, the person so designing, if it appears to such officer that the commission of the offence cannot be otherwise prevented. Section 172 of the BNSS says that a police officer may detain or remove any person resisting, refusing, ignoring or disregarding a lawful direction. The officer must then take the person before a magistrate or, in petty cases, release them within 24 hours. Unlike the earlier CrPC, this provision expressly allows police to detain or remove a person who refuses to comply with a lawful direction. Section 1722 BNSS is new. The CrPC had no equivalent, Senior Advocate Hegde said. The CrPC let police prevent cognizable offences and arrest to prevent them. It did not bind citizens to obey police directions, nor let police detain those who refused. Section 172 adds both. The idea came from state police statutes, not the CrPC. The 24-hour limit was itself a late addition. He added that the law on safeguards applicable to such short-term detentions remains largely untested no short-term detention and the consequences of not following safeguards have been litigated up to the Supreme Court. This position is different from preventive detention which allows a person to be held without trial under special laws such as the National Security Act. Banerjee said that the practice of briefly taking protesters into custody should not be confused with preventive detention powers under the law. He said This so-called detention has no place in law and is wholly illegal. Of course there are preventive detention powers available, but they are subject to strict rigours of the law and cannot be casually applied spontaneously. None of the abductions and excursions to Narela or Kingsway Camp in buses is carried out under legal provisions for preventive detention. When can police detain people? Most protest-related detentions begin with a claim that police are trying to prevent a law and order problem. Often, there is already a prohibitory order in place. On October 2, the Delhi Police imposed Section 163 of the BNSS across New Delhi. If protestors refuse to disperse or continue activities prohibited by such an order, police may invoke preventive powers to remove them from the spot or hold them temporarily. Disobeying such an order is itself an offence under Section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita or BNS, which replaced the Indian Penal Code or IPC. That is the point at which a detention can turn into an arrest with an FIR first information report. Courts have, however, said that such actions cannot be arbitrary. Police must be able to explain why restricting a persons liberty was necessary. The Supreme Court, in Joginder Kumar v State of UP 1994 held that the existence of the power to arrest is one thing and the justification for the exercise of it is quite another. In Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar 2014, the court told police not to arrest automatically in offences punishable up to seven years. In Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v Union of India 2018 the court held that restrictions on protests should be regulatory rather than eliminating the right to protest altogether. What rights does a detained or an arrested person have? Once the state restricts a persons liberty, a number of protections become relevant. Article 22 is a fundamental right under the Constitution that deals with protection of an accused against arrest and detention. It requires production of an accused person before a magistrate within 24 hours information about the grounds of arrest and the right to have legal representation. The Supreme Court, in multiple cases, has held that written grounds of arrest must be furnished. Just last month, the court held that if an arrest violates the safeguards prescribed under Article 22, it would be unconstitutional. Article 221 also provides for the right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of ones choice. Section 38 BNSS allows an arrested person to meet an advocate of his choice during interrogation, though not throughout interrogation. If a person cannot afford a lawyer, free legal aid is provided to them at the States cost. Section 435 of the BNSS bars the arrest of a woman between sunrise and sunset, except in exceptional circumstances and with the prior permission of a judicial magistrate. The Supreme Court in DK Basu v. State of West Bengal 1997 laid down safeguards for all cases of arrest or detention. Officers must wear visible name tags. An arrest memo must be attested by at least one witness. Injuries must be recorded, and family members should be informed. The court also made clear that these safeguards are not merely advisory and officers who fail to comply can face departmental action or even contempt proceedings.

articleTitle: 22-year marriage not consummated, Calcutta High Court grants divorce, Rs 10 lakh alimony
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Calcutta High Court marriage divorce consummate alimony
description: The husband claimed before the Calcutta High Court that the marriage was never consummated as the wife allegedly said that she was not interested in physical intimacy.
body_raw: The Calcutta High Court recently granted divorce to a man after a 22-year marriage that was never consummated and directed him to pay Rs 10 lakh as permanent alimony to his wife. The court noted that the couple lived together as husband and wife for barely a month after their marriage in 2004 and separated after that, barring a brief period when they were required to stay together by a court order. Justices Debangsu Basak and Aryak Dutt held that the marriage was not consummated and that there was no valid reason or evidence of physical incapacity preventing consummation. There is no valid reason for the marriage not being consummated. There is no material on record suggesting that any of the parties were incapable of consummating the marriage. The materials on record suggest that they voluntarily withdrew from the society of the other, the October 5 order read. Lived together for 1 month The man claimed that the couple married in April 2004, but allegedly never consummated the marriage, and they started living separately after the wife left the house within one month. The husband later filed a divorce case on the grounds of cruelty and desertion in July 2016. He said that his wife refused to consummate the marriage, saying that she was not interested in intercourse because her figure would become shapeless and nobody would notice her after that. The mans counsel, advocate Kaushal Paul, submitted that there was an interim period in which the parties were required to live as husband and wife in the wake of an order of the high court. He added that the couple, however, never cohabited and neither was the marriage consummated during that period. The husband did not reside at the house with the wife at the time, the counsel added. On the contrary, the woman, through advocate Prantick Ghosh, argued that the husband did not give any particulars of her alleged cruelty. He also stated that the husband had not given particulars of the dates of the alleged non-consummation of the marriage. No amicable settlement The high court noted that the marriage was proved to have not been consummated and that the wife had admitted in her cross-examination that there had been no cohabitation between the couple. It also mentioned having made efforts to help the couple arrive at an amicable resolution of their disputes, but they could not agree to settle the same. The bench acknowledged that both lawyers tried their best to help the parties arrive at an amicable settlement and went out of their way in the process. The bench found that there was an irretrievable breakdown of marriage. The cruelty which was occasioned in the facts and circumstances of the present case emanates out of denial of conjugal rights and non-consummation of marriage, it added. The court also considered the assets available to the husband and found it appropriate to grant permanent alimony of Rs 10 lakh, payable in four monthly instalments starting November 15, 2026. It noted that the wife was gainfully employed.

articleTitle: Bengaluru gym trainer likely died of strangulation after party: Police
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Bengaluru gym trainer death
description: The police on Monday arrested three fellow gym trainers who were with the victim on Saturday night
body_raw: A preliminary investigation into the death of a gym trainer in North Bengaluru early on Sunday suggested that the 25-year-old man allegedly died of strangulation following a violent altercation with three other gym trainers in the bathroom of a flat, the police said on Wednesday. However, the police are awaiting the final post-mortem report to establish the precise cause of death of M Nandan, who worked at Masiv Gym in Sahakaranagar. The police on Monday arrested three fellow gym trainers - Vishwanath, 22, Sharath, 27, and Nishanth, 24, who were with Nandan at the flat on Saturday night - and booked them for murder. According to police sources, a group of four gym trainers, including Nandan, gathered at a flat in Kempapura following the gyms first anniversary celebrations on Saturday, where they reportedly consumed alcohol and drugs. Investigators suspect the men were heavily intoxicated when an altercation broke out inside the bathroom, escalating into a physical brawl. The police noted broken mirrors and fittings in the bathroom, along with injuries on the victim and the accused. Nandan sustained injuries to his face, while the other trainers also had injuries to their hands and knees, said an officer. Nandan was also found to have several bite marks on different parts of his body. The police are examining the injuries to determine how and when they were caused. Prima facie, authorities suspect Nandan died of strangulation, though final post-mortem and forensic reports are awaited. The police said Nandan was seriously injured after the fight but was not taken to hospital immediately. The men allegedly remained at the flat and attempted to pacify the situation. Nandan subsequently lost consciousness and was taken to hospital, where he was declared dead. Anush Shetty, owner of the flat where the gathering was held, was among those initially detained. The police have issued him a notice for inquiry and are examining his role in the incident. Gym trainers version A senior police officer said the accused gave investigators their account of what happened inside the bathroom. According to their version, Nandan vomited in the bathroom and suffered seizures, and that the injuries and bite marks occurred while attempting to prevent him from biting his tongue-a claim police are verifying against medical evidence. They have told us that Nandan was attempting to bite his tongue, and that they tried to prevent him from doing so by slapping and biting him, the officer said. Police rule out sexual act angle The police are also examining an allegation that Nandan and one of the men may have been involved in a sexual act during the gathering. However, investigators have not found evidence so far to establish that a sexual act took place, a senior police official said. The bite marks and other injuries are being examined as part of the investigation, but the police have not established that they were connected to any sexual activity. The police are also awaiting forensic reports, including the results of samples collected from the accused, to establish whether they had consumed narcotic substances and to corroborate their account of the incident. The arrested men are being questioned to establish the sequence of events inside the flat. The flat owner has told police that he was sleeping in another room and woke up later in the morning, when he found Nandan injured and unconscious. He then contacted a doctor and called an ambulance.

articleTitle: Blood on his face, legs tied: Man found dead in Kolkata cab
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Kolkata cab driver death, Kolkata cab driver murder, Entally cab driver death, Kolkata cab driver found dead, Entally murder case, Kolkata crime news, Entally crime news, Kolkata cab murder probe, Indian Express news, Kolkata news, Kolkata police news
description: The Kolkata police suspect the body and cab may have been dumped in Entally after he was killed elsewhere, but are probing all angles.
body_raw: A cab parked by the roadside in central Kolkatas Entally area drew residents attention Wednesday morning when repeated calls to the occupant went unanswered. When the police arrived and found the vehicle locked from the inside, they called a mechanic to break open the door. Inside was the body of a man with blood marks on his face and both legs tied with a rope. According to police sources, officers traced the vehicles registration number and contacted the app company to identify the man. The man was subsequently identified as Bhagwan Prasad Gupta, 45, the vehicles driver, said a source. The discovery has raised suspicion that Gupta may have been murdered, although the police are yet to officially confirm the cause of death. Officers from Entally Police Station recovered the body and sent it for an autopsy. Officers from the Homicide Section and the Intelligence Branch at Lalbazar, Kolkata Police headquarters, also visited the spot and collected evidence. CCTV, booking history The police said they are examining how and when Gupta died and whether he was killed inside the cab or elsewhere before his body was brought to Entally. Investigators are checking CCTV footage from the area to establish a timeline and identify people who may have entered or travelled in the cab. They are also examining the vehicles booking history and contacting the app company to determine Guptas last passenger, where the cab travelled after the last ride, and its last known location. The police suspect, as one possibility, that Gupta may have been killed elsewhere and that his body and the cab were later abandoned at the Entally location. Investigators are probing this and other possible explanations. According to police sources, investigators are also contacting Guptas family, relatives, and friends to establish his movements Tuesday night, including who he was last seen with and whether he had any known personal disputes or enmity.

articleTitle: Bethlehem Kudumba Unit effect: Arvind Swamy-Sridevi’s shelved film to be revived after decades
articleFeaturedImageAlt: After 'Yavanakathayil' went viral in Bethlehem Kudumba Unit, Joshiy's shelved film Anna is set for revival.
description: After 'Yavanakathayil' went viral in Bethlehem Kudumba Unit, producer Tomichan Mulakuppadam has acquired the rights to revive director Joshiy's shelved film Anna, originally starring Arvind Swamy and Sridevi.
body_raw: Movies getting shelved isnt a new phenomenon in Malayalam cinema. From Randamoozham, Swarnachamaram, Australia, and Karnan to Dhanushkodi, Kaaliyan, and Antichrist, several films never progressed beyond the initial stages. Recently, director Girish ADs blockbuster romantic comedy Bethlehem Kudumba Unit brought one such film, Anna, back into the spotlight. Now, the movie is finally set for revival, with a new team taking over. Veteran producer Tomichan Mulakuppadam - best known for bankrolling blockbusters such as Pulimurugan, Pokkiri Raja, and Ramaleela - recently announced he has acquired the rights to Anna and is gearing up to give it a new lease of life. Taking to social media, he expressed his elation at the endeavour and stated he would announce the cast and crew details later. Also Read No one is to blame Kalaranjini lost her voice after consuming fake blood containing acid Tomichan Mulakuppadam acquires rights to shelved film Anna I am happy to share that I have acquired the rights to the film Anna, which started in the 1990s but was shelved for various reasons. Years later, when the song Yavanakathayil from the film became a sensation again through Bethlehem Kudumba Unit, there were many enquiries and discussions about Anna, he wrote. Tomichan added, It is with the desire to bring the story and associated memories of that film to the new generation through new writers that I have taken over the production rights of Anna. A new beginning for a film that stopped midway three decades ago. More details, including the director and cast, will be announced later. Anna is coming back to the silver screen through Mulakuppadam Films. What happened to Anna? For the unversed, master filmmaker Joshiy was set to helm the film in the 90s, with Arvind Swamy and superstar Sridevi in the lead roles. According to Onmanorama, veteran writer and novelist N Mohanan originally scripted Anna, and Balram of Ambu Films was supposed to produce it. The movie centred on the love story of Hari Arvind Swamy, a Brahmin boy, and Anna Sridevi, a Christian girl. Anna was envisioned with music given the utmost prominence, and legendary composer Ouseppachan and veteran lyricist Shibu Chakravarthy were brought on board for the same. They crafted eight songs for Anna and completed their recordings even before the filming began. ICYMI Fahadh Faasil says wont get half of Rs 300 cr as Bethlehem Kudumba Unit earns Rs 326 cr However, the project soon ran into scheduling problems, as the makers couldnt match the dates of Arvind Swamy and Sridevi. Team Anna even considered replacing Sridevi with Meena. Yet, Arvind Swamys availability remained an issue, further delaying the project. Joshiy also had other movies lined up. Thus, Anna was shelved without any of its scenes being filmed. Nevertheless, the movies music found its way to the public in 1995 when Magna Sound released a cassette containing all eight songs recorded for Anna. Yavanakathayil was one of those songs, which director Girish AD included in Bethlehem Kudumba Unit, allowing Anna to rise from the ashes like a phoenix. Must Read Bethlehem Kudumba Unit review Nivin Pauly leads a sweet, non-creepy age-gap rom-com About Bethlehem Kudumba Unit Featuring Nivin Pauly and Mamitha Baiju in the lead roles, Bethlehem Kudumba Unit opened to rave reviews and emerged as the highest-grossing Malayalam film of all time, earning Rs 330.89 crore worldwide, according to industry tracker Sacnilk. Also starring Sangeeth Prathap, Suresh Krishna, Vinay Forrt, Roshan Shanavas, and Shyam Mohan, the romantic comedy was bankrolled by Dileesh Pothan, Fahadh Faasil, and Syam Pushkaran under the banner of Bhavana Studios.

articleTitle: Mobile phone bursts inside man’s pocket, consumer commission grants Rs 41,139
articleFeaturedImageAlt: mobile phone consumer court
description: The commission held that there was no rebuttal to the complainant's allegations and said that the mobile phone was defective and there was deficiency in service.
body_raw: A consumer commission in Uttar Pradesh recently directed a mobile phone manufacturer and a local electronics retailer to either replace a mobile phone or refund its cost after the phone allegedly burst inside a mans pocket in 2023, causing injury. President Hasnain Qureshi and member Purnima Singh Rajpoot also directed the opposite parties to pay compensation of Rs 36,139 and Rs 5,000 as litigation expenses. As there is no rebuttal of the pleadings of the complainant and therefore it is held that the mobile set was defective and there was deficiency in service, the order read. Phone burst According to the complainant, he purchased the mobile phone for Rs 29,500 in 2020. He alleged that the phone started heating up. After he complained, he was allegedly told that such heating sometimes occurred. After he complained, he was allegedly told that such heating sometimes happens. The phone allegedly heated up again, but his complaint to the local retailer was allegedly ignored. The complainant said that the phone burst while inside his pocket, injuring his thumb. He then lodged a police complaint. The complainant further alleged that the incident damaged photographs and videos from his marriage. He claimed that he was hospitalised after learning about the damage and that he and his wife had to hold another marriage celebration and arrange fresh photography and videography. He sought Rs 51 lakh towards the expenses of recreating the marriage ceremony and Rs 48 lakh as compensation for the shock, depression and treatment he claimed to have suffered. His total claim was Rs 99.29 lakh, though he restricted it to Rs 50 lakh citing the commissions pecuniary jurisdiction. The manufacturer filed its response beyond the prescribed period, which the commission said was of no importance, while the local retailer did not contest the case. The commission held that there was no rebuttal to the complainants allegations and concluded that the mobile phone was defective and there was deficiency in service. It noted that the complainant remained hospitalised and incurred Rs 36,139 in treatment expenses, as supported by the medical records. The commission directed the opposite parties to either replace the mobile phone with a new one or refund Rs 29,500. It also awarded Rs 36,139 towards medical expenses and Rs 5,000 as litigation costs. Takeaway Manufacturers and sellers can be held liable when a defective mobile phone causes injury to a consumer. Where the defect and resulting loss are not rebutted, consumer commissions can order replacement or refund of the product and award compensation for proven medical expenses and litigation costs. For consumer-related grievances, individuals may contact the consumer helpline in their respective states and union territories Uttar Pradesh helpline 1800180030 or call the National Consumer Helpline at 1915 for assistance.
