articleTitle: Hamas calculus, Israel’s gamble: How October 7 reshaped the region, 3 years on
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Hamas
description: Why did Hamas plan the attack, and three years later, where do Israel and Palestine stand? An Expert Explains.
body_raw: On October 7, 2023, a Hamas-led attack in Israel killed around 1,200 people, while 251 were taken hostage. Israels response in the three years since has utterly devasted Gaza and sparked off three other linked wars in Iran, Lebanon, and Yemen. Why did Hamas plan the attack, and three years later, where do Israel and Palestine stand? The Hamas attack on October 7, 2023 UN investigations detail that the complex attack comprised an assault from the land, sea, and air in conjunction with the launch of a large-scale rocket and mortar attack towards cities, towns and villages and military bases in southern and central Israel. Executed across the day, the October 7 operation also saw attacks on several Israeli kibbutzim and the Nova music festival, assaults on Israeli beaches and arterial roads, and triggered the evacuation of nearly 150,000 people from their homes. Three years since, all Hamas-held hostages both dead and alive have been released, with the last batch of releases occurring as a result of a US-induced January 2025 ceasefire. On the other hand, Israels continuing military offensive in Gaza since October 2023 has killed over 70,000 Palestinians by conservative estimates, with Israeli actions characterised as a genocide by several states and human rights agencies, as well as a UN Commission of Inquiry. Israel is presently headed into its first elections since the attack, with the countrys longest-serving PM, Benjamin Netanyahu, seeking yet another term. What was Hamas strategic logic for October 7? Hamas October 7 attack occurred when it did as a result of two specific strategic conditions. First, in the 15 years before October 2023, Israels security calculus vis-a-vis Hamas had settled into a quiet for quiet approach. Besides the broader strategic goal of repelling Israeli occupation, Hamas own focus with Israel prioritised sub-strategic goals such as the lifting of Israels stringent economic blockade on Gaza since 2007 and the release of over 5000 Palestinian prisoners in Israel. There were new unwritten rules of the game in both IDF and Hamas parlance, which would be determined by acceptable and unacceptable acts. Moreover, Hamas own ability to deter a large Israeli offensive in Gaza had been proven by its intense exchanges of rocket fire most prominently for 51 days in 2014. By 2018, Hamas abilities to threaten hinterland Israeli targets had grown sufficiently for its leader Yahya Sinwar to assert that whatever rockets hit Tel Aviv for 51 days in 2024, would be launched within five minutes if Israel carried out any offensive. Since 2018, Israel had also let conditional aid trickle into Gaza as a result of negotiations with Hamas through Egypt, further contributing to Hamas perceptions of a vindication of its posture. This balance was sustained by an Israeli political interest in playing off Hamas against Fatah in the West Bank especially under Netanyahu, who fiercely defended allowing Qatari financial sustainment of Hamas across 2019 and 2020 as necessary to prevent the creation of a Palestinian state. Even hard-right politicians such as Bezalel Smotrich presently Israels Finance Minister and West Bank administrator argued in 2015 that Hamas is an asset, and Abu Mazen Mahmoud Abbas of Fatah is a burden. Second, Israels approach to removing the possibility of a Palestinian state alongside an expansion of its settlement project in the West Bank had taken on a regional character especially since 2020. Both the Abraham Accords of that year as well as subsequent Arab signaling of a de-prioritisation of the Palestinian issue brought the fundamental logic of resistance back to Hamas. Hence, as far as six months before October 7, Hamas then second-in-command Saleh al-Arouri had publicly declared that Palestinians had between two to three years before Israeli settlers in the West Bank increased to two million, making a decisive, multi-front war necessary in the near term. A more specific window of opportunity was created due to Israels then ongoing domestic crisis featuring a tussle between the Netanyahu-led executive and the judiciary. This logic was supplemented by Hamas having increasingly integrated itself into Irans Axis of Resistance. But this architectures functioning was complicated. Irans Axis was built on a non-sectarian strategic logic but with deterrence and not war as the principal objective a regional threat-in-being to counter Israels own regional approach to countering Iran. It became categorically evident on October 7 that Hamas wrested agency from the rest of the Axis, most of whom were then faced with a now or never scenario to fulfill their long-standing objective of defeating the Israeli state. However, even as Hezbollah became the only principal Shia force that initiated rocketmissile exchanges following October 7, then Hezbollah Chief Hassan Nasrallah repeatedly rationalised a limited approach and the rest of the Axis remained hesitant to act until the Yemeni Houthi blockade in early 2024. Hence, immediately after the attack, Hamas returned to seeking sub-strategic concessions from Israel. Consequently, as the Qatari PM has stated on the record, Hamas was willing to release all hostages on the first day of the war. How did October 7 affect Israels security outlook? The October 7 attack dealt a huge dent to Benjamin Netanyahus image as Israels Mr Security. However, in retrospect its domestic political effects were more complicated. Israels security architecture was already working with a long-set outlook vis-a-vis Hamas that had been politically blessed by successive Israeli governments, including Netanyahus. However, Netanyahus domestic political crises and threats from the judiciary incentivised inaction before the attack despite warnings from both Egypt and UAE, while the attack itself necessitated aggressive action instead of accepting Hamas offer for hostage return. This latter posture was further supported by the hard-right lawmakers who propped up his government. Now, Netanyahus electoral gamble is that his post-October 7 aggressive regional approach has yielded successes that have been long necessary for Israeli security. This includes significant dents to Irans Axis Hezbollahs operational decimation in south Lebanon and northern Israels expanded security perimeter a longstanding Israeli priority Bashar al Assads fall in Damascus and a free rein for Israeli military operations in Syria, which has led to an expanded Israeli occupation of the Golan Heights a US war on Iran and Arab restraint in punitive actions against Israel. However, it is the continuity in regional conflict of which these successes are a part that has enabled his opponents to keep the focus on October 7s security failure. Nonetheless, the scale of regional shifts now means that beyond Netanyahu, there is a normalisation of an aggressive security posture. This is a security logic that combines past and future. Regardless of whether Netanyahu survives politically, this assertive outlook now arguably pervades Israels politico-security establishment at large, while Israel continues to resist international pressure against its continuing occupation and expansion of settlements in Palestinian territories.

articleTitle: ‘Peace and closure’: Mirabai Chanu on a medal that took four Asian Games cycles
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Mirabai
description: A coach's remark in a Manipur gym set the target. Chanu and Vijay Sharma needed years, a changed plan for the Commonwealth Games and a Paris miss to reach it
body_raw: When Mirabai Chanu first walked into a gym in Manipur to try weightlifting, a coach looked her up and down and made a casual remark that would stay with her for over a decade You could win a medal at the Asian Games. She surpassed that remark in nearly every way but the one it named. Chanu, who can lift three times her bodyweight, won medals at the World Championships, the Commonwealth Games and, in 2021, a historic silver at the Tokyo Olympics. That consistency, chiselled over years of work and protected through countless injuries, had one gap the Asian Games. Something always kept happening during or around the Asian Games. It reached a point where I would constantly wonder why this was happening, says Chanu. Her longtime coach Vijay Sharma, sitting next to her, chimes in I wont call it a psychological barrier. You can say that it happened by chance. We have discussed this many times. We realised if we attributed it to bad luck, we wouldnt be able to do anything about it. So they did something about it. It started with how they approached the Commonwealth Games. Training loads were kept with Chanus past injuries in mind, and the duo chose not to chase a Commonwealth Games record. A gold with minimal effort was the call. It left her fresh to push at the Asian Games, for the one medal that would complete her. Weightlifting asks for unflinching trust between coach and athlete. Even at these Asian Games, Chanu did not know what weights she was supposed to lift, or where she stood on the medal table. It was Vijays split-second permutations and combinations that ensured a silver arrived while keeping her limits in mind. Vijay was there in Sydney in 2000 when Karnam Malleswari won a bronze medal. Malleswaris gripe since has been that if her Russian coach had trusted her, a better medal could have been Indias. When youre in the arena, you need to make decisions in a fraction of a second. Whatever decisions we take are for the best of the players, says Vijay. He did not allow that breakdown of trust, which he saw with Indias first Olympic weightlifting medal, when he started training Chanu. That trust is essential. In life, whether with a life partner, in business, or in coaching, without trust, there is no bonding, and without bonding, there are no results. The trust that she has in me, even after she has won medals at the World and Olympic level, she still asks me what sets to pick up, says Vijay. I didnt even know that I didnt need a third lift in Japan, admitted Chanu. Sir told me that the silver medal was assured and that we wouldnt need to risk another lift. Once the medal was assured, Chanu could finally feel the weight lift off. It was a collective sense of wrong, felt by both her and Vijay, that was corrected in Nagoya. The fourth-place finish at the Paris Olympics had rankled deeply for both of them, more than two years on, until Nagoya came along. Winning this medal after so many years, across four Asian Games cycles, feels like a dream come true for both me and Vijay sir. It helps cover up the pain of missing out on the medal in Paris. Every time we looked at photos or videos from Paris, it reminded us of what we missed. This medal brings us peace and closure, said Chanu. Their next challenge is the LA Olympics, and a jump to the 53 kg category. Chanu admits that a higher weight class feels more comfortable. Now with the weight increase, itll give some relief from injuries, so we can focus even more on performance and everything else. Whenever I win a medal, I immediately look ahead to the next competition what I need to do, what changes to make. I learn from every medal and championship, and thats where I get my motivation, says Chanu.

articleTitle: Watch: Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka hauled away again after lie-in on Delhi road
articleFeaturedImageAlt: The Congress leaders were detained by cops in dramatic circumstances
description: The showdown erupted after Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge hosted lunch for INDIA bloc MPs at a restaurant on Janpath, less than 2 km from the Jantar Mantar protest site.
body_raw: Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra were dragged away by Delhi Police Wednesday evening as opposition leaders launched Day 2 of their protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The Congress leaders were detained by cops in dramatic circumstances - Rahul Gandhi was manhandled and bundled into a police bus, the second time in as many days. An angry-looking Priyanka Gandhi, who lay on the road with her arms crossed, was hustled away minutes later. She held on to a copy of the Constitution, her arm outstretched outside the moving vehicle. Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra were dragged away by Delhi Police-for a second time in as many days-after opposition MPs kick-started Day 2 of protests demanding CEC Gyanesh Kumar quit over irregularities in the SIR process. Read - The Indian Express IndianExpress October 7, 2026 The showdown erupted after a lunch meet organised by Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge for INDIA bloc MPs. The venue was the all-vegetarian Sagar Ratna restaurant on Janpath, less than 2 km from the Jantar Mantar protest site. Earlier, Rahul Gandhi was trolled online by a section of X users for allegedly having a non-vegetarian roll from Khan Chacha eatery during his eight-hour sit-in at the Akashvani Bhawan on Tuesday. After about one-and-a-half hours, the MPs streamed out of the eatery and went and sat in three buses parked on Janpath Road and headed towards Jantar Mantar. Interestingly, the Samajwadi Party skipped the lunch meeting. Sources in the Congress said that most of their MPs had left Delhi by this morning and couldnt attend the meeting and the subsequent protest. The issue was discussed during the lunch meeting where most other INDIA bloc parties were in attendance. When Rahul spoke to reporters, he said that 45 FIRs had been lodged against him, but he considered them to be medals and wanted a 100 FIRs. Today, we feel that we will protest at Jantar Mantar, which is a designated protest site, and tell the country that for us Gyanesh Kumar is not a legitimate Election Commissioner.As I said yesterday, around 300 Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha MPs wanted to meet Election Commissioners, but they did not meet us. They told us that we cannot protest here Jantar Mantar, Gandhi said. Lunch over, the MPs were being ferried in buses to Jantar Mantar when the cops closed them down at Windsor Place, which is roughly 900 metres from the popular protest site. Some Congress leaders, including Amarinder Singh Raja Warring, Imran Masood, Imran Pratapgarhi, Deepender Hooda and Srinivas B V climbed the roof of the bus in which Kharge, Rahul and Priyanka were travelling, and waved the tricolour, as the procession crawled from Janpath to Jantar Mantar, bringing the high security area to a halt for the second day. An impromptu sit-in took place at the roundabout in front of the Shangri-La hotel. The police soon moved to detain the protesters who countered the security officials. Rahul kept resisting police attempts to put him inside a van for detention. The INDIA bloc leaders jostled with security personnel who tried to detain them and clear the area. The entire Windsor Place roundabout was jammed with buses, cars and Congress youth outfit workers. While he was taken away to the Barakhamba police station, Rahul released a video message, continuing to engage through his social media platforms, besides his on-ground presence. We are not going to stop protesting till Gyanesh Kumar resigns.This is a fight to protect the most sacred thing in this country.There is nothing that Narendra Modi and Amit Shah can do that will stop us, he wrote in a post on his X handle along with a video message. We are not going to stop protesting till Gyanesh Kumar resigns. This is a fight to protect the most sacred thing in this country. There is nothing that Narendra Modi and Amit Shah can do that will stop us. - Rahul Gandhi RahulGandhi October 7, 2026 Later, the Congress said, The bus in which Rahul Gandhi ji was being taken was punctured by Congresss Babbar lions near Agrasen ki Baoli. The leaders were then taken to a police station in central Delhi. In a video attached to an X post, Rahul Gandhi said that Prime Minister Modi, Amit Shah, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat and Gyanesh Kumar can do all this, but we are going to bring them to justice. My guarantee that all four of them will be brought to justice. This is all a panic reaction. This is all fear. They are going to be brought to justice, mark my words, he said. The was the latest in a series of protests by political leaders and civil activists to press for Chief Election Commissioner Kumars resignation since a September 25 Indian Express report that suggested irregularities in the SIR process and differences among the election commissioners. articleTitle: ‘Special camps’ for voters cut after recent demolitions: Delhi poll body chief
articleFeaturedImageAlt: SIR survey in Delhi's Sangam Vihar. (Express Photo by Gajendra Yadav)
description: Delhi election officials will hold special camps to help eligible voters left out after recent demolitions enroll in the electoral rolls during SIR.
body_raw: The Delhi Election Commission on Wednesday said it would ensure that no eligible elector is left out of the electoral roll. The commission said special camps would be organised to facilitate the enrolment of all eligible electors who have been left out of the rolls. Every eligible elector is added and no ineligible entries remain in the electoral roll, the statement issued by the Election Commission of Delhi said. With the objective of maximising the enrolment of young electors, special camps were organised at various colleges and universities across Delhi from October 7 and will continue till October 8, 2026, the statement said. Booth Level Officers BLOs present at the camps will guide students in filling out the forms, collect the completed forms and address their queries related to the Special Intensive Revision SIR of electoral rolls. As per the instructions issued by the Election Commission of India on October 1, a special drive is being conducted to enrol all eligible electors left out of the electoral rolls. BLOs will conduct house-to-house visits to identify eligible persons and facilitate their enrolment through Form 6, wherever applicable. Special camps will also be organised on October 9 and 11, 2026, at all polling station locations across the National Capital Territory of Delhi to enrol eligible electors left out of the rolls. In Delhi, the Special Intensive Revision SIR data showed that 29.86 per cent of electors were marked as absent, shifted or under the others category, while 1.95 per cent were listed as deceased and 0.98 per cent were found enrolled at multiple places. articleTitle: From ITIs to AI: Why India needs to rethink skill development
articleFeaturedImageAlt: NITI Aayog, India, skilling, vocational education
description: NITI Aayog's report calls for reimagining India’s skilling architecture to address the gap between labour market needs and workforce skills. What does India’s skilling journey reveal about this mismatch, and how can the country strengthen its skilling system to keep pace with changing demands of job markets? See infographics for quick key insights.
body_raw: - Ritwika Patgiri Students from Class 9 onwards can choose Kaushal Tracks for specialised vocational training based on local and national job demand, proposed a NITI Aayogs report. The report also calls for universities to offer courses that focus on high-growth areas, such as green industries and electric vehicles, and help workers reskill for changing job markets. These recommendations made in Reimagining Skilling for Viksit Bharat2047 point to a challenge facing India a large section of young people are not making a direct transition from education to employment or skill development. It underscores the urgent need for a shift from generic degrees to applied, industry-aligned specialisations. But what does skilling mean in the context of a changing labour market? Is it simply about acquiring a set of skills or does it involve upskilling, reskilling and adaptation to new technologies and occupations? What does Indias skilling journey reveal about the gap between labour market needs and workforce skills? First, a brief overview of the NITI Aayogs report? Why NITI Aayog calls for reimagining skills The report says that more than 7.67 crore people have undergone skill-based training since 2014-15, adding that the Union Budget for 2025-26 allocated Rs 34,000 crore towards skilling-related expenditure across multiple central ministries. Despite this, outcomes remain uneven, says the report. Based on data from the 78th round of the National Sample Survey, the report maps workforce and learners into five segments, together representing approximately 60 crore citizens i schooling, ii tertiary education, iii formal and informal work, iv not in education, employment, and training NEET youth, and v women. The report underlines the significance of establishing stronger links between education, skills and actual employment, as only 8.25 per cent of graduates are employed in roles aligned with their qualifications. Skill training can happen through both institutions, like Industrial Training Institutes ITIs and on-the-job training. However, close to only 8 of the Indian firms provide on-the-job training, according to the NITI Aayogs report. The cost of providing on-the-job training for firms is often higher and they prefer trained individuals. This makes the role of skill institutions important. Therefore, the report proposed to incorporate vocational education and employability skills from schools to universities, with a stronger focus on applied, industry-aligned specialisations, along with greater use of apprenticeships and work-integrated degree and diploma programmes. The report also called for greater focus on sectors expected to generate demand, including green industries and electric vehicles, while providing reskilling for workers in declining occupations. Investing in human capital These recommendations hint at a broader shift towards viewing education and skill development as an investment in human capital. India has the largest youth population in the world, about 65 of its people under the age of 35, representing the potential of the demographic dividend. According to the human capital investment theory, economist Gary Becker argued that the various ways to invest in human capital include schooling and on-the-job training. He argued that earnings increase with age at a decreasing rate, and this increase is positively associated with the level of skills. Unemployment rates, in turn, are negatively associated with the level of skill. Similarly, Theodore Schultz argued that investment in education and training of young people yields returns over a longer period of time. In India, skill development has been perceived as a way to enhance employability and minimise the gap between labour market needs and workforce skills. For instance, according to data from Employment and Unemployment Surveys of National Sample Survey Office NSSO and the Periodic Labour Force Survey PLFS, formal training increased from 1.6 in 2011-12 to 4.1 in 2023-24, non-formal hereditary training from 1.8 to 11.6, non-formal self-learning from 1.8 to 11.6, and non-formal on-the-job training increased from 1.7 to 9.3. However, close to 65 of people aged 15-59 remain without any form of training.This points to a significant skill deficit in India and a gap between skill workers possess and those required by the labour market. A 2022 study by the National Skill Development Corporation NSDC estimated a significant deficit of 29 million between the demand and supply of skilled workers in India, particularly in sectors like IT, BFSI, healthcare, semiconductor manufacturing, and green jobs. This has been attributed to the failure of the countrys education sector as well as the performance of the numerous ITIs. Indias skilling push Skilling can be defined as a process through which individuals gain a particular skill or set of skills. However, the nature of skills required in the labour market keeps evolving with technological advancements and changing occupational demands. Upskilling refers to acquiring relevant advanced skills within a field or occupation to keep pace with changing technologies, roles, and responsibilities. Reskilling, on the other hand, involves learning new skills for different areas or roles. Economist Amit Basole notes that in India, the definition of skill is entangled with notions of dignified work. First, jobs that require mental skills are often considered more prestigious than those that prioritise manual skills. Second, the nature of caste hierarchies has influenced the allocation and social valuation of occupations and skills based on them. Finally, certain skill-based institutions are considered more prestigious than others, reflected, for instance, in the distinctions between IITs and ITIs. The 11th Five-Year Plan 2007-2012 marked a shift in policy focus on skill development. The National Skills Policy was introduced in 2009, followed by the launch of the National Skill Development Mission by the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship MSDE in 2015, which targeted training 400 million individuals by the end of 2022. During this time, vocational training institutes grew exponentially and a number of schemes were introduced, including the Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana, Deen Dayal Upadhyay Grameen Kaushalya Yojana, and the National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme. Despite this, the country spends only around 3 of its educational budget on vocational education. The number of ITIs, established in 1950 under the Craftsmen Training Scheme, increased from 9776 in 2014 to 13888 in 2026. The number of National Skill Training Institutes, Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Kendras, and Jan Shikshan Sansthans also increased. However, Basole notes that the character of the expansion changed because new ITIs were mostly private in nature, compared with the initial years till the 1980s when the government played a dominant role in their administration and expansion. More importantly, the expansion has not necessarily translated into comparable improvements in the quality and market-relevance of training. Why many ITIs seats are vacant It has also been found that students entering ITIs are more likely to have completed Class 10 and come largely from OBC, SC, and ST communities. Basole cautions against interpreting this pattern as a sign of inclusivity. Students from marginalised backgrounds face barriers in accessing educational opportunities and are more likely to drop out after Class 10 and 12. While relatively better-off students are more likely to pursue degree programmes or other forms of better or higher education, the caste-representation in ITIs is more likely a fallback option rather than an aspirational choice. The challenge is compounded by the large number of vacant seats in ITIs. According to NITI Aayogs 2023 Transforming Industrial Training Institutes report, in 2021, more than 50 seats in Andhra Pradesh and 58 in Assam stayed vacant, while only 47 of seats were occupied in Delhi. The reason for the large number of vacant seats has been attributed to a range of factors. The trade mix offered by ITIs remains heavily concentrated in manufacturing and technical occupations. For instance, the trade of electrician is offered by almost all ITIs, followed by the trade of fitter. Yet, around 65 of electrician seats and nearly 72 of fitter seats across ITIs are unoccupied, according to NITI Aayog. Notably, Indias growth story is largely driven by service, and ITIs have not been able to expand training relevant to service sectors, including financial services and information technology. Similarly, relevant trades such as AI, automation, and green technologies have not received much emphasis. As of 2022, only 0.09 of all the ITI students were placed, according to the NITI Aayog report. This represents a very dismal picture. Moreover, the gendered nature of trades offered by ITIs and a very distinct gendered pattern in the type of trades men and women apply for constitute other factors behind the vacant seats at ITIs. In addition, the shortage of instructors at ITIs is yet another constraint. What India can do to strengthen its skilling system So, what can be the way out for India to enhance its skill development? The evidence points towards several areas for reform. For instance, studies reveal that ITIs located near industrial belts are more likely to create employment. Trade mix and curricula need to evolve in keeping with the changing requirements of relevant industries and service-sector jobs, as well as emerging areas like AI and green skills. The gendered nature of ITIs also requires a transformation. This requires a more structural change where changing gendered roles and perceptions can lead to changes in gendered occupational trades. Other structural changes include greater spending on both general and vocational education. There has also been a rapid decline in the duration of skill development courses. As more people are completing their degrees and earning their certificates, these training programmes sometimes as short as 10 days have not resulted in acquiring gainful skills. Finally, international experiences can provide useful insights. For instance, Germany introduces an early vocational education model at the upper secondary level. Post read questions 1. What explains the persistent mismatch between the skills acquired by Indias workforce and those demanded by its labour market? Suggest measures to bridge this gap. 2. The expansion of Indias vocational training infrastructure has not necessarily translated into better employment outcomes. Discuss with reference to Industrial Training Institutes ITIs. 3. How can India move from a degree-centric education system towards an education model that integrates vocational training, apprenticeships and work-based learning? 4. How can India make its vocational education system more responsive to the growth of the services sector and emerging areas such as artificial intelligence, automation, electric vehicles and green technologies? 5. Gender and caste continue to shape participation and outcomes in Indias vocational education system. Discuss the structural factors responsible and suggest measures for making skill development more inclusive.
