articleTitle: From ‘quantum-enhanced’ to ‘quantum-safe’: Why banks are preparing in advance for the new big threat
articleFeaturedImageAlt: banking sector quantum computing, Indian banking sector, banking sector artificial intelligence, Indian banking sector cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, quantum computing, Indian express explained, explained news, current affairs
description: As AI dominates current cybersecurity concerns, a far greater threat looms over banking: quantum computing. We explain what the technology is and why financial institutions are preparing for it now.
body_raw: The banking sector is moving its focus towards cybersecurity as artificial intelligence AI poses threats to financial systems. But regulators have also stepped up, mandating cyber preparedness across the sector. The Reserve Bank of India RBI issued a new cybersecurity and technology-resilience framework for commercial banks in July, setting requirements for IT governance, cyber-risk management and incident response, while the Securities and Exchange Board of India SEBI introduced an IT Resilience Index for market infrastructure institutions in August to measure the robustness of their critical IT systems and identify weaknesses early. While these measures may help address the threats confronting the sector today, a new type of threat is beginning to emerge - one that could challenge the mathematical foundations of some of the encryption used to protect digital systems quantum computing. What is quantum computing? Traditional computing stores and processes data in a unit called a bit, which can have a value of either 0 or 1. In quantum computing, the unit is called a quantum bit, or qubit. Unlike a classical bit, a qubit can exist in a combination of 0 and 1, a property known as superposition. Quantum systems can also exploit another property called entanglement, in which the states of different qubits become closely correlated. Quantum algorithms are designed to manipulate these quantum states so that the probability of useful answers is amplified, and that of the incorrect answers is reduced. This can give quantum computers a significant edge over traditional computers for certain types of problems. Their significance comes from particular problems for which quantum algorithms can provide a major computational advantage. They have the potential to solve certain problems in minutes or hours that would take conventional machines millennia to complete. While this could have striking use cases, it also opens the door to a whole new set of threats. The cybersecurity concern stems from the fact that sufficiently powerful quantum computers could solve some mathematical problems that underpin widely used public-key cryptographic systems much more efficiently than classical computers can. Why does quantum computing threaten banks encryption? Right now, we are talking about AI threats, right? In a couple of years, we will be talking about cryptographic threats due to quantum computing. We will be talking about a lot of other things that are not even there in the market yet, Sarthak Dubey, Co-founder and COO of Mitigata, a full-stack cyber resilience firm, told The Indian Express. What people have been talking about quantum becomes a very major risk starting, say, 2030, he added. Modern cryptography protects digital communications by relying on mathematical problems that are extremely difficult for conventional computers to solve. Some widely used public-key systems, such as RSA RivestShamirAdleman and elliptic-curve cryptography, rely on problems related to integer factorisation and discrete logarithms. Indias financial ecosystem is heavily digitised through the Unified Payments Interface UPI, Aadhaar, real-time gross settlement RTGS, and national electronic funds transfer NEFT. The quantum threat is not that a quantum computer would hack a payment system. Rather, it could undermine cryptographic building blocks used across the digital infrastructure for functions like authentication, secure communication, key exchange, and digital signatures. However, cybersecurity and traditional computing in general are based on a particular set of mathematical logic. For example, RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring very large numbers, while elliptic-curve systems rely on the difficulty of solving certain discrete-logarithm problems. These problems are computationally difficult for classical machines, but could be much easier for a sufficiently capable quantum computer. Essentially, when we talk about the existing ways of security, there are encryption mechanisms that keep systems safe and secure in certain ways, that keeps your data secure in certain ways. And there are ways to decrypt them, which requires a significant amount of compute, and a significant amount of hardware power to make sure that you are able to decrypt those particular encryptions and get into that particular system, said Dubey. Now, with quantum, and what people call the quantum deadline, is that by 2029 or 2030 the quantum computers would be smart enough to decrypt any of the historical encryptions that are present, he explained. Several technology companies and governments have been working towards transitioning their systems well before such a capability emerges, although there is no universally agreed date for when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer will arrive. Why banks cannot wait for the quantum computer One reason why financial institutions cant just wait for quantum computers to become powerful enough is a threat called Harvest Now, Decrypt Later, or HNDL. Under this model, an attacker can intercept and store encrypted information today, with the expectation of decrypting it once sufficiently powerful quantum computers arrive. This makes data that needs to remain confidential for many years particularly vulnerable. According to the Digital Threat Report 2025-26 by CERT-In, CSIRT-Fin and SISA, the broader quantum threat has yet to reach full-scale realisation, but HNDL strategies are already active. This is why the transition to post-quantum cryptography PQC - encryption algorithms resistant to attacks from quantum computers - has to begin before the threat materialises. The more immediate task in preparing for the quantum era involves identifying where vulnerable cryptography is being used, and replacing it before sufficiently capable quantum systems emerge. This involves creating an inventory of cryptographic systems, identifying the most sensitive and critical data, testing quantum-resistant algorithms, working with technology vendors and ensuring that systems can switch between cryptographic standards without requiring a complete rebuild. This last capability, known as crypto-agility, is the ability of an organisation to replace cryptographic algorithms and protocols as security requirements change. For banks, this is crucial because their technology infrastructure is spread across legacy systems, cloud environments, third-party vendors, payment platforms and multiple layers of security infrastructure. How imminent is the threat? While the new threat sounds scary, it is at least a few years away. India has only a handful of quantum computers, though the technology is rapidly developing through startups, academics, and government initiatives such as the National Quantum Mission launched in 2023 with an outlay of Rs 6,003.65 crore. The mission aims to develop indigenous quantum-computing capabilities in stages, moving from 20-50 physical qubits in the initial phase towards systems with larger numbers of qubits over the longer term. Despite this, most projects are either under development or under small-scale testing. Were currently seeing only a handful of such systems being developed. This is led mainly by institutes like the IISc Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, or through startups like QpiAI. Most are under 10-qubit and are still under development, so it may take a few more years to undergo testing and be operational, said the executive from the Bengaluru-based startup cited earlier. Others remotely access such systems developed by bigger names such as IBM and Amazon Web Services for research and developmental purposes. Globally, too, quantum threats have not become widespread yet but remain an active concern, as suggested by Big Techs endeavours to bulk up security systems. They are researching on, and have started deploying post-quantum cryptography algorithms into their products, as well as stepping up protection against HNDL strategies. Governments and financial regulators are taking similar steps. In the US, the National Institute of Standards and Technology NIST has already finalised post-quantum cryptography standards and is urging organisations to begin the migration process. The G7 has also developed a roadmap for transitioning the financial sector towards post-quantum cryptography, while the European Union has called for member states to begin the transition by the end of 2026, with high-risk use cases moved to quantum-resistant cryptography as soon as possible and no later than the end of 2030. Indias quantum-safe roadmap India has begun building a policy framework around this transition as well. The Department of Science and Technologys quantum-safe roadmap sets out a phased approach for moving the countrys digital ecosystem towards post-quantum cryptography. For critical sectors such as banking, financial services and insurance, it envisages foundational work by 2027, migration of high-priority systems by 2028 and full adoption of post-quantum cryptography by 2029. The expert committee under RBIs Quantum Secure and Adaptive Financial Ecosystem Q-SAFE initiative released in May aims to examine the implications of quantum technology for the financial sector, and recommend a roadmap to quantum-secure it. NITI Aayogs roadmap for transforming India into a quantum-powered economy released in 2025 also identifies financial modelling, fraud detection and encryption among potential applications of quantum technology in finance. This creates a two-sided policy challenge for India the country has to protect its digital infrastructure from a technology that could eventually disrupt existing cryptography, while simultaneously building the domestic capabilities that could make quantum computing economically useful.

articleTitle: The hidden crisis in Indian classrooms: Why teachers are quitting before year five
articleFeaturedImageAlt: World Teachers' Day 2026
description: UNESCO lists attractive career pathways with equitable access to professional development as a key to keep teachers motivated. Does it mean that primary school teaching is not considered an attractive pathway?
body_raw: World Teachers Day is held annually on October 5, exactly a month after we celebrate our teachers and their work. UNESCO commemorates the anniversary of the adoption of the Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers in 1966, which set the benchmarks regarding the rights and responsibilities of teachers, and standards for their professional preparation and employment. In 2026, while we mark its 60th anniversary, UNESCO brings to our attention the new difficulties that have emerged for teachers from digital technologies, climate change, migration and displacement. These pressures adversely affect teachers work and status, which have always been insufficiently valued in all systems. Their lower status is marked by limited professional autonomy and voice in policymaking. UNESCOs Global Report on Teachers 2023 warned us that teachers are leaving the profession within the first five years of practice, especially at the primary level. The report classified teacher shortage as a pervasive phenomenon, which is a result of several factors including low motivation, sluggish recruitment practices, weak professional preparation, difficult working conditions, and low status. These, in turn, have consequences including increased workloads on the remaining teachers, compromised sense of well-being, and discouragement of prospective teachers. The UNESCO report mentions a shortage of 7.8 million teachers in South Asia, including India. Let us pay attention to two factors, namely teacher motivation and preparation, to understand why teachers are leaving, especially at the primary level. UNESCO lists attractive career pathways with equitable access to professional development as a key to keep teachers motivated. Does it mean that primary school teaching is not considered an attractive pathway? Well, it is not even a pathway because it is one of the most stagnant recruitments in our system. The experience of teaching at the primary level is not counted in the eligibility to become a school principal. Secondary teachers who get appointed as principals make further progress by playing a role in policymaking as they eventually join the bureaucracy. More than 70 years after Independence, we realise that in educational policymaking, school-based decision-making and administration, the wisdom of primary teachers has remained absent. The wisdom and knowledge that they must be gaining by teaching and managing the beginners - which include millions of first-generation learners - simply get lost. The loss is two-fold, as the system loses out on a resource and has to pull on with a large number of teachers whose enthusiasm and aspirations dissipate. Let us turn to the factor of teacher preparation, an Achilles heel for the Indian system. It is a connecting point between school and university systems but a weak one. Indian universities have shown persistent reluctance in playing a catalyst role in teacher preparation, especially for the primary level. A small-scale but major breakthrough was made in the 1990s when Delhi University DU institutionalised its first-ever four-year integrated professional degree programme of elementary teacher education, namely, Bachelor of Elementary Education B.El.Ed.. It marked DUs attempt to locate teacher preparation for elementary level, earlier a constitutional dream, later a commitment, within the ambit of a central university. B.El.Ed. graduates emerged as elementary teachers who drew their identity from being the teachers of children rather than transmitters of a school subject. B.El.Ed. thus became a landmark as its graduates developed professional commitment and resilience to remain in the system and improve it, highlighted by the UNESCO report as an important means to address teacher shortage. This small achievement brought to the fore a dilemma that teacher preparation encapsulates in India. Should we train teachers or educate them? In educational discourse, training has been associated with tricks of the trade that the trainees acquire by practising certain actions such as modulation of voice while explaining something. Training emphasises trainee-teachers dependence on being trained by others in skills and practices, but remains weak on the important principle of autonomous pursuit of knowledge. The emphasis in teaching is upon a relationship between the teacher and their students in a carefully developed learning ethos. Teaching demands from the teacher a persistent interest in the learning process of their students, which involves command over knowledge and recognition of the specificities that the students bring with them. The specificities emerge from disparities involving caste, poverty, gender, language, tribal affiliations, and so on. Teaching emphasises the focus on interaction between the minds of a teacher and their students. Approaching teacher preparation as training has its origins in the colonial system of education centred on the limited purpose of the transmission of textbook content. The roots of training orientation have proved strong, as one notices its presence even in the reports of progressive commissions. The term teacher education gained mild popularity as it was used in the recent policy documents, but the system retained the training orientation as the basic features of the programs of teacher preparation remained intact. The recent changes in teacher preparation, made under the framework of NEP 2020, reinforce the colonial format of training. The policy aims at extreme homogenisation by replacing all the teacher education programmes with the Integrated Teacher Education Programme ITEP, which is a new name for yesteryears BA As the university system in India moved to a four-year UG degree programme, the teacher education programmes received a casual and unspecialised treatment. The general higher education prescriptions are being applied to them. Thus, ITEP is wobbling between the tedious and meandering calculations of credits and dual degree arrangements, giving structural priority to content rather than specificities of the learners and teachers autonomy. With inadequate preparation and the pressure of new challenges, the teachers find it difficult to meet the demands that teaching a group of young minds poses. They quit early or remain demotivated. No wonder that the UNESCO report does not include India in the list of hopeful countries that could address the teacher shortage by 2030. Honouring a few teachers is not enough. We need to modernise their preparation and take policy-level steps to address the lower status of primary teachers. The writer teaches education at Delhi University

articleTitle: 2026 Chemistry Nobel: Mirror-image molecules and the chemistry of life
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2026, Nobel Chemistry Prize 2026, Chemistry Nobel 2026, Nobel Prize Chemistry winners 2026, Nobel Chemistry winners, Chemistry Nobel winners, Nobel Prize in Chemistry explained, Nobel Chemistry history, first Nobel Prize in Chemistry, Nobel Prize Chemistry discoveries, Nobel Prize Chemistry predictions, Nobel Chemistry from India, Chemistry Nobel Prize winners, Nobel Prize winners 2026, Nobel Prize Chemistry facts, indian express, express explained
description: Certain molecules exist in two forms — like your left and right hands. But the building blocks of life use only one. The scientists Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai showed how to make just that form in labs — something crucial for the manufacturing of medicines.
body_raw: Certain molecules exist in two forms, each a non-superimposable mirror image of the other - like the left and right hands of human beings. Chemically, the two forms are the same in the sense that they are composed of the same set of atoms, connected in the same order. The difference is only in the relative three-dimensional arrangement of those atoms, such that one happens to be the mirror image of the other. This structural asymmetry, called chirality, becomes particularly interesting in biology. Many of the fundamental molecules in biology, like the amino acids that make up proteins or the sugars in DNA, appear in only one form. The mirror image versions of these amino acids or the sugars do exist, but they are rarely used in these biological settings. This preference for homochirality in life forms has intrigued scientists for long. This years Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to two scientists, Henry Kagan and Kenso Soai, for demonstrating how this homochirality can emerge. The normal chemical processes used to produce a chiral molecule results in the production of both forms, called enantiomers. Kagan developed a way of manipulating these processes in such a manner that one form was produced in much greater proportion than the other. Soai took a step further and designed the first chemical reaction in which only one of the enantiomers was produced. Outside of biological processes, such a result had never been achieved. The first breakthrough The propensity of biochemistry to prefer one particular enantiomer over the other was initially thought to be something unique for life forms. After all, when chiral molecules were produced in laboratories, a mixture of both enantiomers was obtained in almost even proportions. However, way back in the early 1900s, German chemist Willy Marckwald had been successful in carrying out a chemical reaction in which the proportion of the yields of the two enantiomers was slightly asymmetric. Marckwald had used a catalyst - a chemical that speeds up the reaction without itself getting consumed into it - which itself was chiral. And this had led to one mirror-image form being produced more than the other. However, subsequent attempts to increase the asymmetry in the yields of the two enantiomers remained unsuccessful. Besides, scientists still did not understand how the use of a chiral catalyst was affecting the reaction in a manner that one enantiomer was produced in greater quantity. It was Kagan, working in the 1980s, who eventually answered these questions. Before him, it was believed that there was a linear relationship between the catalysts chirality and the proportion in which the two forms of the product were produced. In other words, if the catalyst itself contained a disproportionate amount of one form, this would get reflected in the proportions of the final product as well. Kagan was able to show that this was not true, and that much greater asymmetry in production could be achieved even if the catalyst was only mildly chiral. In the process he was also able to demonstrate the internal dynamics of how this was happening. The next step This breakthrough created a new excitement in the field. While studying one of the chemical reactions that had produced one particular enantiomer in large quantities, Soai realised that there were significant similarities in the catalyst used and the final product. That prompted him to explore autocatalytic reactions - chemical reactions in which the final products themselves act as catalysts. None of the autocatalytic reactions known at the time Soai started experimenting with them in the 1990s were known to produce asymmetric formation of enantiomers. After about a decade of trying, he finally succeeded in carrying out an autocatalytic reaction that resulted in the production of one particular enantiomer, which then formed copies of itself in a self-replicating process. The final product contained 99.5 of one enantiomer, a result comparable to the kind of preference seen in biological processes for a particular version of a chiral molecule. Mysteries of life The work of Kagan and Soai has demonstrated that homochirality can be obtained in the laboratory as well. It was not exclusive to nature. Their work does not solve the origin of the puzzle of life - how biological processes themselves preferred homochirality. But it did open up fresh avenues for scientists to try and understand the chemistry of life. Possibly the biggest practical implication of their work has been in the pharmaceutical industry. Many drug molecules are chiral, and it matters immensely which particular enantiomer has to be used. This is because the human bodies prefer only those enantiomers. The other variety of molecule might not just be ineffective, they can even be harmful. Before this Nobel Prize-winning work showed how one single enantiomer could be produced, pharma companies had been manufacturing the drug molecules as a mixture of both enantiomers, and then the desirable enantiomer was separated through a separate process. This was an expensive, wasteful and often technically difficult way of achieving the final result. The asymmetric synthesis of a particular enantiomer, as shown by Kagan and Soai, is already being used widely by the pharmaceutical industry. This is relevant for the manufacturing of all other substances that are meant to interact with living organisms, including flavours, fragrances and agricultural chemicals like pesticides.

articleTitle: ‘We don’t distinguish between nations’: Coast Guard chief on rescue operations
articleFeaturedImageAlt: ‘We don’t distinguish between nations’: Coast Guard chief on India’s sea rescue mission
description: Speaking to the reporters ahead of the 12th edition of the national level Search and Rescue Exercise (SAREX-2026) to be conducted off Paradip coast on Thursday, he said several nations look up to India in the event of a crisis.
body_raw: Director General of the Indian Coast Guard ICG Paramesh Sivamani on Wednesday underscored the forces commitment to saving lives at sea, saying it does not distinguish between nations while carrying out an effective search and rescue SAR operation. Speaking to the reporters ahead of the 12th edition of the national level Search and Rescue Exercise SAREX-2026 to be conducted off Paradip coast on Thursday, he said several nations look up to India in the event of a crisis. We have enhanced our capacity, redefined the procedure and fine-tuned the standard operating procedure over the years. We have established a very robust system of SAR and all the nations in the Indian Ocean Region look up to Bharat in case there is a crisis or in a volatile situation that requires a SAR, said the ICG chief. Stating that they have built up the SAR capabilities from scratch, Sivamani said they have ensured that the ICGs prowess of executing a good SAR operation is there for a larger good of humanity. Whenever there is a crisis and our ships and aircrafts are required to the spot. we do that immediately, he said. During the inaugural event of SAREX, the ICG chief also emphasised that the future of maritime SAR hinges on advanced technological integration, real-time information sharing, and seamless inter-agency synergy. Sivamani stressed the imperative for enhanced vessel tracking, robust distress-alert management, data-driven operational decision-making, and accelerated asset mobilisation. He also underscored that operational lessons derived from past missions and multi-agency exercises must directly translate into heightened mission readiness and response capabilities. The SAREX-2026 exercise will witness participation and observation by 32 delegates from 30 foreign friendly nations. The multi-agency exercise aims to validate operational preparedness, enhance international interoperability, test joint response mechanisms, and foster the exchange of best practices-reaffirming the preservation of life at sea as the paramount objective of every mission. The 24th National Maritime Search and Rescue Board meeting was also held on the occasion and it deliberated on strengthening national and international SAR frameworks, recognising that maritime emergencies transcend geographic boundaries and necessitate synchronised coordination among global Rescue Coordination Centres and maritime safety agencies. Minister of State for Defence Sanjay Seth, who inaugurated the event, called upon all participating agencies and international partners to reaffirm their shared commitment to safeguarding lives at sea and to strengthen the spirit of cooperation that underpins effective search and rescue across the region. Invoking the principle of One Earth, One Family, One Future, he said collective efforts can build a safer, more resilient and more cooperative maritime community. Speaking on Indias efforts to strengthen its search and rescue capabilities, Seth said Indias journey in Satellite-Aided Search and Rescue has progressively evolved from Low Earth Orbit Search and Rescue LEOSAR to Geostationary Search and Rescue GEOSAR and now towards Medium Earth Orbit Search and Rescue MEOSAR.

articleTitle: Inside Visakhapatnam spying case: Pakistani women operatives lured, blackmailed naval personnel, probe finds
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Inside Visakhapatnam spying case: Pakistani women operatives lured, blackmailed naval personnel, probe finds
description: 2 arrested, 16 under scanner as investigators piece together how Pak-based operatives used social media and WhatsApp to orchestrate honey-trap.
body_raw: Investigators probing allegations of spying in Visakhapatnam claim to have pieced together how intelligence operatives from Pakistan trapped and then blackmailed civilians and navy personnel to gather information about the movement of vessels and submarines. According to investigators, around six months ago, a woman operative allegedly posed as a shipping firm employee and struck up a conversation with Annam Sai Varaprasad, 28, a civilian hired on a contract basis to drive naval officers vehicles at the Visakhapatnam naval base. The woman messaged him on his social media accounts, investigators said, adding that though he was initially suspicious, he allegedly continued the conversation. She told him she was from a neighbouring state. At first, the conversation focused on his personal life where he lived and why he was not married. Then, investigators said, she asked about his work, his salary, and the kind of vehicles he drove. Eventually, the woman allegedly shared sexually explicit content with Varaprasad and promised to visit Visakhapatnam soon to meet him. As the conversation progressed, she allegedly managed to extract information about the officials he drove. From then on, he was threatened that he would be reported to his employers and arrested. Investigators said what followed was blackmail to provide information about the locations of various naval assets, the deployment of officials, etc. The platform for their communication shifted from social media to WhatsApp. However, Varaprasad had basic security clearance and lacked access to observe and report on classified assets, naval ships docking, and submarines arriving or leaving, investigators said. The Andhra Pradesh Polices Counter Intelligence Cell and naval officials monitored him for over a month before his arrest on October 6. Officials are also examining his phone to check if he received payments through cryptocurrency, investigators said. According to investigators, Varaprasad allegedly shared details of a trainee sailor, Pradeep Mukharjee, 31, whom he previously met at the Visakhapatnam base. He too was allegedly trapped by a Pakistan-based intelligence operative, who posed as a medical professional. Threatened with arrest and legal complications after they allegedly exchanged sexually explicit messages, he too shared information about the Vizag and Coimbatore facilities, where he was attending a training course, investigators said. He was allegedly forced to share OTPs to activate WhatsApp accounts of Pakistani operatives, and was threatened with dire consequences on a voice call if he stopped cooperating, investigators said. These WhatsApp numbers were then used to lure and trap at least 16 others, using a similar modus operandi. They targeted employees posted in Kerala, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Gujarat, Goa, Delhi, Tamil Nadu, Chhattisgarh and Bihar, investigators said, and information sought included movement of naval ships and submarines arriving and leaving. Andhra Pradesh Counter-Intelligence Cell officials said that after it was established that Varaprasad and Mukherjea allegedly shared information and helped operatives trap others, they registered a case against them on September 2 and put them under surveillance. On October 1, simultaneous raids at the homes and residences of 18 persons, including 13 naval personnel, were conducted in an operation named Operation Firewall 2026, and 12 teams supported by officials of the anti-terrorist squads of several states, navy intelligence officers, and local police seized phones, electronic devices, and documents. Authorities are investigating the 16 people to determine their level of involvement and have arrested Varaprasad from Visakhapatnam and Mukherjea from Coimbatore.

articleTitle: Kerala’s IUML picks Hindu leader as state vice-president. Why it matters
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Kerala’s IUML picks Hindu leader as state vice-president. Why it matters
description: The elevation of C Syam Sundar, a former DYFI state leader who has been with the IUML since 2010, comes as the party navigates allegations of communal polarisation from the Left and pressure from Muslim clerics over its positions.
body_raw: At a time when it faces Opposition allegations of communal polarisation and a push towards conservatism from within the Muslim community, Keralas United Democratic Alliance ally has made an unprecedented move - elevating a Hindu leader to one of its top positions. On Wednesday, the IUML announced that 61-year-old C. Syam Sundar was its new state vice-president as part of its organisational reshuffle. A former state leader of the Democratic Youth Federation of India, the youth wing of the Communist Party of India, Syam Sundar, a prominent Nair leader from central Keralam, has been with the IUML since 2010. The decision comes after the IUML divested all ministers and legislators of various organisational roles. Speaking to the media after his elevation, Syam Sundar said he was happy with the new responsibility. Im the first non-Muslim to become the state vice president of the IUML. I have been with the party since 2010 and started my journey with the IUML as a local party worker. Over the last 15 years, the party has given me various roles, which I have discharged with utmost sincerity, he said. For the party, picking Syam Sundar for one of its top positions assumes significance, especially given the timing. The party finds itself in a difficult position - while the CPI M accuses it of communal polarisation, the IUML is also having to defend conservative positions amid growing pressure from Muslim clerics. Who is C Syam Sundar Syam Sundar belongs to a prominent upper-caste Hindu Nair political family from Alappuzha - the states first Assembly Speaker, R Sankara Narayanan Thambi, was his uncle. At the IUML, Syam Sundar has been given charge of the Idukki and Pathanamthitta districts, where the party does not have a significant presence. Although this is the first time a Hindu leader has taken a prominent position in the IUML, the party has had non-Muslim leaders and electoral candidates in the past. Last year, the outfit inducted Jayanthi Rajan, a Dalit woman, as a national assistant secretary, with the party even fielding her from the CPIM stronghold of Koothuparamba in this Assembly election. Although Jayanthi lost the election, she had managed to put up a formidable fight against the Left. The IUML also backed a young Christian leader from the Congress, V S Joy, in the election in Thavanoor in Muslim-majority Malappuram. The support helped Joy beat the CPIM-backed independent and four-term MLA K T Jaleel in a seat where the Christian vote bank accounted for only 1.4 per cent of the total electorate. For the election, IUML put its organisational machinery behind Joy, a non-Catholic Christian who had earlier struggled to find acceptance in Catholic-dominated constituencies when the Congress decided to field him there.

articleTitle: Two of three MPSC protests continue, one withdrawn after Bombay High Court hearing
articleFeaturedImageAlt: MPSC protests continue, MPSC paper leak, MPSC protests, MPSC protests intensify, MPSC chairman Vivek Bhimanwar, Pune news, Pune, Maharashtra news, Indian express, current affairs
description: At SM Joshi bridge, six protesters have been on hunger strike for the past four days—Shivraj More and Priyanka Chaudhari of the Youth Congress, Nitin Gite, Omkar Patil, Rushikesh Gangurde, Gajanan Shelke and Somnath Chavan.
body_raw: Two of the three protests ongoing in Pune demanding reforms in the Maharashtra Public Service Commission MPSC are ongoing while one protest has been withdrawn after the Bombay High Court on Monday suggested that students should go home and study as the court was seized of the matter. The larger protest ongoing at SM Joshi bridge, completing seven days, is being forefronted by Nationalist Congress Party-Sharadchandra Pawar NCPSP MLA Rohit Pawar. This group has been demanding the resignation of MPSC Chairman Vivek Bhimanwar. The other protest is ongoing at Lal Bahadur Shastri Road, while the protest at Alka Talkies has been called off by the third group. At SM Joshi bridge, six protesters have been on hunger strike for the past four days-Shivraj More and Priyanka Chaudhari of the Youth Congress, Nitin Gite, Omkar Patil, Rushikesh Gangurde, Gajanan Shelke and Somnath Chavan. The court was hearing a Public Interest Litigation filed by two residents of Pune citing inconvenience to Punes public due to the protest. Pawar said that the petitioners in court were connected to a BJP corporator. In its order the Court found substance in the argument by agitators that accountability has to be fixed in the paper leak case and the matter requires consideration. Maybe the police had self-confidence as the case was in the High Court that the hearing would begin at 11 and at 1115 the decision would be in their favour. That is why there was a huge police force here in the morning, Rohit Pawar said after the hearing. The HC bench of Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait M Sethna remarked orally that the protesters should continue with police permission and relocate if need be. Referring to the court order, Pawar said, Now in Pune city there is no dedicated protest place. The police check whether there are any homes, buildings, schools, hospitals, and if not then there is no problem giving permission. We have chosen this spot because there is nothing other than trees here, it is in between two crematoriums, Pawar said. Meanwhile Pawar also said one of the protesters on hunger strike, Rushikesh Gangates sugar had dropped to a dangerous level, and that no government doctors had visited the site throughout the day. Pawar added that discussions had taken place between him and the state government on Wednesday, and that the government might send some ministers for discussions with the protesters in Pune. We will not go to Mumbai, he said. Congress MP Praniti Shinde, Samajwadi Party MLA Rais Shaikh, Sujat Ambedkar of the Vanchit Bahujan Aghadi, and satire singer Neha Singh Rathore were some others who joined the protest on Wednesday night and spoke to the students.

articleTitle: KPSC chairman Sahukar, member Geetha took bribes to leak answer keys
articleFeaturedImageAlt: Karnataka Public Service Commission job racket, KPSC recruitment scam, Shivashankarappa Sahukar, Karnataka KPSC scam, KPSC chairman daughter recruitment, Suma Sahukar income certificate case, KPSC veterinary doctor paper leak .Karnataka veterinary recruitment scam. Shivashankarappa Sahukar CID probe, KPSC question paper leak, Karnataka High Court KPSC case, KPSC corruption allegations, Basavaraj Kannale KPSC scam, Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar arrest, 400 veterinary doctors recruitment scam, Karnataka government job scam, Express investigation, KPSC recruitment controversy
description: Sahukar reportedly leaked the keys to an aspirant for a Rs 10 lakh advance, who subsequently secured the third rank, while Geetha allegedly provided them to the first-rank winner for a Rs 20 lakh advance.
body_raw: An Enforcement Directorate ED probe has revealed that the now-suspended Karnataka Public Service Commission KPSC chairman Shivashankarappa Sahukar and KPSC member B V Geetha allegedly leaked answer keys for the January 6 veterinary doctors recruitment exam in exchange for bribes. Sahukar reportedly leaked the keys to an aspirant for a Rs 10 lakh advance, who subsequently secured the third rank, while Geetha allegedly provided them to the first-rank winner for a Rs 20 lakh advance. They were arrested by the ED on Tuesday following a probe into allegations of money laundering by KPSC officials through job frauds in the Commission with a specific reference to the fraud in the recruitment of veterinary doctors for Karnataka. The EDs findings with respect to Sahukar and Geetha were presented in court on Wednesday, where the agency submitted that the two had obtained the answer keys for 80 questions prepared for the entrance exam from the now-arrested KPSC Controller of Exams and IAS officer, Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar, and supplied it to as many as six candidates. Incidentally, Gangwar and a middleman Basavaraj Kannale were earlier arrested for allegedly leaking up to 80 questions to as many as 11 aspirants for bribes ranging from Rs 20 lakh to Rs 40 lakh. In the case of the previous arrests, it was the questions that were leaked. Here, in this case, it is the answer keys, the ED counsel Madhu N Rao told the court. This is a different modus operandi from the first cases, he added. The ED probe has found that four other candidates - the eight, ninth, 11th and 12th rank winners - were also given access to answer keys by Sahukar and Geetha. The probe found that Geetha gave the names of six aspirants to Exam Controller Gangwar and he, in turn, looked at the seating arrangement for them in the exam hall and then provided the answer keys for the specific set of question papers they would receive on the exam day, the ED counsel said. Only 80 answers For 100 questions were given, and the candidates were asked to memorise them. This is why these candidates have all got the same answers wrong in the exam, the counsel added. The ED has shown prima facie that the two accused were misusing their positions for leakage of answer keys to the two candidates for consideration of illegal gratification of Rs 20 lakh and Rs 10 lakh respectively, the special court said while remanding Sahukar and Geetha to EDs custody till October 19. The ED probe also prima facie discloses that Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar, VH the third rank candidate, her father, NB the first rank candidate and his father, and Shivashankarappa Sahukar and B V Geetha were connected with monetary transactions. the court observed. The ED has taken the two accused into custody until October 19 to probe transactions with other selected candidates and to find the money trail from the bribes.

articleTitle: Pregnant woman, 2 children among 3 killed as building collapses in Delhi
